Likewise some animals, as said, remain in water and cannot live outside it, like water tortoises, the crocodile, the hippopotamus, and the kind of frogs. Some, however, remain in water and give birth or breed on land, and some remain on land and are nourished by water. The dolphin and the whale and all having windpipes by which they breathe remain in water. They are intermediate between land creatures and sea creatures, and share in both, since they take in water through the windpipe and air through the lung. These animals take in water for the sake of food and along with food, and have an instrument, namely gills, in place of breathing, by which they expel water, taking in moisture with food, and have windpipes. Soft-bodied creatures and soft-shelled ones take in the moisture of food and are marine according to another manner, namely because of the constitution of their body and their life. Stone-bearing fish remain paired, male with female. Some fish, too, remain in caverns.

Pliny, on fish, in the same place: Theophrastus reports that near the irrigated lands of Babylon, where rivers descend into caverns having water, certain fish remain. From there they go out to feed, walking on their fins with a frequent motion of the tail, and, when hunted, flee back into their caverns and stand there turned to face outward. Their heads are said to be like those of the sea-frog, the rest of their body like gudgeons, their gills like those of other fish. He reports too that in the Black Sea there is one kind that follows the farthest waters of rivers and makes caverns for itself in the earth and lives in these even when the rivers recede and the shore dries up. They prove, then, that these live by being dug out, by the motion of their bodies. In Paphlagonia, too, fish most pleasing for food, land-dwelling, are dug out of deep pits, in those places where no standing waters remain.

div.head: DE CONVERSATIONE PISCIUM PER AQUE LOCA DIVERSA

cit.quote: Aristotle: of aquatic animals, some remain in sea water, some are riverine, some belong to standing pools, and some, like frogs, to marshes; of sea creatures, some are pelagic, some coastal, some rock-dwelling. Some sea creatures, too, are near the shores in winter, but in the deep sea in summer, since they seek now warmth, now cold. Whence some in winter go from the depth of the sea near land, seeking warmth, and some, fleeing the places near land, enter the depth of the sea, fleeing heat. Again, near land, the depth is better, since good pasture is there. For because of the rising of the sun, soft plants grow there. Places near land, too, are more temperate. And so the flesh of fish dwelling there is more flavorful. Many fish, however, hide in caverns and are not caught at all, except at determined times. Some, as said, hide in the depth of the sea in winter, and after their hiding grow very fat, and some prepare a cavern for themselves in sand, some in mud, and put out nothing but their mouth. They do not hide, however, for the most part, except in winter. Fish of soft shell, then, and those that remain among stones, hide in caverns during days of severe cold. Some, however, remain in caverns in summer, like the 'glaucus,' for about sixty days, and are caught after the rising of the Dog Star. Particular places, then, suit fish, since some grow fat near land and some in the depth of the sea, and some in both. The diversity of regions, moreover, diversifies fish, not only in abundance of food, but in the frequency of mating and conception and in giving birth, as with plants and trees and animals. And so many fish frequently lay eggs in certain places and not in others.

Pliny: the 'hippurus' and the black bream. Not caught in winter, except for a few days of summer and always the same days. Likewise the moray and the sea-perch, the conger, the perch, and all the rock fish are said to hide themselves in earth, that is in a hollowed-out shallow of the sea, through the winters; the electric ray and the sole are said to do the same, pounded [into the sand]. Some, again, from impatience of the heat, hide in the middle of summer's heat for sixty days, like the 'glaucus,' the hake, and the gilt-head. Among river fish, the catfish is affected by the rising of the Dog Star, and put to sleep at other times by lightning. They think this also happens in the Cyprian Sea, and otherwise the whole sea senses the rising of that star, which appears most in the Bosphorus. For seaweed and fish are carried to the surface, everything turned from the bottom up. Many fish, indeed, spend the summer in the Propontis and do not enter the Black Sea; only turbot enter. Likewise soles enter with turbot, nor is cuttlefish found where squid is found. Among rock fish, the wrasse and the blackbird-fish are lacking, just as shellfish are, when oysters abound. All, however, hibernate in the Aegean Sea; of those entering the Black Sea, only the mackerel do not return. But these alone go up the river Danube and from it, by its underground channels, flow down into the Adriatic Sea. And so they are seen there, descending, but never seen coming up from the sea.

Isidore, on fish: this indeed is not thought to happen without a certain gift of nature, that each kind has territories prescribed for itself, which no member of its own kind exceeds and no stranger invades. This kind of fish is nourished and born in that bay of the sea, that one in another. Finally you will not find the kinds of fish confused, but what abounds here is lacking elsewhere. Nor, however, is their abundance shut in by mountains, or their passage hindered by intervening rivers. Rather, a habit is impressed by nature, so that each one keeps itself, as it were, within the bounds of its own country, and regards going beyond its own inhabitants as suspect. There are, however, some kinds of fish that do not change places for ease of disposition, but from the necessity of tending their young. For they go in summer to the strait of the Black Sea, since this bay becomes sweeter than the rest of the sea's bay. For the sun does not linger as long over this strait as over the rest, and for this reason it does not exhaust all the water that is sweet and drinkable. This, then, is the reason the Black Sea is more pleasing to them, where they can both breed and give birth, since the tender young could scarcely bear the hardship of a foreign region, whereas the great mildness of the air fosters them there. And so, once their task is accomplished, all together return in the same company by which they came. Who announced these places to the fish, or who granted them their perceived times or the arrangement of their journey? Surely he who pours the rule of his authority into the senses of all things, who grants to dumb creatures the order of natural discipline.

div.head: DE VARIATIONE PISCIUM SECUNDUM ANNI TEMPORA

cit.quote: Pliny, in the same place: certain fish change their white color in winter and become blacker in summer. The 'phycis,' too, changes - white the rest of the time, varied in spring. And this fish alone builds its nest from seaweed and lays its eggs in the nest. All feel the very cold of winter, but especially those thought to have a stone in their head, like the bass, the sea-perch, and the sea-bream. And when winters are harsh, many blind ones are caught; some lie hidden in caves in winter, especially the 'hippurus' and the black bream. They are said not to be caught in winter; the electric ray and the sole are said to hide themselves through the winters in a hollowed-out shallow of the sea. Some, however, from impatience of the heat, hide in the middle of summer's heat, like the 'glaucus' and the hake. At the rising of the Dog Star, fish are carried to the surface, and so on, as above.

Aristotle: the fish called 'garus' is very soft, but wind and cold harden it, as they do a tree, yet it also decays in very hot places. Certain sea creatures are near the shores in winter and spring, but in the deep sea in summer, since they seek now warmth, now cold. A certain kind from which the crayfish is generated, before it lays eggs, is of good flesh, and of poor flesh afterward. This kind too, in the manner of a serpent, sheds its skin in spring. Certain animals live in water, then change into another form and live outside. Dry seasons, as said, harm fish, but rainy ones benefit and fatten them. Fish having a stone in the head are harmed by winter, since the stone is chilled in the head and coagulates. Fish, when ice occurs, die, and for this reason are caught in rivers and lakes. In summer, too, especially the long fish are caught, since they grow fat from the north wind. The fish called 'rodez' swims by day and rests by night, unless the night is moonlit, for then it swims and does not rest.

Aristotle: certain aquatic creatures swim head-first, like the crayfish, some by the tail, and some are creatures that walk, like the kind of crabs, whose nature is aquatic. Some, too, swim in company, some alone. All sea fish that have feet swim with them and with fins, like the whole kind of soft-bodied creatures, that is of soft flesh, which kind indeed moves quickly in swimming: the crayfish, among hard-fleshed fish, moves with its tail in a swift motion, just as by the motion of its fins. The crocodile, however, moves with its tail and foot. There is also a fish of the oyster kind, that is of hard shell, which swims and crawls with its tail. A certain sea creature has a small right foot and a large left one. And so, when it walks, it carries its whole body on the left. Fish fins are suited to swimming, since they are in the manner of oars. Some fish of long body, however, have no fins and swim only by the bending of the body. It moves, indeed, in water as serpents crawl on land. Certain aquatic creatures, however, are attached to rock and are not separated from it, unless compelled by something, through attraction, to motion; some, however, are attached to rock, but when they seek their nourishment they are free. Many, too, are free and do not move from their places. There is a certain creature attached by a strong shell attachment, and when the air is clear, this animal will be free and will walk about. But when the winds stir, it will attach itself to rocks and rest, and will not move. A certain fish, however, that does not move, like the 'escheleti,' has something similar to roots growing in the earth. Some, too, arise without roots, and if moved from their places, die. A certain fish goes up from the sea into rivers and marshes, like the 'castonoz.' Others, however, do the opposite, like the 'haloz.' The 'rodez,' as said, swims by day and rests by night, unless the night is moonlit. Fish, like birds, move their jaw only up and down, since that motion is suited to biting and cutting. But sideways motion is suited to the kind of fish. There is a fish that feeds on mud and, for this reason, being heavy, often swims, so as to wash the mud from its flesh. Sea creatures of hard shell walk and feed and draw their heads out from the shell, and when afraid, put it back. Shoals of fish have a leader and move to the place where food and pasture are good, because of the sweetness of the water.

Ambrose: certain kinds of fish change places from the necessity of tending their young. At the fitting time, from different places, they come together to very many bays of the sea, as if by common counsel, in a joined company. They catch the blast of the north wind, make for the northern sea, and enter the strait of the Propontis with violent force, and cross many seas, seeking some benefit for their own kind. They cross to the strait of the Black Sea, as said above, in summer, since the bay is sweeter, because the sun does not linger so long in this strait as to exhaust all the sweet and drinkable water in which sea creatures delight. Whence they also follow the rivers and go up into the higher waters, and thus fish of a foreign kind are frequently caught in rivers. There, suited by place and time, they breed and rear their tender young, and once this is done, all together return in the same company by which they came.

Pliny: it is made evident by the leanness of some fish, when they are caught of the same kind, that others are quite fat. A sign of their old age, moreover, is the hardness of their scales, which are not the same in all. Seneca writes that a fish placed in Caesar's fishponds died after its fortieth year.

Aristotle: dryness, as said above, harms fish; rain, too, harms some, since it blinds them when there is much of it. Pestilential illness, however, does not appear in fish as it does in men and other animals, though certain fish are subject to illnesses of their own. There are also fish that die when bitten by the 'draco,' for the sea-dragon is venomous. There are also fish that die of heat around the rising of the Dog Star. Under the gills of the 'kabari,' as said above, many lice are found, by which it is killed. Again, fish, when ice occurs, die, and for this reason are caught in rivers and lakes. There is also a fish having a stone in its head, which is harmed by winter, since the stone is chilled in the head and coagulates, and so that fish falls, that is, dies. The fish called the sword-fish, similar to the scorpion in stinging, causes great pain to other fish, and so they often leap, just as the dolphin leaps when pricked by its own spine. Besides, a certain fish, as said above, which also arises without roots, dies if moved from its place. The fish called 'garus,' very soft, decays in very hot places. Certain sea creatures shed their old age. For the lobster and crayfish shed their shells, sometimes in spring, sometimes in autumn. All agree, too, that soft-shelled creatures shed their old age. It is also said this happens to those of hard shell, since, when they shed, their shell becomes very soft. Old fish are poor at leaping, since the greater part of what was held in their belly has already dissolved. The old age of fish, moreover, is known by their size and by the hardness of their scales.
Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: fish die in ice, and are also extinguished by the taste of oil.

Pliny, in the same place: there are marvels, moreover, of enmity and concord among fish. The grey mullet and the sea-bass burn with mutual hatred. The conger eel and the moray gnaw off each other's tails. The lobster fears the octopus so much that if it sees one nearby, it dies outright. The conger eel devours the lobster, and in turn morays tear apart octopuses. Nigidius is the authority that the sea-bass gnaws off the mullet's tail, and that they are on friendly terms during set months. All those whose tails are thus cut off, however, live. Examples of friendship, on the other hand, are found among those that keep company with one another. The male whale, when his eyes are sometimes overwhelmed by the excessive weight of his eyebrows, is guided by a fish that swims ahead, showing him shoals dangerous by their size, and thus performs the office of eyes for him.

Aristotle: for many kinds of fish it is fitting always to be with many companions. Some are separated and solitary by themselves. For many it is not possible to be with any companions. For some love one another mutually and some do not. All shoals of fish, however, have a leader. The fish called the sword-fish, as said, similar to the scorpion in stinging, causes great pain to other fish, so that it makes them leap. The dolphin leaps for this reason too.

Seneca, in the Natural Questions, book 8: Balbillus is the authority that, when he himself, as prefect, held Egypt, at the uncovered mouth of the Nile, which is the greatest, it was a spectacle for him: dolphins rushing together from the sea and crocodiles from the river in an opposing column, waging, as it were, a battle for their respective sides. The fleeing creature was bold, and the boldest creature was timid, and the crocodiles were wounded by the calm and, by their bite, harmless animals. For although their upper body-part is hard and impenetrable on that side, even to the teeth of larger animals, the inner part is nevertheless soft and tender. This the dolphins, diving under or straining against them, cut open with the spines they bear projecting on their backs. Once many had thus been cut open in this way, the rest fled as if their battle-line had turned.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: [crayfish walk] like herds, and divide up wars among themselves. For monstrous creatures of this kind fight most fiercely among themselves, like rams, and opposing sides fortify themselves with a multitude of allies. Wars occur among such animals, as among the rest, for four reasons, namely because of natural pride, because of food, because of mating, because of offspring. And all shoals of fish, indeed, have a leader. No fish living by predation, however, swims socially, like the pike and its like. But all male fish devour one another, except one, as said above.

Aristotle: 'malacia' is the name given to the kind of fish that is soft-fleshed, made only of flesh. Among their external members they have feet and a head, which is between the belly and the feet. And all of this kind have four feet divided between two, except one kind called the many-footed one. Soft-bodied creatures swim head-first, and all those having a soft shell, like the crayfish. And some are walking animals, like the kind of crabs, since their nature is aquatic. The kind of soft-bodied creatures increases in warm places and is more in the open sea than near the shores, especially in places where insipid waters multiply. In the body of a soft-bodied creature there is no bone, nor any earthy part distinct in itself. Sea creatures of hard shell walk and feed and draw their heads out from the shell, and when afraid, put it back. There are also, in the sea, certain creatures about which it is doubtful whether they are animals or plants, for they are continuous with the places in which they are found and decay if moved from them. And every hard-shelled creature is, moreover, similar to a plant, though compared with a walking animal. And among these are creatures entirely lacking sense, and some having weak sense. Immobile shelled creatures feed themselves from fresh water. And there is a fish, as said, having a stone in its head, which is harmed by winter, since the stone in its head is chilled and coagulates, and so the fish falls, that is dies. Of fish, as said, some are marine, some riverine, some of lakes, and some have their mouth opposite, some in front, some on the back. Some move from their place, some do not. The fish, as said, called 'garus,' is very soft, but wind and cold harden it, as happens to trees, and it decays in very hot places. In certain sea creatures there is no blood, as with the cuttlefish and the crayfish and all those that have four or more feet.

Pliny: squid, cuttlefish, octopuses, and other creatures of this kind, of which, that is, mention will be made below. Oysters. The same nature, too, that belongs to the sea-anemone belongs to many, and to sea-cucumbers, sponges, and starfish.

Isidore: among these, moreover, there are certain kinds of fish called amphibious, so named, as already said above, since they have the practice of walking on land and the function of swimming in water.

Pliny, in the same place: of sea fish, some are like the turbot, the sole, the flounder, which differ from the turbot only in the position of their bodies. Others are long, like the moray, the conger. And so there are also distinctions of fins, which are given to fish in place of feet. None has more than five, some three, some two, some none. Only in Lake Fucinus is there a fish that swims with eight fins. Two entirely for the long ones, like earthworms and eels and conger eels. None for morays, which also have no gills. All these use the sinuous thrust of their bodies, making use of the sea as serpents do of dry land, and so such creatures are also more tenacious of life. And among the flat ones, too, some have no fins, like the stingray. For they swim by their very breadth, and those called soft-bodied, like octopuses, since their feet serve in place of fins. Of flat fish, some have cartilage instead of a spine, like the skate, the stingray, the angel-shark, and those Greece calls by the names of ox, shark, eagle, and frog, among which number are the dogfish, though not flat. All such are more fleshy and feed lying on their backs. And while other fish lay eggs, this kind alone, like those called cetaceans, bears living young, except the one called the frog. It is a most reliable sign of safety to have seen flat fish, since they are never present where malicious beasts are, for which reason divers call them sacred.

Aristotle: long fish do not swim, but crawl in the water, as serpents do on land, and live a long time. Long fish, as said above, grow fat from the north wind, and so many of them are caught in summer, but broad fish grow fat from the south wind.

Aristotle: animals dwelling in water are of a more varied form than those on land, since the nature of moisture is more suited to creation than earth, and this is especially true of sea creatures. For in the sea, too, there are more corpulent creatures than in fresh water, since the nature of the sea is warm and shares in all its parts, namely earth, moisture, and wind.

Ambrose: notice, O man, how many more things there are in the sea than on land - count, if you can, all the kinds of fish, whether small or very large. What shall I add of blackbirds and thrushes and peacocks too? Whose colors we see expressed in birds, as the blackbirds are black, the peacocks' backs and necks are painted with varied colors, the thrushes are mottled with white, and the rest, whose forms and names the land has claimed for itself. For these first appeared in the sea and in various rivers. If indeed the water, first, at the divine command, produced the creeping things of living souls. Add also this grace, that the things we fear on land are harmless in water: the lion is terrible on land, but gentle in the waves. The moray, which they say has something else harmful, is a more precious dish. The frog, repulsive in the marshes, is beautiful in the waters, and provides food for almost everyone. The weasel's smell is heavy on land, sweet in the waters. What shall I say of the tenderness of ravens, or even of wolves? The lamb does not know to fear these wolves. So great is the grace of the waters, whose young the very lions flee? What too shall I recall of the purple-fish, which clothe the banquets and dinners and garments of kings? It belongs to the waters, then, what is adored in kings. Add too: you see even sea-pigs pleasing, since there is nothing common that water does not wash clean, whence men cannot judge them common, as they would those born on land.

Pliny: [certain] winged animals. The evident cause is the abundance of moisture. In the sea, however, so broadly open, soft, and fertile in growth, nature, taking causes of generation from on high and always giving birth, produces even many monstrous things, tangled and coiled in themselves now one way, now another, now by a gust, now by a wave, into seeds and beginnings, so that the common belief becomes true, that whatever is born in any part of nature is also found in the sea, besides many things found nowhere else - not only likenesses of animals but of things, as one may understand by observing: a grape, a sword, saws, and even a cucumber similar in both color and smell, so that we should be less amazed that the heads of horses project from such small shells. There are seventy-four species of fish, apart from those covered in shells, which number thirty. Of bloodless fish there are three kinds, as said above; of these, the soft-bodied ones have their head between their feet and on their belly, with eight small feet. But the cuttlefish and the squid have two feet among these, the longest and roughest, with which they bring food to their mouths and steady themselves in the waves as if with anchors.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis: some fish have multiple gills, others simple. And some swim head-first, others tail-first. Certain fish, moreover, as Pliny says, are naturally of such lightness that, unless their heads made up the greatest portion of their bodies, they could not sink in the water. In the depth of the sea there are many kinds of fish that never or scarcely come into human sight. There is an armed fish, in the manner of a soldier, and there is a fish resembling a monk.

Pliny, book 9: aquatic creatures too have several kinds of covering. Some are covered with hide and hair, like seals and hippopotami. Some with hide only, like dolphins. With a bark-like shell, like tortoises. With the hardness of stone, like clams and oysters. With crusts, like lobsters. With crusts and spines, like sea urchins. With scales, like fish. With rough skin, like the angel-shark, with which wood and ivory are polished. With soft skin, like morays. Others with none at all, like the octopus. Those clothed with hair bear living young, like the sawfish, the whale, the seal. Likewise of those lacking hair there are only two that bear living young, the dolphin and the viper. Of fish, as said before, thirty kinds are covered in crusts. A sign of old age is the hardness of the scales.

Aristotle: of fish and serpents, some have smooth hide, some rough, some scaly, some spiny. Some fish, too, have hide full of scales. Those having smooth hide, however, are few. The 'cheleti,' however, have a shell, but rough, since their formation is cartilaginous and bony. For the earthy part naturally passes into the hide. Of bloodless animals, one kind is soft-bodied, that is soft, lacking a shell, and its flesh is on the outside. But what is hard on the outside, in the manner of the cuttlefish, one kind is soft-shelled, like the crab; another is hard-shelled, like the oyster and the ringed creature. There is also a fish of the oyster kind, that is of hard shell, which swims and crawls with its tail. But the creature called 'thico' is of much more surplus than other animals, since its whole body is hidden in a shell. The formation of its shell, however, is between the formation of a shell and of hide. Its shell is attached to stones, and in its body there are two small passages, difficult to see, and through them it receives moisture. And when its body is opened, one membrane is found, whose formation is spread around the circuit of the shell, and in that membrane is the flesh. Its flesh, however, is not like the flesh of any sea animal. The membrane, indeed, is extended on both sides up to the outer passages, namely the passage by which it takes in moisture and the passage by which it expels it, and through one of them it receives its food. The difference between hard-shelled animals and trees is this, that moisture is closer to their life, and water is closer to them, that is to shellfish, than earth is. And for this reason the nature of hard-shelled animals is closer to life than trees are. And just as is the relation of trees to earth, so is the relation of hard-shelled animals to moisture. Hard-shelled and soft-shelled creatures, too, are of cold nature and have no blood. All kinds of hard-shelled creatures have a fleshy part inside the shell, except the sea urchin. And some are of rough shell. Some have woolly shells, and differ in thickness and slenderness. Hard-shelled sea creatures walk and feed. Certain fish having slender and scanty eggs are of weak shell. But what is of long body among them lacks a shell and does not lay eggs. The shells of fish thicken and harden for their protection. And whatever among them is leaner and older is of harder shell.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham: fish hiding in caverns shed their old age, that is their skin. Those, however, that are of hard shell do not, from the fault of age, in spring and autumn. In the western sea there are fish from whose hides men make ample and beautiful garments for themselves.

div.head: DE CARNIBUS PISCIUM ET ADIPIBUS EORUM

cit.quote: Avicenna: the nature of fish is cold and moist. Some, however, are hot by comparison with others. Salted ones, indeed, are hot and dry, and the more aged they become, the more they increase in both. Fresh fish generate watery phlegm and soften the sinews, and are not suited except to a very hot stomach. And their blood tends toward fineness. Salted fish species draw out what is embedded in the flesh. Water of salted fish benefits ulcers and cleanses them of pus. Heads of dried, salted fish benefit apostemes of the uvula. Eating fresh tarragon [or a similarly named preparation] causes blindness of the eye - indeed, so does all fish. Fish glue is added to broths and prevents coughing of blood. Every fresh fish, eaten while warm, increases mating. When enemas are given repeatedly with the juices of salted fish, it greatly benefits pain of the gills [or throat]. All fish broths soothe the bowels. Heads of salted fish, roasted, are placed on the bite of a rabid dog and the sting of a scorpion, and help. Likewise all fish and their broths. The broth of any fish benefits poisons drunk and stings.
Aristotle: old fish, however, are poor for salting.
Pliny, book 32: the melted fat of all river and sea fish, mixed with honey, greatly benefits clarity of the eyes.
Avicenna: fish-water benefits the eye and sharpens sight when mixed with honey.
Dioscorides: the fat of river fish, dissolved with honey mixed in, in the sun, clears dimness of the eyes.

Avicenna: fish glue is hot and dry, adhesive and drying. It is put in poultices and in medicines for leprosy-like conditions. It is also smeared on burns and benefits scalding of the bladder. It is also put in plasters for ulcers of the head and ulcerous scabies. Likewise given in drink with vinegar for coughing blood.

Haly Abbas: sleepy fish, if placed on one who suffers from headache, will benefit him. Fish fat, too, melted, if mixed with honey and used as an eye-salve, clears and strengthens the sight, and benefits incipient watering of the eye.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: fish flesh on the back and front is harder than in other parts of the body. All stone-bearing fish are fat. And indeed all fish that swim by their breadth, like the flounder and the scallop, grow fat when the south wind blows. Those, however, that are elongated, like the pike, grow fat when the north wind blows. If wood is rubbed with the lung of a sea fish, it seems to burn like oil. Whence oil has customarily been made from the lungs of certain of them.

Isaac Judaeus: the whole nature of fish is naturally cold and moist, productive of phlegm, suited to those of hot and dry constitution and to lean people, especially in summer and those inhabiting hot regions. It is unsuited to cold and moist constitutions and to fleshy people, especially if they are of soft flesh. For they naturally chill and moisten the body. Fish vary, moreover, according to the diversity of the waters in which they live, and according to the diversity of the winds to whose region they are exposed.

Aristotle: places near land are more temperate. And so the flesh of fish dwelling there is stronger. Near land, too, the depth is better, since good pasture is there, for because of the rising of the sun, soft plants grow there, especially in gardens. But the flesh of fish that are in the depth of the sea is more moist. And all stone-bearing fish are fat. Dryness of season harms fish. The greater part of them, however, grow fat in rainy seasons, for then they find much food. Rainwater itself, too, is beneficial to all of them, and for this reason they grow fat in rivers and lakes, and summer rainwater suits them most. Some, however, grow fat in places where there is a green cloud of water. For fish that eat flesh find much food in green water, whence, caught there, they are better. Some, too, grow fat from the north wind, like the long fish. Some, however, from the south wind, like the broad fish. They do not grow fat, however, in cold places. Fish of hard or soft shell, when they grow fat, are good; some fish, however, are the opposite. But all fish having shells, when they breed, are for the most part poor. Old fish, too, are poor. River and lake fish are good after breeding and mating, especially if they have had much food. In all kinds of fish, however, the males are better than their females.

Isaac Judaeus: the diversity of fish is also divided in many ways by the method of cooking. For they are eaten either roasted, or fried in oil, or cooked in water and oil and seasonings, or boiled in water alone. Roasted and fried fish are of less viscosity and moisture. Whence, if neither, they are moistening, harder to digest, in that they burden the stomach. Yet roasted are more praiseworthy than fried, since fried have a certain viscosity because of the oil. Fish, however, prepared with oil and water and the like, are more digestible than the rest and loosen the bowels. Cooked with vinegar, they will be cooling, though less moistening. Those, however, boiled with water alone, are more praiseworthy than all, since the water of the cooking in which they were cooked has taken away their viscosity, especially if eaten with oil-fish-sauce, mint, celery, rue, caraway, pepper, ginger, and the like.

div.head: DE ELECTIONE PISCIUM MELIORUM AD ESUM

cit.quote: Avicenna: the better fish are those that are not very large, nor have hard or dry flesh, and in which there is no excessive or thick or acrid fat, nor sliminess, nor bad taste or smell, and which do not quickly develop an odor when separated from the water. Of fish having hard flesh, the smaller is chosen. Of soft ones, however, that which is larger up to a certain limit. And that indeed which has hard flesh is better salted; recent is better. Likewise, according to place, better are those that dwell in rocky places. Then those in sandy places and fresh waters, in which there is no filth, nor mud, nor lake-dwelling nor field-dwelling ones. Likewise those that dwell in waters exposed to the blast of winds above them are better than those that are the opposite, and those that dwell in places of much agitation and waves are better than those that inhabit still waters. Sea fish are best and of fine flesh, especially when their habitation is on rocky or even sandy shores, and those that go from the sea into fresh rivers, whose current is contrary to them, are naturally fine and of much exercise. Further, according to food, better are those that feed on good plants and roots, than those that eat filth thrown out from cities and roots of bad plants, although these may ultimately be of good taste. The better manner of eating fish, moreover, is with seasoning, that is condiment, such as with vinegar and the like. Then those roasted on a shell. Fried ones are suited to those having a strong stomach. And roasted ones indeed are more nourishing and of slower descent, boiled ones the opposite. Their cooking is better done thus: that the water be brought to a boil, then they be thrown into it. Of salted fish, the fresher are better. Then those nearer to the time they were salted. Water in which salted fish is boiled is of vehement cleansing power and is used in drying enemas.

Aristotle: fish, as said, since they have hearing, must be hunted in quiet. They are hunted better before the sun's rising, since then they do not see well. Each kind of fish, moreover, has something proper to its own hunting. For many love something that is known to them as food, and are hunted by means of it. They flee, however, at the smell of certain things. Many of them do not touch the vessel by which they are caught, unless it is new. Some, however, are caught by means of foul-smelling things. Many fish hide in caverns and are not caught at all, except at determined times. When ice occurs, fish die, and for this reason are caught in rivers and lakes. When hunters wish fish dwelling among stones to come out, they rub the mouths of the stone-caverns with salted things, and then the fish come out quickly and are caught this way. Some, however, love the smell of burnt things and smoke, and so cuttlefish flesh is burnt, and fish are caught by their smell. Some, however, when they perceive a voice or noise, flee to the depth. A certain fish is strangled by dirty water, since its gills are small, and so they stir up the water when they want to hunt it. Some, however, when afraid, hide their head in their own body. And some, like the scallop, if anything approaches its foot, suddenly closes its eye. Long fish are caught especially in great numbers in summer, since they grow fat from the north wind.

Pliny, on fish, book 9: all female fish heavy with roe are easily caught; they wander about mostly in shoals, of whatever scaly kind, and are caught before sunrise. For then the sight of fish is deceived, though on clear nights they see equally well as by day. They also say that if a deep pool is disturbed repeatedly, this affects the catch, so that more are caught on the second draw than the first. At the taste of oil, the catch of fish is most abundant, the sun passing being the sign for fish. And when winters have been harsh, many blind ones are caught.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis: fish are hunted in caverns, especially where the place is warm. But when they desire food, they come out a little to feed, especially at the full moon, and then they are hunted. Some, however, dwelling among stones, are forced to come out by having their caverns rubbed with salted things. There is, moreover, a fish which, when someone wants to pull it from its place, tightens itself and is drawn out with difficulty. It does the same too when struck by a wave or strong wind, and if a part of it falls off, it will grow again from the remainder, similar to what it was. When the sea thickens, often several fish are caught in one net. Some fish, however, do not enter an old and dirty vessel, but come to a new one, and from far off. Some, too, are caught by the smell of burnt things producing smoke. Fishermen hunt fish fleeing from the sea to the river in winter by making a pit near the bank, so that a stream runs from the bank to the pit. For they place wood and grass over it, and thus fish entering by the way of the stream are caught. Further, in summer they hunt them by placing much wood and stone in the middle of the river, so that water can pass through, and make one opening in it, in which they place a hollow instrument, and thus catch them through it. In the net, moreover, there are certain things that naturally tend downward, like lead, and some light things, which raise the net from the bottom and make it float. Likewise sleeping fish are caught by hand, and struck while asleep with a three-pronged iron, as said, and are better caught before sunrise, since then their sight is most deceived. Some, too, are weakened when they breed, and for this reason are more easily caught at that time. Some do not touch the vessel by which they are caught, unless it is fresh, for they have the sense of touch. Others, however, that do not have it, are caught more quickly. There is also a method of fishing whereby a ditch is made next to a river, so that water enters, and wood is placed there; for then fish come from the river and hide there for quiet, especially in winter. Every fish, as said, naturally having a stone in its head, is more harmed in winter than one that does not, since that stone chills the brain. For this reason, as the cold sets in, such fish seek the depths.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: in sum, note that fish are sometimes caught by net or seine, sometimes by hook, sometimes by trident, sometimes by otter, sometimes by weir or wicker trap, sometimes by basket, sometimes by draining the fishpond.

div.head: DE LUXURIA HOMINUM IN CAPTURA ET ESU PISCIUM

cit.quote: Seneca, in the same place, book 1: the works of luxury are incredible. Fish swim in the bedchamber, and are caught right under the table, to be transferred straight onto it. A red mullet seems hardly fresh unless it dies in the guest's own hand. The color of the dying is watched, which death itself, as the breath struggles, turns through many changes. Redness first, then pallor spreads over it - a long, sleepy expectation of idle luxury. They refuse to touch one unless caught that very day, one that, as they say, still tastes of the sea itself. And so it is rushed in at a run, and so a path is cleared for the porters hastening with panting and shouting, and men run to the mullet's death: to what has delicacy come? The belly of the pampered has come to this arrogance, that they cannot taste unless they have seen it swimming and gasping at the very banquet, and feed their eyes before their gullet. Every day the frenzy of luxury devises something more refined and elegant, scorning the accustomed. We used to hear that nothing was better than a rock-mullet; now we hear that nothing is more beautiful than one dying. Give me, one says, a glass vessel in my hands, in which the mullet may leap and quiver. See how its redness, sharper than any vermilion, blazes up? See what veins it drives through its sides? And so these men are not content with the tavern's fare in teeth, mouth, and belly, but are gluttonous in their eyes too.

Pliny, in the same place: already, indeed, out of the whole of nature, the sea is most ruinous to the belly, in so many ways, at so many tables, with so many flavors of fish, whose prices are set at the peril of those who catch them.

Isidore: men imposed names on cattle and wild beasts and winged creatures before they did on fish, since these were seen and known first. Names for fish, however, were established only afterward, as their kinds gradually became known, either from resemblance to land animals or from their own particular appearance, or habits, or color, or shape, or sex. From resemblance to land animals, as frogs, calves, lions: from the habits of land animals, as sea-dogs, from land dogs, since they bite, and sea-wolves, since they pursue others with shameless voracity. From color, as the umber-fish, since they are the color of shadow. And the gilthead, since it has the color of gold on its head. And the varied ones, from their variety, which are commonly called trout. From shape, as the sunfish, since it is round and consists entirely of a head. From sex, as the 'masculus,' since it is the male of the whale itself. For by mating with it this beast is said to conceive. Hence too the males of snails are so called, by whose milt oysters conceive. And so there are one hundred forty-four names of animals living in water. Pliny says: divided into the kinds of sea-monsters, of serpents common to land and water, of crabs, shellfish, lobsters, mussels, octopuses, soles, and crustaceans, such as the squid and things like it. From these, too, many, by a certain understanding of nature, recognize the order of their own seasons.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: many kinds of fish, especially river and pond fish, are indeed quite commonly used among us, of which nothing is found written in the books of the philosophers, or perhaps they are called by other names, unknown to us, among them - such as the salmon, the pike, the tench, the perch, the 'vendesia,' the roach, the gudgeon, and the rest.

div.head: DE NATURIS PISCIUM IN SPECIALI SECUNDUM ORDINEM ALPHABETI ET PRIMO DE ABRENONE ET ACHANDE ET ACCIPENDRO ALBIREZ ALPHORAZ

cit.quote: Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'abrenon,' also called 'abarenon,' is a fish, as Aristotle says, very fecund in eggs, and does not lay them, as others do, by contact with the male, but by a certain natural instinct rubs its belly against the sand, which is rough to the touch and salty to the taste. And so it lays the eggs thus conceived, and after the due time brings forth its young.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, in the book On Animals: the fish called 'abren,' at the hour of a sea storm, keeps its young safe in its belly, and after the storm vomits them out again.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, the same: the 'achandes' fish, anxious for its young, clings to ships at sea, and because of it the ships become entirely immobile.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the sturgeon is, as Pliny says, a most noble fish among the ancients, which alone, contrary to the habit of all fish, has scales over its whole body turned toward its mouth.

Pliny, book 9: among the ancients the sturgeon was held the most noble fish, the only one of all with scales turned toward the head, moving against the current when swimming; now it is held in no honor, which indeed I marvel at, since it is rare to find; some call it the 'elops.' The 'albirez' is a sea fish having a skin so thick and hard and firm that soldiers use it in place of helmets. The 'alphoraz' is a fish that is not bred, but in a muddy place, where there is no water, is created from the putrefaction of the mud itself in the manner of a small worm. Afterward, when it rises into water, it grows into a fish, but lasts only a short time and quickly dissolves.
Isidore: the herring is a fish suited to the liquid of fish-sauces, whence it also got its name.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the herring, moreover, is said to live from the pure element of water alone, as the salamander does from fire.
Pliny: [herring] benefits the bite of a dog or sea-dragon.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the herring is a rather small sea fish in the western sea, which is the strait between greater Britain and Germany. This fish, like almost every kind of sea fish, has its own season in which alone it is good, namely from August until December; when freshly caught it provides more delicate fare. Salted, however, it can remain wholesome for human use longer than other fish. It also, alone among almost all fish, lives on water only, nor can it live except in water. For as soon as it comes into contact with the open air, it dies. Nor is there any delay between contact with air and death. Its eyes, like a light, shine at night in the sea, but this power of theirs dies with the fish itself. Wherever they see light above the waters in the sea, they swim together in shoals. And by this cunning, while they are lured to nets at the times mentioned, as if ready to be caught by a divine gift, they are led into the service of men. In the winter months, however, they hide in the secret depths of the sea until the due time, and this around Germany.

Isidore: the eel is named from its resemblance to a serpent [anguis]; its origin is from mud. Whence, when caught, it is so slippery that the more firmly you press it, the more quickly it slips away. They say that the eastern river Ganges produces eels thirty feet long. Likewise eels killed in wine, if men drink from that wine, produces distaste for wine in them.

Pliny: eels live eight years, and endure even without water for six days when the north wind blows, fewer when the south wind blows. But they do not tolerate winter in shallow water, nor in muddy water. And so they are caught especially around the rising of the Pleiades, most of all in muddy rivers; they feed at night, and, lifeless, do not float on the surface like other fish, in the sun. Further, in place of feet, two fins are given to entirely long fish, like eels and conger eels. Likewise eels rub themselves against rocks, and these scrapings come to life, nor is there any other way they are generated. Eels, moreover, live longer than other fish once taken from the water.

Pliny, book 10: in all eels there is neither a male nor a female kind, and they generate from themselves neither living young nor eggs, just as the kind is neuter also in oysters and other creatures attached to a shallow bottom or a rock.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the eel is said to be born from the mud of other fish. It is hard to skin, has a very tough death, so that even skinned it still lives, and is stirred by the sound of thunder. It delights in clear river waters and is caught most when the Pleiades are hidden, since then the water is stirred up by opposing winds; it is rapacious toward small fish of lesser power, especially, however, when they are found in spawn. Lifeless, alone among fish it does not float, except when, putrefied in the water, it dissolves. It is more digestible cooked with other food; otherwise its flesh is harmful; roasted on the fire it is more suitable, since its harmfulness evaporates there; its fat is a remedy for the ears.

div.head: DE ARANEA ET ARIETE ET ARIMI

cit.quote: Isidore: the weever [aranea] is a kind of fish, so named because it strikes the ear [aure feriat]. For it has spines with which it stings those who come near.

Avicenna: the sea-spider seems to have a disposition close to that of the scorpion. And so the bite of this and of other venomous sea reptiles, they said, should be treated with theriacs, by which cold venom is treated, and with the medicines and theriac of small rodents.

Pliny: the weever, with the sting of the spine on its back, is dangerous and venomous. The 'aries' [ram-fish] is fattened like a robber; now hidden in the shadow of larger ships standing at sea, it waits for anyone the pleasure of swimming might invite; now, its head raised above the water, it watches fishermen's boats, and, swimming up secretly, sinks them.
Aesculapius, in the book On Animals: the fish called 'arimus,' when a man sees it, makes him drunk and stirs him to quarrels and disputes; but once he has eaten it, his anger is calmed.

Physiologus: the 'aspidochelone' is a certain sea-beast, called in Latin the 'asp-turtle.' It is a great whale, having on its hide something like sand, such as is by the sea-shore. Whence very often, when it raises its back above the waves, it is believed by sailors to be nothing other than an island. And so, landing and going down onto it, they fix stakes, tie up ships, light fires to cook their food. But this creature, once it senses the smell of fire, sinks the ships into the deep. There is also this other nature of this beast: when it is hungry, it opens its mouth and breathes out from its mouth something like a sweet-smelling odor, which the smaller fish, sensing it, gather into its mouth, and when it is full, it closes its mouth and swallows them. The gilthead is so called because it has the color of gold on its head.

Isidore: the whale is a beast of immense size, named from emitting and pouring forth water. For it throws its waves higher than the other beasts of the sea. 'Balin,' moreover, means 'to emit' in Greek.

Pliny, book 9: they report that whales are not seen in the ocean off Cadiz before winter. They hide, however, in summer in a certain calm and spacious bay, delighting remarkably to give birth there; they know that the killer whale is hostile to them, a beast whose form cannot be represented by any other image than of a mass of flesh, savage with teeth. They break, then, into their hiding places and, with a bite, tear apart their calves, or their young, or even those not yet pregnant, and, charging like the beaks of light warships, pierce them. But those, immobile for turning, sluggish for fighting back, and burdened by their own weight - then indeed heavy in the womb, or, if giving birth, weak from the pains of it - know only one aid, to flee into the deep and defend themselves throughout the whole ocean. The killer whales, on the contrary, strive to meet them and oppose themselves, and, in cramped narrows, to slaughter them, drive them into shallows, dash them against rocks. Battles of this kind are witnessed as if the sea itself were angered against itself, with no winds in the bay. Yet there are waves, from the panting and blows, such as no whirlwind could stir. Whales have their mouth in their forehead. And so, swimming at the water's surface, they blow out clouds of spray from the top. Whales have no gills, nor do dolphins. These two kinds breathe through blowholes, which lead to the lung - in whales from the forehead, in dolphins from the back. Likewise those clothed with hair bear living young, like the sawfish, the whale, the seal.
Pliny, in the same book: whales and dolphins sleep. For they are even heard snoring.

Solinus: the Indian seas hold whales beyond the size of four acres. But those they call 'fasciturae' rise up, monstrous, beyond the mass of huge columns, above the masts of ships, and, having drawn in waves through their blowholes, belch them out so that the cloudy deluge often sinks the hulls of ships sailing by.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: whales, lacking gills, breathe through a blowhole, which is rarely found among sea creatures; they carry their young when they are weak and infirm, and if they are small, take them into their mouth. They do the same when a storm is approaching, and vomit them out again after the storm. When, for lack of water, their young are prevented from following their mother, the mother ejects water taken into her mouth toward them like a river, so as to free them thus stuck to the land; she also accompanies the grown ones for a long time. They mature quickly, however, and grow for ten years.

div.head: DE BORBOTHA ET BOTHA ET BRENA

cit.quote: Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: certain river fish, somewhat similar to eels, for they are slippery and are skinned as eels are. They have black skin, sweet to eat, and a liver better and more effective than that of all other fish. Their head is large in proportion to the body, their mouth wide and very broad. But when it exceeds twelve years of age, it grows into a large body. And then its name changes, and it is called the 'solaris,' of which more will be said below. The flounder are river fish that swim only by the breadth of their body. For they are very thin and very broad. They have fins around the edge of their broad body, and grow fat when the south wind blows. And when this fish is hunted by fishermen, seeking the bottom of the water, it stirs up the water above itself, so that it cannot be seen. And especially, its body lying flat when it clings to the ground, it is most like the ground on top; but it has red spots on its back.
Alexander Neckam: the 'brena' is a river fish which, when it sees the pike threatening it, turns aside to muddy places, stirring up behind it the clearness of the waters it has.

Isidore: crabs are so named because they are shell creatures having legs, animals hostile to oysters. For they live on their flesh, by a wonderful cunning. Some report that if ten crabs are bound with a bunch of basil, all the scorpions in the vicinity will gather to that spot. There are, however, two kinds of crabs, river and sea.

Ambrose: the crab feeds on oysters, but since it cannot open a closed oyster by any force - and it is dangerous if the oyster's shell should close on it - it resorts to schemes and plots an ambush with fresh cunning. For it watches to see when the oyster, in places sheltered from every wind, opens its two-leaved shell facing the sun's rays, so as to enjoy in the open air a certain pleasure in its innards, and then secretly inserts a pebble, preventing the oyster's closing, and thus, finding the barrier open, safely inserts its claws and feeds on the inner flesh.

Pliny, book 9: crabs, among soft-bodied creatures, seek sunny shores in winter. In summer they withdraw into the shaded depths; they are harmed in winter, grow fat in autumn and spring, and more so at full moon, since at night the star tempers them with its warm glow. Crabs have a long life; eight feet, all bent obliquely. In the female the first foot is doubled, in the male single. Besides, they have two arms with toothed pincers. The upper part of these moves in front, the lower being immobile; the right arm is always larger. They fight among themselves, like rams, charging with opposing horns. They are a remedy against the strikes of serpents. Crabs, like sea-lobsters, hide and are concealed for five months at the same time. Both shed their old age at the beginning of spring, in the manner of snakes, by renewing their shells. Lobsters, indeed, live in rocky places, but crabs in soft ground: sometimes they all gather together and cannot overcome the mouth of the Black Sea. Wherefore, having come out, they go around it, and a worn path becomes visible. Further, in fear, they return backward with equal speed, the sun passing through the sign of Cancer being the signal for crabs; and of these same crabs, when the body is lifeless, it is said they are transformed into scorpions on dry land. Crabs and lobsters mate by the mouth.

Pliny, book 11: bees are killed if cooked near the smell of crabs. Crabs look sideways, their eyes fixed, enclosed in a fragile shell. Octopuses, cuttlefish, squid, and crabs have eight feet, which move their arms in the opposite direction, their feet in a circle or obliquely.
Pliny, in the same: [crabs] are the only round animals; the rest of the animals have two feet as leaders; crabs, however, have four.

Aristotle: the crab has eight feet, by which it moves with equal motion, lacks blood, is hard outside and soft inside. Nor is that hardness crushable; indeed it withstands fire. On the sea-shore that lies within Judea small crabs are found, called 'soldiers' because of the swiftness of their running, for they run so fast that they cannot be caught. And when one is opened, no flesh or surplus at all is found in its body, since they have no pasturage. The kind of crab called the 'cantel' has ten feet with spines. And the feet of all kinds, whether eight, ten, or twelve, are bent to the sides, like the feet of a ringed animal. The spines, however, of whatever has them, are bent inward. Kinds of crabs have two spines and two feet, and the right spine is sharper and stronger than the left, in most cases. The smaller crab, that is the male, mounts the female from behind, and then the female bends toward him on her side, and then mating is completed. Females are of larger members than males, and the distance of the covering is greater than in males. And it lays eggs through the place of surplus: none of these has a member entering the body of the other. The small crab is generated from earth and mud, within the empty places of other animals' shells. And when it has grown somewhat, it moves itself from that place to a larger shell. The crab and the lobster shed their covering in old age. Both take fish in the depth of the sea with their two lips and divide them into two parts and bring them to their mouth. Crabs have two teeth from the first front ones, between which is a member resembling a tongue, then an opening, then a small stomach in proportion to the size of the body, and after the stomach a belly and intestines. There are also other teeth in certain crabs. Crabs have two lips, that is appendages, not for walking, but in place of hands, for taking and holding and bringing to the mouth. They do not stay in a place near land, but in the cracks and holes of stones. What is deep sea for them. They have very weak feet because of the scarcity of their walking. At the time when crabs cannot walk well, they do not shed once, but many times.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the crab has feet and arms and pincers in place of hands, and moves backward, never knowing how to walk before its own face. Males have two spines between belly and tail, which the females lack. Those having eggs in their belly are a remedy against the strikes of serpents. At mating time the male mounts on the female's back. But she, sensing his motion behind her as he wishes to mate, bends over on her side and turns to him. And thus mating is completed; they hide in winter for five months. In spring they shed their old age like a snake. A crab, given milk to drink, lives many days without water. But when it has grown old, two stones of white color mixed with red are found in its head, which are said to be of such power that, given in a drink, they heal pangs of the heart. Crabs fight among themselves with their little horns, the sun passing the sign of Cancer. In the western sea, as Solinus says, there are crabs that drown men they have seized. They have hard backs like crocodiles. The crab changes color when cooked, since what was green or black becomes red.

div.head: DE OPERATIONE CANCRORUM IN CIBO VEL MEDICINA

cit.quote: Avicenna: 'sea crab' is properly said of that species of sea crab that has all its members hard as stone. What is burnt from it is finer than other burnt things and cleans the teeth and removes ringworm and freckles. It also dries ulcers and benefits scabies. Likewise it stops tears and, with salt, dissolves nail-disease. A collyrium is also made from it, and scabies of the eyelids is rubbed with it. It also prevents quartan fever. River crab greatly benefits those wasted away. The shell of the sea crab is finer than the shell of the oven-crab [or, than the shell of the land-crab]. It is drying and cleans ringworm and freckles and scabies. River crab is difficult to digest and very nourishing, and it itself corrects [that difficulty]. Its decoction with honey draws out thorns and sharp things stuck in the flesh, but the sea kind is finer. Besides, its ash is good for cracks from cold, and what is burnt from it is put in medicines for vitiligo and ringworm, and helps. Likewise river crab dissolves large abscesses when placed on them. Its flesh benefits consumption, especially with donkey's milk, and its broth too. Its ash is good for cracks of the anus. And it benefits the bite of scorpions and small venomous reptiles, applied as a plaster or eaten. The same ash, too, with honey, benefits, drunk, against the bite of a rabid dog. From the shell of the sea crab a wax-salve is made for scrofula. A plaster made from it is of strong healing power and benefits ulcers. And it cleans scabies.

Avicenna, book 4, in the same: river crab, with milk, or its decoction, is drunk against venomous bites. Scrofula, too, is healed by river crab cooked or burnt with honey. Crabs of this kind, crushed and drunk in water, stop the bowels. They provoke urine in white wine with the gills removed. They also expel stones, crushed with myrrh. Further, crushed especially with donkey's milk, they heal ruptures and convulsions. The same, crushed in water and oil, benefit if rubbed on before the onset of fevers. Sea and river crabs' ashes, burnt in boiling water with wax, heal and this treatment also restores hair. River crabs, crushed, draw out things embedded in the body. Their juice with barley flour heals ulcers in the ears or elsewhere on the body.

Pliny: the ash of crabs with oil is effective against leprosy. Their broth is held most effective against 'doricnium' poison. Their ash, drunk, benefits those endangered by fear from the bite of a rabid dog. River crabs, crushed and drunk fresh in water, benefit against all poisons, especially against the strikes of scorpions with donkey's or even goat's milk. But their ash too, kept in store, benefits against poisons and against the bites of a rabid dog. In all these, sea crabs are less effective, as Trachylus is the authority. Nothing, however, is equally opposed to serpents as crabs, and pigs that have been struck heal themselves with this food. When the sun is in Cancer, serpents are said to be tormented by the stings of scorpions; the flesh of river snails resists this, raw or cooked. Some, for this reason, also keep them salted, and apply them to the wounds themselves. Crabs' eyes, bound to the neck, are said to heal watering of the eyes. Likewise the juice of river crabs with barley flour is most effective for wounds of the ears. Ruptures and convulsions, too, river crabs crushed in donkey's milk especially heal.

Isaac Judaeus: Galen holds that crabs and all fish having shells are laxative, because of their saltiness and sharpness. Hence they are harmful to the stomach, especially because of their fibrousness.

div.head: DE CAUCIO ET CAPITATO ET CARPERA

cit.quote: Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'caucius,' also called the catfish, bites baited hooks facing away and does not swallow them, but strips the bait off.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: according to Pliny it is written with 'g' and 'l' in the first syllable, and this is better, as 'glaucius.' The 'capitatus' is a rather small fish, having a head close to the size of the rest of its body, and a mouth also round and wide; this fish, dwelling in rivers, gladly hides beneath stones and among rocks. The carp is a fish with, as it were, golden scales, in lakes or rivers, so named as if 'the one that gives birth by plucking,' for when, dictated by nature, she senses she has eggs ready in her belly for laying, she approaches her mate and signals with her mouth, with a light nudge, so that he may help the laying; then he, in place of semen, emits milt, which she takes into her mouth; at once she lays her eggs, destined to become offspring. For she cannot lay eggs unless she has first received semen through her mouth. The semen, however, once received, seems to help not only the laying but also the conceiving and forming of the eggs, whence offspring is hoped for in the coming year. In the semen of the carp there sometimes grows, in the first year of its life, a certain small black worm, and afterward a wasting sickness of its own arises, and this usually after August, and it dies of that wasting. The remedy is fresh, river water, whose offspring comes from a small amount of water, if in individual pits of ten cubits, freshly made, individual carp are placed with their mates just before spawning. It is the common opinion that their offspring comes about this way. But after they have spawned, they are removed. The offspring too, strengthened after three or four months, is taken from the pits and put back where it may grow with the mature ones. This fish has many cunning tricks, so as to escape when caught in a net; for when it has entered the net, going around it seeks an opening, and if it does not find one, it strives to leap into the free air above the net, so as to fall outside. Sometimes it seeks refuge beneath the net. Sometimes it holds grass in its mouth at the bottom of the water, so that the net passing over is thrown off. Sometimes, too, coming from above with force, it fixes its head more firmly in the mud, so that the net, passing over by way of its tail, is foiled in the catch. Its brain is said to grow or shrink according to the waxing and waning of the moon. And although this is true in every fish, it is more so in this one, just as among four-footed creatures it is more so in the wolf and the dog.

Ambrose: the whale is a fish of infinite size, such that, if it ever floats on the waves, you would think islands were moving. Whence they are reported to be seen not on the shores, but in the depth of the Atlantic sea, so that in their sight sailors in those places are recalled from their presumption of sailing.

Ambrose: great whales, bodies indeed equal to mountains, know a sea beyond the bounds of the world, one that no islands interrupt, where, for the sake of navigation's usefulness, the sea shuts off boldness; they are reported to keep themselves there and to love it as their native soil.

The same: whales too, like dolphins and seals, and weasels and the dogfish, bring forth living young from their own body. And if anyone should attempt an ambush against them, they defend them. They suppress the fear of their tender age with a mother's affection. And they open their mouths and hold them suspended with a harmless tooth. They are also said to receive them into the interior of their body and hide them in the womb, until they can bring them to safety, or thus guard them by placing their own body in the way.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the whale, as is reported, when it plays in the sea, is a sign of a storm. The same is also called the 'balena.' Of this kind is the 'aspidochelone,' of which mention was made above.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, in the same place: in the whale, an earthly nature dominates more than a watery one. For when it grows old, it gathers roots, shrubs, and small trees upon itself, which grow and multiply upon it.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the whale is the largest of fish, having a large and wide-open mouth in its forehead and narrow passages of the mouth. In youth it has black teeth, in old age white. These fish sometimes belch out swallowed waves in such a way that the cloudy deluge often sinks a fleet of sailing ships. But also, when a storm arises at sea, they raise themselves above the waves, so as to sink ships with their commotion and whirlpools; sometimes they lift sand on their backs, on which, as a storm sets in, sailors, rejoicing that they have found land, cast anchor and rest in false security, and, the beast sensing the fires lit, suddenly, disturbed, submerges itself and drags the men down with their ships into the deep. The whale, after it exceeds three years of age, mates with the female whale, and in that very mating is at once mutilated in the power of its genital organ, so that it can no longer mate. But, entering the deep of the open sea, it grows so large that it cannot be caught by any human skill; within three years of its age, then, it can be caught. They are caught thus: fishermen, marking the place where a whale is, gather there with many ships, and, having made a concert of pipes and trumpets around it, lure the pursuing creature, since it delights in sounds of this kind; and when they see it lingering by the ships, stunned by the sound of the melody, they secretly throw onto its back a certain instrument like a rake, sharpened with iron teeth, and secretly flee. Without delay, if it has been given a definite wound, the whale seeks the bottom of the sea and, rubbing itself against the ground on its back, violently drives the iron deeper into its wounds, until, the fat pierced through, it has penetrated the living flesh within. And thus the salt water of the sea, following the iron, enters the wound and kills the wounded creature. Fishermen, then, approach the dead whale floating on the sea with ropes and drag it to shore with great rejoicing.

From the book On the Nature of Things, of an uncertain author: the whale, however, as is read, does not eat as other fish do, by chewing and breaking up food with its teeth, but only by swallowing and holding it within its body.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: [the whale] swallows little fish, which it draws in with its fragrant breath and, devouring them, sends into its belly. For it has in its throat a certain skin like a membrane, pierced with many passages, which does not allow anything large to enter the belly.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, in the same place: the whale, moreover, ejects semen in its mating with the female, and what is surplus from that semen floats on the water and is gathered as ambergris.

Platearius: [on ambergris, that is] of the whale. And it is hot and dry in the second degree. It is white, and if found of a chalky color, it is better. It is adulterated, however, with powder of aloeswood and storax and musk and certain other things. But this is recognized, since adulterated ambergris can be kneaded like wax, but true ambergris cannot. It has, moreover, the power of strengthening and is effective against fainting and epilepsy.

Avicenna: ambergris, as I judge, is a strong exudation in the sea; the strong grey kind is better, then the mottled, then the citron-colored. And it is adulterated with gypsum and wax and ladanum. The black kind is bad. It is often, moreover, taken from the belly of a fish that dies from eating it. It is hot and dry, and seems to be hot in the second degree, dry in the first. It benefits the decrepit, because of the fineness of its warming power. It benefits the brain and the senses and the heart.

Constantine the African, in the book of Degrees: ambergris comes out from the belly of a certain very large beast. Some, however, say that it is born on the sea floor: hot and dry, existing in the second degree, it strengthens cold constitutions.
Pliny: of the kind of shellfish, the firmer are those in which great variety of playful nature appears. So many differences of color, so many shapes, among which pearls hold first place.

Isidore: shells and snails are so named because they are hollowed, that is emptied, as the moon wanes. For the parts of all closed sea creatures and shellfish swell with the moon's growth, and are emptied with its waning. For the moon, when waxing, increases moisture, and when waning, moisture diminishes. 'Concha,' moreover, is the name in its original form; 'cochlea' by diminution, as it were a little shell. There are many kinds of shells, among which also the pearl-bearing one, called 'eceloa,' of which mention will indeed be made below.
Fulgentius, in the book of Mythologies: the sea shell mates with its whole body opened at once, as Juba relates in the Physiologus.
Haly Abbas, on the shell, in the same place: 'sadephum,' that is the sea shell, is better white.
Rhazes: burnt sea shells, by abrasion, clean the teeth. A plaster made from unburnt or ground ones heals burns from fire.

Pliny: snails, both aquatic and land-dwelling, put themselves out of their dwelling and extend and draw back their two, as it were, horns; they lack eyes. And so with their little horns they feel out their path ahead.

Pliny, book 30: the flesh of snails is useful to the stomach. But they should be lightly heated in water without breaking their body, then roasted on embers and taken with wine and fish-sauce; the most praised are the African ones and those from the islands of Capri. It has recently been discovered that this benefits very many. This too is observed, that they should be taken in an odd number. Their power, however, causes heaviness of breath. They also benefit those coughing up blood, with the shell removed, crushed, drunk in water. The most praised, however, are the African ones. The Sicilian ones are modest, since their size makes them tough and without moisture, and the Balearic ones, which they call 'canaricas,' since they are born in caves, are praised, and those from the islands of Capri. None of them, however, are pleasant to eat, whether old or fresh; river and white ones have an offensive smell, and likewise the wild ones are useful to the stomach and loosen the bowels. On the other hand, the sea ones are more useful to the stomach. Most effective, however, for stomach pain, more praised are those swallowed live with vinegar. Snails eaten benefit those whose mind is disturbed or whose reason is alienated, or those with vertigo, with three cups of raisin wine. Individual snails, too, crushed and warmed with their own shell, given in a drink. Likewise the flesh of these same snails, cooked in barley gruel, is praised for pains of the sides. The same also check the bowels. Their flesh eaten dispels inflammation. And the same, eaten, hasten childbirth. Fresh river snails eaten are said to cure quartan fevers. The same, however, stir up lust when kept in salt and given in a drink with wine. The ash of all snails constricts and warms. Likewise ash of snails, of the kind found widely, broad and small, with honey, removes blemishes from the face. Snails also benefit those coughing up blood, shell removed, crushed, in a drink of water. Most effective, however, are certain ones for stomach pain, swallowed with vinegar. Snails swallowed raw or crushed with lukewarm water, three cups, if sipped, calm cough. They also heal pain of the loins, crushed with their shells and cooked in wine with pepper. Their ash, taken with wine, is useful for dysentery sufferers, and, drunk with dry wine, checks the bowels. The same ash, that is of snails burnt alive, heals all ulcers of the feet. With flaxseed and nettle added, smeared with honey, it heals epileptics. Broad snails drunk are said to remove pains of the feet and joints. Certain ones, too, crushed and applied, are useful for extracting reeds and any other darts from the body.

Pliny, in the same book: the flesh of river snails resists the poison of scorpions, raw or cooked. Some, for this reason, also keep them salted and apply them to the wounds themselves. They also prescribe drinking crushed raw snail flesh in warm water for bloody cough.

div.head: DE CONGRO ET COREM ET CORVO

cit.quote: Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the conger eel is a sea fish, long like the moray, but much larger in body; this one, when a strong wind blows, grows fat, and its flesh is most sweet to eat. It is hostile to the moray and other fish, and is so strong that it tears apart the octopus with the strength of its teeth.

Pliny: the conger eel is a long fish, like the eel or moray, using the sinuous thrust of its body, making use of the sea in swimming, as a serpent does the land in crawling. The conger and the moray burn with mutual hatred, gnawing off each other's tails between them. Congers lie hidden in caves during the winter months and are not caught except in the days of summer. Fins, which are given to fish in place of feet, are two, entirely, for the long ones, like eels and congers. That the octopus gnaws its own arms is a false belief; this in fact happens to it from congers. For congers tear apart the octopus. But the lobster fears the octopus, and the conger fears the lobster; congers also crawl onto dry land.
Aesculapius, in the same place: the 'corez' is a fish that hides itself in caverns during time of rain. For while rain falls upon it and it takes it in, it is blinded and afterward dies.
Isidore: the sea-crow [corvus] is so named from the voice of its heart, since it grunts in the chest and, betrayed by its own voice, is caught.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, in the same place: fish called 'sea-crows,' when they breed, are betrayed by their own voice, since they always utter groans or grunts, and are thus caught.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'dentix,' also called 'dentrix,' or the sea-bream, has its name from the fact that it has large, many, and hard teeth, with which it is fierce against oysters and harmless fish.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'dentix' is the same as the sea-bream, of which mention will also be made below in its own place. The 'dies' is a sea fish, as Aristotle says, so named because after its full growth it lives only one day; it has, however, two fins and two feet and lacks blood.

Isidore: 'eceloa' is the name given to the pearl-bearing shell, in whose flesh the precious stone hardens. For those who have written on the nature of animals report of these that, at night, they seek the shore and conceive a pearl from the celestial dew, whence they are also named 'eceloae.'

Solinus: shellfish, at a certain time of year, wanton with conception, produce dew as if a husband, for desire of which they gape open, and when a moonlit rain especially falls, they drink in the desired moisture with a kind of yawning. Thus, then, they conceive and become pregnant, and from the quality of the nourishment the character of the pearl results. For if what they received was clear, the little spheres become white.
