But if turbid, they either languish with pallor or grow cloudy with redness, so their offspring comes more from the sky than from the sea. Finally, the more often they receive the seed of the morning air, the clearer the pearl becomes; the more often that of evening, the darker it becomes. If lightning should suddenly flash, they are spoiled by the untimely disturbance and, closing in fright, suddenly contract miscarrying defects. For either tiny gravel-like specks will form, or empty shells. This stone is soft in water, but hardens once removed. Never, however, are two found together, whence they are also called 'unions' [uniones]. Shells of this kind have such a sense that they fear their offspring being blemished. And so, when the burning sun sends forth its rays, lest the stones be darkened by too much heat, the shells sink into the depths; this foresight, however, is aided by age. For whiteness is lost with old age, and as shells grow larger, the pearl turns yellow. They also fear the ambushes of fishermen, and for this reason hide more often among the rocks. They swim in shoals, and the one most experienced among them leads the shoal, and if she is caught, the rest scatter.

Isidore: the 'echeneis,' a small, half-foot-long little fish, took its name from the fact that it holds a ship back by clinging to it. Though the winds rush and the storms rage, the ship still seems to stand rooted in the sea and not to move - not by holding it back, but only by clinging. The Latins called this fish the 'remora,' since it forces the very ships to stand still.

Pliny, book 9: ships are believed to move more slowly when the 'echeneis' clings to their keels, whence its name was given. For this reason it is also notorious for love-potions, and for delaying judgments and lawsuits - crimes it makes up for with one praise, that it checks the flow of the womb in pregnant women and holds the pregnancy to full term; yet it is not admitted as food. Mucianus says this fish is broader than the purple murex, with neither a rough mouth nor a round one, nor a beak projecting at the corners, but with a simple shell gathering itself in on either side. Trebius Niger says it is a foot long and five cubits in girth, and that it delays ships. He says too that this power of it, kept in salt, is such that, applied, it draws out gold that has fallen into the deepest wells - an immense and hidden proof, nature overcoming its own power.

Pliny, book 32: alas, human vanity, when the very beaks of ships, armed with bronze and iron for ramming, can be checked and held fast, bound, by a half-foot-long little fish: it is said to have held back the flagship of Antony as he was hurrying to go around his fleet and exhort them, until he transferred to another ship. And so Caesar's fleet passed straight through it with greater force. It also held back the ship of the emperor Gaius. And certain men, leaping from the ship, found the little fish clinging to the rudder, and showed it to Gaius, who was indignant that this was what had held him back, though he was proceeding with the service of four hundred oarsmen. Those who saw it then afterward said it was like a large slug.
Pliny, book 9, in the same: Aristotle says it has feet, the likeness of fins being thus positioned.

Aristotle: a small fish in the sea prevents a ship from moving away, by a natural power, and many men use it for many purposes, for hatred and for love. Its fins resemble feet, for indeed it has no real feet.

Ambrose: the sea urchin is a small, base, and contemptible creature in the sea; yet when it senses an approaching storm of winds, it seizes a strong stone and carries it like ballast, and drags it like an anchor, lest it be shaken by the waves, and thus, unable to free itself by its own strength, it is steadied by another's weight. By this sign sailors too take it as a mark of coming disturbance and take precautions for themselves, lest the storm catch them unprepared. It also stops the largest ships, running with full sails, in the middle of the waves, as if rooted, and it is not without the gift of the creator that so much power can be at its disposal.

Pliny, in the same place: sea urchins are of the crab kind, in which spines take the place of feet. Their way of moving is a kind of rolling. And so they are often found with their spines worn down. The eggs of all are bitter, five in number. Their mouth is in the middle of the body, turned to the ground. They are said to foresee the fierceness of the sea and to cover themselves with pebbles they have seized, steadying their mobility with weight, unwilling to wear down their spines by rolling. When sailors see this, they at once secure their ships with several anchors.
Alexander Neckam: the sea urchin, then, in the middle of the sea, gives to another a stability it cannot give to itself. For it begs from pebbles what it can abundantly bestow on ships.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the sea urchin is a small fish having spines in place of feet, like the crab, but fins under its belly, which resemble feet. In its mouth, in place of teeth, it has heavy spines. This, moreover, is wonderful beyond measure, that although it is only half a foot long, not by any violence but by clinging alone it holds back a ship two hundred feet long with all its weight inside, so that it cannot be moved even a fraction. Nor is there any other explanation for so astonishing a marvel, except that God is proclaimed wonderful in his creatures. This fish cannot be eaten, since it brings death by dissolving a man from the state of his constitution.

Dioscorides: the taste of sea urchins is good for the stomach, softens the bowels, and is diaphoretic. Their raw hide is usefully mixed into remedies for scabies. Burnt, it cleans dirty wounds, and also makes growing wounds subside.

Pliny: the sea urchin, or 'echeneis,' bound to pregnant women, holds the slipping pregnancy to full term, and so it is kept in salt. The same fish also inhibits lust. Besides, sea urchins are most beneficial against 'doricnium' poison, and for those who have drunk the juice of hemlock, especially taken in its broth. The same, with vinegar, also remove night-blisters. Sea urchins with their spines, crushed and drunk with wine, remove stones, and eaten as food benefit this in other ways too. Crushed shells of sea urchins, applied in water, resist incipient ringworm. Sea urchins, too, living, burnt and drunk in sweet wine, check discharges. Sea urchin ash, with their own flesh cremated, with oil, fills in bald patches.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, in the same place: the 'ephemeron' is a fish born without mating, and, once it has lived three hours of the day, dies.

Isidore: the 'scarus,' or 'escarus,' is so called because it alone is reported to chew the cud of its food, for other fish do not ruminate. They report, moreover, that it is clever, for, enclosed in a wicker trap, it does not burst out head-first, nor thrust its head into the hostile withies, but, turned backward, loosens the opening with repeated strikes of its tail, and so returns backward out. And if by chance another 'escarus' outside should see its struggle, it is said, seizing its tail with its mouth, to help the struggling one to escape.

Pliny: [this] fish is said to chew the cud and feed on plants, not other fish. It is most common in the Carpathian Sea. It never willingly crosses the chosen headland of the Troad. Brought from there, however, by the emperor Tiberius Claudius, Optatus Elipertius, prefect of the fleet, scattered and sowed it between the mouth of the Tiber and the shore of Campania, and for about five years care was taken that any caught be returned to the sea. Afterward it is found frequently on the shores of Italy, not caught there before.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: all fish have serrated teeth except the 'scarus,' which alone among aquatic creatures has full, flat ones; this one uses its front fins as hands, bringing food to its mouth.
Pliny, book 9, in the same: Arcadia marvels at its own 'exocoetus,' named from the fact that it comes out onto dry land for the sake of sleep.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'exox,' or salmon, is the largest fish of the Danube, so large it can scarcely be pulled on a cart by four or three horses; it has one intestine, few and small bones in its body, cartilaginous rather than solid, but is said to have many bones in its head. Its flesh, however, is said to be most sweet in taste and very similar in appearance to the flesh of a pig. Over its whole body it is smooth, and has nothing rough in its body or its habits, but is most gentle and timid. Indeed it cannot defend itself even from the smallest little fish, but is at once driven to flight. The sturgeon most readily rubs itself against this fish, for the sake of playing. The salmon, as soon as it senses this, flees from its hiding places, which it is accustomed to dig out for its own protection on the shores; but sometimes the pestering sturgeon drives the hiding salmon out and pursues it as it flees, and because both are large and cannot even hide in the deepest waters, running about and stirring up the water ahead of them, they are often caught together by fishermen. This fish, once caught, is given very strong wine or milk to drink, since, made drunk with wine, it can live for many days, and this is done so that it may be carried to distant lands for the sake of food. It drinks, however, four measures of wine before it becomes drunk.

div.head: DE FASTALEO ET FASTEN ET FICE

cit.quote: Aristotle: the 'fastaleon' is a kind of fish that alone, among all other kinds, does not eat its own kind. For all fish eat one another, except the 'fastaleon.'

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, in the book On Animals: the 'fasten' is a fish that, when it draws water tight in its mouth, makes it sweet from this. Whence smaller fish follow it into its own mouth, but it thus catches and swallows them.
Pliny, book 9: the 'ficis' is a fish that changes its color, white the rest of the time, but varied in spring. This alone among fish builds its nest from seaweed and lays its eggs in that very nest.

div.head: DE GARDONE ET GLADIO ET GLAUCO

cit.quote: Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the roach is a river fish, of most pleasant taste, similar to the 'vendesia,' but distinguished from it by the redness of its eyes. Both, however, are of moderate size.
Isidore: the swordfish is so named because it has a sharp beak, and for this reason it sinks pierced ships.

Aristotle: the 'hastarus,' that is the swordfish, is similar to the scorpion and the equal of the weever, and it causes great pain to other fish. And so they leap very often. For the dolphin too leaps because of pain, since it is pricked beneath the fin by its spine, which is called the sword.

Pliny: [a creature] the size of the weever-scorpion; this one drives its spine, repeatedly, beneath the fin of the tuna and of the one called the swordfish - even one exceeding the dolphin in size - and afflicts it with such pain that ships are often leapt over.
Isidore: the 'glaucus' is named from its color, since it is white. For the Greeks call white 'glaucon'; this one rarely appears in summer, except only in cloudy weather.
Pliny: for certain fish, unable to bear the summer heat, hide for sixty days in the middle of the hot season, like the 'glaucus' and the hake.
Aristotle: for certain fish remain in caverns in summer, like the 'glaucus,' for forty days, and are caught after the rising of the Dog Star.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the gudgeon is a small white river fish, but sprinkled with black spots. Some have said it feeds on carcasses, but this is found by fishermen to be fabulous; rather, they are said to dwell in the clearest water and to be nourished by pasture, though in food they are reckoned base and contemptible, since they are watery and least solid.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the gudgeon is a small fish of round shape, with small scales resembling silver; this one, where it has sandy waters with small pebbles for its nourishment, provides more suitable food. The 'granus' is a sea fish that, contrary to the nature of all animals, has one eye on the top of its head, with which, keeping watch above, it is always wary of ambushes.

Isidore: the 'hamio' is a rock fish, marked on its right and left sides with continuous crimson stripes and other differently colored ones, and is called 'hamio' because it is caught only by hook [hamus].

Pliny, in the same place: they call 'hamia' a fish whose growth is perceived day by day, along with the tunas; with these too the bonito enter the Black Sea in shoals toward sweeter pastures, each with its own leaders.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'hamius' is a rock fish, as Isidore says, that is, it carries a stone within; this one is quite handsome, having on both sides small stripes of continuous crimson color, but the rest of its body of varied and pleasing colors, entirely mottled like silk cloth. The sea-swallow is similar to the bird of this name; this one swims in water like a fish, in the manner of a squid, and, having wings, rises to the pleasant heights of the sky.

Isidore: the 'icinus' of the sea took its name from the land 'icinus,' which common folk call the hedgehog, whose little shell is said to be spiked with spines in the manner of chestnuts when they fall from the trees still covered. Its flesh is soft and similar to vermilion.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'icinus' is itself the sea urchin, of which mention was made above. The same also seems to be the 'echeneis,' although Isidore treats these separately, as if of two things; the same is also called 'ericius' or 'iricius' [hedgehog].

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the sea urchin is a sea fish, having its head and mouth below, as Aristotle says, and the exit of its surplus above, which is contrary to the habit of other animals. It uses spines, however, in place of feet. Its front parts are separated and its lower parts continuous; it is a horror to other fish, since it is bristling with spines, whence it does not easily become prey to any fish. Its flesh is intensely red, similar in color to vermilion, as Pliny says.

Aristotle: the sea urchin has no flesh. For indeed all hard-shelled animals have a fleshy part inside the shell, in the belly, except the sea urchin, for this one entirely lacks flesh, and this is proper to it. It has, however, black parts in its belly. And there are many kinds of this creature, among which is the kind that is eaten, in which many eggs are found. There are, however, two other kinds, which are found in the open sea and are few, and of these one kind is of large body, another of small body and many hard spines. In a certain region of Greece there is a kind of sea urchin of white shell and spine, and of eggs, which is larger than the other kinds. The edible sea urchin moves much and has a visible mark on its spine. And all kinds of sea urchins have eggs, but in some they are small and are not eaten. The sea urchin hears weakly, and less than animals having a shelled hide and walking on feet. All hard-shelled animals appear full of eggs in spring and likewise in autumn, except the edible sea urchin; this one indeed appears at any time, but especially at the full moon and in the days of heat, and this except for certain ones of a certain place, which breed only in winter and are of small body, full of eggs. There are, moreover, many distinct eggs in the belly of the sea urchin, and each is placed by itself in one membrane, and they are of black color, and small in all kinds. The sea urchin is properly hot, since a shell surrounds it. But since it is an animal having blood, it therefore feels cold greatly and needs warmth. In every kind the eggs are equal in number, an odd number, namely five. Likewise the number of teeth, likewise of bellies. And the eggs of some are larger, of some smaller. The sea urchin, moreover, is of an entirely round body, and uses its spines as other animals use feet and hands. The sea urchin's head and mouth are below, and the exit of its surplus above, namely on its back. It has, moreover, five teeth, and between them fleshy parts in place of a tongue; after that it has the opening of the stomach. Then a belly divided into five parts, full of surplus. The kind of sea urchin is continuous from its lower part. In its upper part, however, where the spine-covering is, it is separate, and it uses its spines in place of feet, and the size of the spines comes from this, that the growth of the body passes into them, because of the scarcity of natural heat. For, since the food is not digested, much surplus is generated in their bodies. Hair and similar things, however, are generated only from surplus. The hardness of the spines and their bones is like stone because of the abundance of coldness that has congealed. For this reason it happens that as land hedgehogs grow, they become very hard, similar to stone, especially in the northern region, since there are more hedgehogs of this kind there than in the southern region, and in a region of many winds more than on a plain, since they are chilled more in places of this kind, and moisture comes out from them, which, when dissolved by heat - since a hedgehog cannot exist without heat - the cold does not merely harden but thickens the body.

div.head: DE CALAO ET CARCORA ET KILOK

cit.quote: Aristotle: the 'calaos' is a sea fish, varied in appearance. Rain, which for other fish is usually a remedy for life and an aid to fattening, is given to this one for its destruction. For if there is much rain, it is blinded in its eyes, and, consequently, unable to seek food, dies of hunger. The 'carcora,' however, is a fish that, once caught, lives a long time and feeds itself from itself, since above its intestines is a certain moisture of water. The 'kilok' is a sea fish, hiding in a very rough shell, whose opening is in the middle of its body. It senses, however, whatever approaches it, and attaches itself to stones with its hind feet. With its front feet, however, which it uses as hands, it preys on whatever fish pass by it. But if something passes that it believes it cannot overcome, it swells and contracts itself and clings more firmly to the stone to which it is attached.
Isidore: the sea lion is so named from its resemblance to the land lion.
Ambrose: the lion is terrible on land, but gentle in the waves. The sea hare is a timid creature on land, but formidable in the sea, for it quickly brings corruption that cannot easily be removed.
Isidore: the hare [sea hare] is so named from its resemblance to a hare's head.
Pliny, on the sea hare: dire poisons do not cease in the Indian sea, and this creature, pestilential even to the touch, at once causes vomiting and dissolution of the stomach.

Pliny, book 32: the sea hare, given as food or drink, is poison. There is no animal that does not perish from its touch. A man touched by it smells of fish and dies, and likewise the hare dies when touched by him. Thus each is poison to the other. They affirm it cannot be caught alive in India.

Avicenna, in the fourth canon: the sea hare is venomous; if given in a drink, there follow tightness of breath, redness of the eyes, dry cough, spitting of blood, difficulty of urination, blood in the urine, violet-colored urine and stool likewise, or pain in the stomach, excessive vomiting of bile and blood, jaundice, and distress and pain of the kidneys, foul-smelling sweat, and horror of food. And when the sufferer sees fish, he is terrified of them and finds the taste of foul fish in his mouth and in belching, with a salty flavor. Many, however, who escape this fall into consumption. Goat's milk benefits its cure, which is the ultimate help. Also donkey's milk and a woman's milk from the breast, and the broth of river crab, and roasted sea urchin or its blood; strong remedies, moreover, are fresh, hot river catmint and goose blood and stale human urine and the like. The sign of health, however, is when, seeing fish, he is no longer terrified of them and eats. And when he falls into consumption, let the consumption be treated.

Avicenna, in the second canon: the sea hare is a shelled, muddy creature, inclining somewhat toward redness. Its blood is hot and cleanses ringworm. Its burnt head generates hair for baldness, especially with bear fat, and is very good for tetter. When a plaster is made from it, as it is, it removes hair and down. Likewise it clears the sight, applied as a plaster or like a collyrium. It is numbered, however, among venomous medicines and kills, causing ulceration of the lung.

Pliny: if pregnant women look upon the female sea hare, their stomachs turn and they miscarry at once. The remedy is the male, hardened for this in salt, so that it may be worn on the arm. The sea hare is indeed poisonous. But its ash restrains useless plucked eyelashes. The same hare heals scrofula, so that it is quickly removed. From a fresh sea hare, too, some order that gout be rubbed. Its blood and gall, if mixed in oil, are effective against carbuncles and gangrenous sores.
Physiologus: the sea lobster, according to Pliny, is four cubits long, is harmed in winter, grows fat in autumn and spring, and more so at full moon.

Pliny: lobsters are protected by a fragile crust. Among that kind lacking blood, they hide for five months. Likewise crabs, which are hidden for the same period. And both shed their old age at the beginning of spring, in the manner of snakes, by renewing their shells. In the waves, however, lobsters swim, floating in the manner of crawling creatures. If no fear presses upon them, they move in a straight course, their horns - which have a rounded knob at the tip - stretched to the sides and raised; in fear, they move obliquely to the sides. They fight among themselves with their horns. Alone among animals, unless boiled alive in boiling water, its flesh, being fluid, forms no firm mass. Lobsters of this kind live in rocky places. In the Indian sea, lobsters reach four cubits. The lobster fears the octopus so much that if it sees one nearby, it dies outright. The hostile conger eel also tears apart the lobster.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham: the river lobster [crayfish], contrary to the field-locust, has longer front feet, and does not ruminate in the front part, as other animals do, but toward the rear, namely at the far end of its stomach, with teeth attached to it in its belly.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the pike is a river fish with a wide mouth and very sharp teeth, a devourer of smaller fish. Yet the tench, sparing in scales and armed with very rough gills, resists it, so that it does not overpower it, nor does it become prey to its teeth. The pike, moreover, feeds on venomous things, like toads and the like, and yet is said to be wholesome food for the infirm. If ever the wicker trap in which it has been enclosed is lifted from the water and it sees the light of day, it rarely or never happens that it survives long afterward, but, having sought a way out, escapes.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the pike is a fish, as the book of things says, also called the water-wolf: this one, if it has river waters and food sufficient for its life, grows over the course of time to a very great length. Its food is fish and whatever creeps in the manner of frogs. It eats fish nearly its own size. For once it has overcome its prey, it swallows the head first with its mouth, and, once that is digested, gradually takes in what follows until it has consumed the whole. It also refuses to spare even its own kind, either from natural cruelty or because it is greedy for food and impatient of plunder. For it even pursues its own offspring, once they have taken on the form of a fish. There is, moreover, a certain fish having sharp scales and sharp fins, which, if the water-wolf seizes by the head, it quickly swallows down, but if from the tail end, it cannot, since the roughness stiffens against it in that direction. The pike carries in its brain a stone similar to crystal, but this only once it has lived a long span of years. This fish is impregnated, as Aristotle says, when the north wind blows; likewise the fish that grow to great length. The pregnant female goes up the waters as far as she can from the place where she is accustomed to dwell, and there lays her eggs, so that her own offspring will not be an obstacle to her prey. And this is because of natural cruelty, or because of jealousy over food and plunder; others have said she goes up for the sake of sweeter water, since water is always sweeter the closer it is to the spring. The pike is of such greed that, when it cannot swallow whole a fish that its own size cannot accommodate, it takes in half of it.

Isidore: the sea-bass [lupus, wolf] is named from its voracity, in which it resembles the land wolf, since it pursues others with shameless voracity. It is, moreover, a fish clever at avoiding capture. For, surrounded by a net, it is said to plough the sand with its tail and thus, buried, to pass through the net.

Pliny: the sea-bass has less cunning in taking precautions, but great strength in fighting back once caught. For once it is stuck on a hook, by a violent thrashing about it loosens the wound, until the hook falls out.

Pliny, book 9, in the same: all fish feel the very cold of winter, but especially those thought to have a stone in their head, like the sea-bass and the sea-bream. And when winters are harsh, many blind ones are caught. Of sea-basses, the most praised are those called 'woolly,' for the whiteness and softness of their flesh. Sea-basses are better in a rich river between two bridges than elsewhere. The sea-bass lays eggs twice a year. Nigidius is the authority that the sea-bass gnaws off the grey mullet's tail, and that they are on friendly terms during the summer months.
Pliny, book 10, in the same: it is reported, as said, that the grey mullet and the sea-bass hear most clearly, and so live in shallow water.
Pliny, book 32, in the same: Ovid too reports that the sea-bass, surrounded by a net, ploughs the sand with its tail and thus, buried, passes through the net.
Aristotle: sea-basses, when they enter the open sea, afterward return and rise to the surface with great speed, like the dolphin. But all sea-basses of great body pant, drawing in air.
Ambrose: sea-wolves, then, are gentle in the sea, whom the lamb does not know to fear. And according to Isaiah, wolves and lambs graze together.

div.head: DE MEGARE ET MILAGINE ET MILVO

cit.quote: Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'megaris' is a sea fish two palms long. It is held cheap in the regions where it is caught, but when salted and taken to more distant places, its rarity makes its price. Yet, freshly caught and unsalted, it makes more delicate fare for those eating it. It is said, however, to be harmful, especially to those with fever. Whence the poet says: and the megaris will be harmful to all.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, in the same place: when the young of the flying fish fly, it is a sign of a coming storm at sea.
Isidore: the 'milago' is a fish so named because it flies above the water. And as often as it is seen flying outside the water, it signals a change of weather.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the flying fish flies above the waves as a sign of joy, that the storm has ceased: this contrary to the habit of other fish and sea monsters, which appear to play, as it were, on the surface of the water when a storm is rising.

Pliny, book 9: the 'milvus' [kite-fish], so named by inference, gleams by night in calm weather like a lantern, its fiery tongue thrust out through its mouth. It raises from the sea horns of about a foot and a half, from which it took its name.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, in the same place: when the 'milvus' fish is pregnant, the sight of it stuns and clouds a man's vision, and provokes lust in the one who sees it.

Isidore: the grey mullet [mugilis] has its name from the fact that it is very agile [multum agilis]. For when it senses the fishermen's ambush prepared, turning back at once, it leaps over the net so that you would see the fish as if flying.

Pliny: the mullet's nature is laughable in its fear, believing itself entirely hidden with its head concealed. Yet the same fish has such skill that, in Phoenicia and in the Narbonensian province, at mating time, a male is released from the fishponds into the sea with a long line tied through his mouth to his gills, and, drawn back by that same line, the females follow him to the shore, and again, at breeding time, the males follow a female. In the Narbonensian province, in the territory of Nemausus, in a lagoon called Laterna, men fish for mullet in partnership with dolphins. For the people, from the shore, rouse one another with as much shouting as possible to the spectacle to come, whose calls the dolphins quickly heed, the north wind carrying the voice further, but the south wind bringing it back more slowly against itself. And then, too, unexpectedly, a battle line flies to their aid, which quickly appears and is at once arranged in the place where the fight against the mullet has been joined; they block them off from the deep and drive the frightened fish into the shallows. Then the fishermen surround them with nets and lift them with forks. Yet the speed of the mullet leaps over these nonetheless. But the dolphins catch them and, content for the present with having killed, put off eating until after the victory. The mullet and the sea-bass burn with mutual hatred. According to Nigidius, the sea-bass gnaws off the mullet's tail, and they are on friendly terms during the summer months. Mullets, fearing the force of other fish, leap over ships, and are of such remarkable speed that they sometimes leap clear over passing vessels.
Pliny, book 10, in the same: it is reported, moreover, that the mullet and the sea-bass hear most clearly, and so live in shallow water.
Pliny, in the same: the mullet knows there is a hook in the bait and is not ignorant of the trap, yet such is its greed that it knocks the food off with a blow of its tail.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba: the mullet is a most swift fish in river waters, but naturally careless. For its foolishness is mocked, since, in fear, with its head hidden, it believes its whole body is hidden and safe. This fish is hostile to the pike only in winter, and the reason for this is believed to be that food is then scarce, for which they fight. In summer, however, they have abundance, and so are then brought back to concord.
Pliny, book 32: ash from the head of mullets and mules frees sciatica sufferers.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the octopus is a sea fish, taking its name from the matter itself [many-footed]; its feet extend from its side; it mates in winter, and, alone among other fish, builds itself a nest from twigs; it lays eggs over two months, and this only one egg, small, the size of a nut; the female sits for forty nights and warms the egg she has produced, from which countless fish are made. Were this not so, their kind would greatly decrease, since they consume one another and are of much eating. The octopus overcomes, by cunning and even more by strength, the crayfish, a sea monster that is strong and robust. The sign of its victory is this: for when they are found caught together in a net, the crayfish is frequently found dead or fatally wounded. There is also a certain kind of octopus, naturally cunning, which swims on the surface of the water and places the shell of its back in the sun, so that it may dry out and become harder, so as to be able to withstand the salt waters of the sea and the harshness of the rocks.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the octopus is itself the 'polypus' according to Pliny, of which more will be said fully below, where sea monsters are discussed.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the red mullet is a sea fish, as Pliny says, of modest size, of great nobility, given for food only to nobles. It is, however, most rare, and only the northern ocean produces it. There are, however, several kinds of these. Some feed on seaweed and oysters and mud and the flesh of other fish. The nobler ones, however, are marked with a double beard on the lower lip. Their food is whatever has formed along the banks in the calm of the air. The nobles of gluttony relate that a noble mullet dying is a spectacle to behold, with a numerous variety of colors.

Seneca, in the Natural Questions, book 7: incredible, as already said above, are the works of luxury; fish swim in the bedchamber, and are caught right under the table, to be transferred straight onto it. A red mullet seems hardly fresh unless it dies in the guest's own hand. The color of the dying is watched, which death itself, as the breath struggles, turns through many changes. Redness first, then pallor spreads over it - a long, sleepy expectation of idle luxury. They refuse to touch one unless caught that very day, one that, as they say, still tastes of the sea itself: and so it is rushed in at a run. And so a path is cleared for the porters hastening with panting and shouting, and men run to the mullet's death. To what has delicacy come? We used to hear that nothing was better than a rock-mullet. And now we have heard that nothing is more beautiful than one dying. Give me, one says, a glass vessel in my hands, in which the mullet may leap and quiver. See how its redness, sharper than any vermilion, blazes up, see what veins it drives through its sides. And so these men are not content with the tavern's fare in teeth, mouth, and belly, but are gluttonous in their eyes. For they feed their eyes before their gullet.

Pliny: red mullets, like the mullet, feed on seaweed and oysters and mud and the flesh of other fish, and are marked with a double beard on the lower lip. The cheapest kind of these they call the 'mud-dweller.' This one is always accompanied by another fish named the sargus, which devours the food stirred up as the mullet digs through the mire. They think this fish's name, 'fenestella,' comes from the color of soft slippers. They spawn three times a year. In these, at least, spawning appears that often. The nobles of gluttony relate that the dying mullet is a spectacle to behold, with a certain many-colored and numerous variety, its reddish scales fading through manifold change, especially if observed enclosed in glass. Licinius Mucianus reported a mullet of eighty pounds caught in the Red Sea - such is the market found with luxury on the shores near the city - and this is nature's way, that elsewhere other fish hold first place.
Pliny, book 32, in the same: the mullet becomes more tender at the touch of the sea hare, and becomes more pleasant and useful.

Isidore: the mullet [mullus] is so named because it becomes soft [mollis] and most tender; they report that its food inhibits lust and dulls the keenness of the eyes, and that men who often feed on it smell of fish. If a mullet is killed in wine, those who drink from it afterward acquire a distaste for wine.
Alexander Neckam: the mullet delights in human dung, so much so that it lies in it, and the fish's flesh borrows its color from the dung.

Pliny: the mullet is beneficial against stingrays and land or sea scorpions and dragon-fish and venomous spiders, applied or eaten as food. And the ash of a fresh one's head is effective against all poisons and especially against mushrooms. Again, ground ash from the heads of mullets frees sciatica sufferers. They are burnt, however, in an earthen vessel and are said to be applied with honey. I find, however, that mullets are harmful to the sinews as food. Their food, too, is reported to dull the keenness of the eyes. In women's menstrual troubles, however, the mullet helps. Aged mullets, crushed and taken in a drink, provoke vomiting. Ash of salted mullets disperses carbuncles. A mullet killed in wine, as said, brings on a distaste for wine in those who drink it afterward.

Isidore: the Greeks call the moray 'myrena' because it coils itself into circles; this is said to be of female sex only, and to conceive by a serpent. For this reason it is called out from the water by fishermen with a hiss, as if by a serpent, and caught. It is killed with difficulty by a blow of a club, but at once by a rod; it is certain that it has its life in its tail. For struck on the head it is scarcely killed, but on the tail it dies at once.

Pliny: the moray is a long fish, covered with soft skin; it hides in winter and is not caught except in the days of summer, like the conger and all rock fish. It comes out onto land, like the octopus; the weasel is its rival. Some fish are given fins in place of feet, some have none, like morays, which also lack gills. These make use of the sea by the sinuous thrust of their bodies, as serpents do the land. On dry ground, too, they crawl. The moray lays eggs in any month, whereas other fish lay at a fixed time. Its eggs grow with the greatest speed. When they slip out onto a dry shore, common people think they are filled by mating with serpents. Aristotle calls the male, which fathers them, the 'zimirus.' The difference is said to be that the moray is variegated and weak, the 'zimirus' of a single color and robust, and has teeth outside its mouth. They say that at the taste of vinegar these creatures are especially driven into a rage. Documented proofs of cruelty have been found in this creature. Vedius Pollio, a Roman knight and friend of the deified Augustus, used to plunge condemned slaves into his fishponds of these, not because the wild beasts of the land were insufficient for this purpose, but because he could not otherwise witness a man being entirely torn apart at once.

Pliny, book 32: Pythiatius reports that a moray, once caught on a hook, turns itself and cuts through the line with the serrated spine it has on its back. Licinius Macer reports that morays are of female sex only and conceive from serpents, and for this reason are called out by fishermen with a hiss, as if they were serpents, and caught.

Pliny: the first to devise dishes of morays was Tyrus, who served a thousand morays at a single triumphal banquet. For he was unwilling to exchange them for a price or other goods. In northern Gaul, all morays have on the right jaw seven spots, gleaming golden in the shape of the constellation of the north, only while alive; they are extinguished together with life. Their hide is very thin, whereas that of eels, on the contrary, is thicker. [A certain kind of octopus, named for its foul head odor], is for this reason especially hunted by morays. Likewise the moray is better in Sicily than elsewhere. Its eggs grow in the sea with the greatest speed. The conger and the moray burn with mutual hatred, gnawing off each other's tails between them.
Pliny, book 32, in the same: a moray caught in a net seeks out the meshes and, with the manifold bending of its slippery back, loosens the net until it escapes, as Ovid reports.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis: morays, as Pliny says, gladly keep themselves among reeds and branches, so that, if by chance they are enclosed in a net, they may escape by manifold twisting; these have a venomous bite, but the bite is healed by the ash of their own heads. It is dangerous to take them as food unless they are first very well and very long cooked in wine and seasoned with aromatic spices, especially pepper, for they abound in venomous moisture, whence they also do not easily submit to cooking. Likewise, according to Basil, the viper calls the moray out from the waters onto dry land for mating.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, in the same place: the moray conceives not from one of its own kind, but from a serpent called out by a hiss onto dry land, and yet produces offspring resembling not the serpent at all, but itself.

Ambrose: the viper indeed calls the moray from the sea to the shore with a hiss, and vows away its venom; the moray comes at once and mates with it. And afterward the viper takes back its venom. Otherwise the moray, which they say has something harmful, is a more precious dish.
Pliny: the bite of a moray is healed by the ash of its own head; moray's ash, with three obols of honey, also dissolves lichen-sores and leprosy.

Isidore: the murex is a sea-snail, named from its sharpness and roughness, which by another name is called the 'conchylium,' since, cut open with iron, it emits tears of purple color, from which purple dye is made, and hence it is called 'ostrum,' since this dye is drawn out from the moisture of the shell. Mucianus, however, reports the murex to be the same as the 'echineus,' of which mention was made above.

Pliny: murices are sea shellfish, which hide around the rising of the Dog Star for thirty days and come out at the appointed time; they have in the middle of their throat a precious liquid useful for dyeing garments. But this color is found only in a single white vein. The rest of the body, however, is barren. This color, too, is drawn out only from the living, since dying they vomit up the dye along with their life; they have neither a spherical mouth nor a round one, nor a beak projecting at the corners, but close on both sides in the manner of a shell.
Pliny: murices, or purple-fish, form from a more sluggish saliva, like slime and the foam of the sea, as it warms up once rain has fallen, and these breed in spring.

Pliny, book 32, in the same: the ash of murex shells, mixed with honey, is usefully applied to ulcers of the head. The same ash is also a good tooth-powder and clears blemishes on women's faces, applied with honey, and, applied for seven days, smooths wrinkling skin, provided that on the eighth day it is soothed with egg white. The same, with oil, is effective against parotid swellings and scrofula. And it resists ringworm in both ways, whether it is needed to disperse incipient cases or discharge developed ones. Likewise murex ash with oil removes swellings. And the ash of these shells with honey effectively heals women's breasts.

div.head: DE MURE AC MUSCULO ET MUSTELA

cit.quote: Pliny: the sea-mouse comes out onto land and, digging a pit there, lays its eggs and again covers them with earth. After thirty days, however, returning, it opens the pit again and leads its young into the water. The young of these lack sight at first, as do the young of almost all aquatic creatures.

Isidore: the 'musculus' is so named because it is the male of the whale. For by mating with it this beast is said to conceive. There are, moreover, 'musculi,' small mollusks, by whose milt oysters conceive.

Pliny: [the] pilot-fish and the whale. When the whale's eyes are sometimes overwhelmed by the excessive weight of its eyebrows, this fish, swimming ahead, shows it shoals dangerous by their size, and performs the office of eyes for it.
Pliny: the sea-'musculus,' which precedes the whale, has no teeth, but bristles instead, inside, for which reason it is also said to be called the 'shaggy' one.
Pliny, in the same book: weasel-fish are counted among table fish; among the Alps, Lake Constance produces these, rivals of morays.

Aristotle: the weasel-fish, like the dolphin and the seal, bring forth living young from their own body, and when they have given birth, if they sense anyone attempting an ambush against their young, they defend them. They suppress the fear of their tender age with a mother's affection, and open their mouths and hold their young suspended with a harmless tooth. They are also said to receive them into the interior of their body and hide them in the womb, until they can bring them to safety, or defend them by the interposition of their own body.

div.head: DE NARCO ET NAUTILO ET NUBE

cit.quote: Aristotle: this fish, on Aristotle's testimony, is of such power that, through the mediation of the line and rod, numbness and insensibility reach the hand of the fisherman holding the hook. Indeed the whole body grows numb, unless he casts down the hook quickly. Hence it is that the poppy and other such things are also called 'narcotic.'

Pliny, book 9: the nautilus, which others call the 'pompilus,' is counted among the chief marvels of the sea. For, lying on its back, it rises to the surface of the water, raising itself gradually so that, once all the water is expelled through its siphon, it swims easily as if lightened of ballast. Afterward, twisting back its first two arms, it stretches between them a membrane of marvelous fineness, with which, sailing before the winds, and rowing itself along with its remaining arms, steering itself with the middle of its tail as with a rudder, it thus goes forth, delighting in its resemblance to light warships; if any fear should intervene, it submerges itself, having taken in water.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'nubes,' according to Aristotle, is a fish, living in water attached to a rock, from which it does not depart or separate, unless compelled by the attraction of an inward pull.
Isidore: the sunfish [orbis] is so named from its shape, namely because it is round and consists entirely of a head.
Pliny: [of] fish, the one called the sunfish is round and without scales.

Isidore: the oyster [ostrea] is so named from the shells [testis] by which the softness of the inner flesh is protected. For the Greeks call the shell 'ostreum'; the oyster, however, is neuter in Latin, its flesh feminine. There is, moreover, in the oyster a most precious pearl naturally embedded, which is hardened in it by seawater. This is even difficult to find among kings, and yet, lying as if worthless on the shores, is gathered by common folk from rough rocks and cliffs.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: the oyster, as Ambrose and Isidore say, sometimes opens its shell, to glory in the delights of a milder breeze. But the crab lays sudden ambushes for it and throws a stone into its shell, so that it cannot close it, and thus gnaws away the oyster's flesh. The oyster indeed, lying on dry land or in a dry place, already opens its shell, as if at home, at the time the tide returns.

Pliny: it must be admitted that no sense is present in creatures enclosed in a stony shell, like oysters; they arise from putrefying mud and foam, around ships that stand for a long time and fixed stakes and wood. It has recently been discovered that a fertile fluid flows from these, in the manner of milk.

Pliny, book 10, in the same: that hearing is present in sea oysters is not likely, but they are said to submerge themselves at a sound. The sense of touch, indeed, is present in all creatures, even in those that have no other sense. For in oysters, too, and in earthworms, whence I would judge the sense of taste to be present in all.
Pliny, in the same: oysters, indeed, have no eyes at all; certain shellfish have them, but doubtfully.

Pliny, book 32, in the same: oysters delight in fresh waters and where many rivers flow in. They are born, however, also in rocky places lacking the influx of fresh water. They grow large by the influence of the stars around the beginning of summer, pregnant with much milt and lying hidden, and where the sun penetrates to the shallows. This seems to be the reason why smaller ones are found in other places, for shade prevents growth, and in gloom they desire food less. They vary in body: in Spain reddish, in Illyria dark; black both in flesh and shell, especially those of Circei; in whatever nation, wherever they are found, they are thick, and not slippery from their own saliva, to be judged rather by thickness than by breadth; caught neither in mud nor sandy ground, but on a solid bottom. They also delight in travel and in being transferred to unfamiliar waters; in the Indian sea, oysters a foot long are found.

Pliny, book 32, in the same: oysters are especially opposed to the poisons of the sea hare, and to them is given the palm among the dishes of the wealthy; they alone restore the stomach, and cure loss of appetite. And luxury adds cold, mixing the peaks of mountains, buried in snow, with the depths of the sea. They gently soften the bowels and, cooked in honeyed wine, free one from tenesmus that is without ulceration. They also cleanse ulcers of the bladder. Cooked in their own shells just as they came, closed, they are marvelously beneficial for discharges. The ash of their shells calms the uvula and the tonsils, mixed with honey. In the same way, parotid swellings, ringworm and hardness of the breasts, ulcers of the head, with water. It smooths the skin of women, however. It is also sprinkled on burns and is pleasing as a tooth-powder. It treats itching and eruptions of phlegm with vinegar. Raw oysters, if pounded, heal scrofula and chilblains of the feet.
Aristotle: there is, moreover, a fish of the oyster kind, that is of hard shell, which swims and crawls with its tail.

Dioscorides: purple oysters, from which purple dye is made, are shellfish which, when burnt, have a drying power, and are similar in power to other shellfish. For I too have used them for rheumatic and long-lasting wounds, and those that are hard to fill with new flesh, and hollow and very deep ones, applying them burnt with old fat.

div.head: DE PAGRO, PAVO, PECTINE ET PERCA

cit.quote: Isidore: the sea-bream [pagrus] is a fish that the Greeks call 'phagrus' for this reason, that it has hard teeth, such that it feeds on oysters in the sea.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the sea-bream is itself the 'dentix,' of which mention was made above.

Pliny, book 9, in the same: indeed all fish feel the very cold of winter, but especially those thought to have a stone in their head, like the sea-bass and the sea-bream. And when winters are harsh, many of them are caught blind, as has already been said above of the sea-bass.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the sea-peacock is so named from the peacock bird, since it resembles it in its colors. For it is painted with varied color on its back and neck. Sea-scallops are armed with claws, and shine in the dark like fires. In great cold and great heat they hide away, since they need temperate air to live, since their claws cannot endure the excess of extremes among the elements.
Aristotle: of the sea creature called the scallop, if anything approaches its feet, it suddenly closes its eye.
Pliny: scallops arise spontaneously in sandy ground.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the perch is a river fish of varied color, most swift in its course, armed with scales and fins that are sharp and very rough, with which it also defends itself against larger fish, so that predators do not attack it: beyond other river and pond fish it is especially suited as food for the infirm.
Alexander Neckam: the perch, seeing the pike threatening it, bristles with its fins and thus escapes.

Pliny: the 'pinna' is a fish of the shellfish kind, born in muddy places, always standing upright, and never without a companion, which they call the 'pinnotheres.' Others call it the 'pinnophylax,' that is a small pig-fish, in some places a crab, an attendant at its table. It opens itself with its light-organs, an eyeless body, offering shelter inside to tiny fish. Others at once rush in, and where boldness has grown from license, they fill it. But it, closing its mouth, examines whatever it has enclosed, and gives a share to its companion. Which makes me marvel all the more that some have thought no sense is present in aquatic creatures.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'pinna' is of the shellfish kind and has a round body. Male and female walk together in company. The 'pinna' opens its shells to the moon and offers itself to small fish as if dead. These, at once exulting - where, as said, license has grown into boldness - fill its shells. But then, sensing itself full, the 'pinna' kills whatever it has caught and enclosed.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: a fish known and common among us, flat, that is, and two-colored. For on one side white, on the other black, of which, as of many others, I have found nothing in the aforementioned authors, unless perhaps they are called by other names among them than among us.

Isidore: the sea-pig, also called the 'suillus,' is so named because, while seeking its food, it digs the ground beneath the water in the manner of a pig. For it has the opening of its mouth near its throat, and unless it plunges its snout into the sand, it cannot gather its food.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the sea-pig is an edible fish, similar in great part to the land pig. For it has a very similar head, and members in its body and ribs arranged in a similar way. Almost its whole flesh turns to fat. Its tongue is free, like a pig's, but they differ in voice. It has its mouth's opening near its throat, and, digging on the sea floor, seeks its food there. On its back are certain spines, having a most potent venom, and causing great torment with their stings. But their gall is a remedy for the stings.
Pliny, in book 32: among the poisonous fish are the sea-pigs, whose spines on the back cause great torment to those injured. The remedy, however, is mud from the rest of these fishes' own bodies.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the stickleback [pungitivus] is the smallest of almost all fish, stinging with certain spines according to its name. Among these the male is red around the gills, but the female lacks that redness. Both, however, are bare of spots. Common folk believe these little fish grow in the water without seed. And, more remarkable still, that other fish too are propagated from their seed, whence they also call this fish the mother of fish. For they say that if a new pond is made and no fish is put into it, these little fish are found in it in the first year, and in the second year a different kind of fish is propagated from these same ones.

Pliny, book 9: the purple-fish has that flower sought for dyeing garments in the middle of its throat; this liquid is quite small, in a white vein, whence it is drawn out precious, gleaming with the color of a darkening rose beneath. The rest of the body is barren. Purple-fish live for the most part seven years. They hide, like murices, around the rising of the Dog Star for thirty days. By mutual rubbing they exude a certain waxy stickiness, like murices too. Fishermen strive to catch purple-fish alive, since they vomit out that dye along with their life, and from the larger shells they remove it by pulling the shell off; the smaller ones, however, they crush with their shells, and thus at last the Tyrians collect that dew. The purple-fish's tongue, a finger's length, with which it feeds by boring through other shellfish, is of such hardness in its point. They are killed by fresh water, and if ever plunged into a river; otherwise, once caught, they live for as long as fifty days on their own saliva. All shellfish grow with the greatest speed, especially purple-fish, reaching full size in a year. Purple-fish, however, are caught with small and sparse woven baskets like traps, cast into the deep. There is bait in these: closing, biting shellfish such as we see, half-dead ones, but, returned to the sea, reviving with a greedy gaping. Purple-fish seek these out and attack them with extended tongues, but the bait, its point provoked, closes and compresses itself, biting down. Thus, hanging on by their own greed, the purple-fish are lifted out, and the aforesaid vein is removed - the highest praise being for a color like congealed blood in appearance, blackish, yet gleaming when held up to view. Of shellfish, purple-fish and the true 'conchylia' are of the same material, but differ in their tempering. There are two kinds: the smaller shell is called the 'buccinum,' from its resemblance to the trumpet [buccina] by which sound is produced; the other is called the purple-fish, its beak projecting like a little dog's snout, with the snout's side folded inward, from which the tongue is put forth; for this reason it is raised up to a whorl with spines set in a circle, about seven of them, which are not found in the 'buccinum.' But both have as many whorls as they have years. The 'buccinum' clings only to rocks and is gathered around cliffs; purple-fish are called by another name, 'pelagiae' [of the deep sea]. There are several kinds of these, distinguished by their food and habitat: the 'lucense,' fed on rotting flax, and the 'algense,' on both; better is the 'teniense,' gathered on the shore of the Tenian sea. This one, too, however, is lighter and clearer still. The 'calculose' is named from the pebbly sea-bottom, wonderfully suited to true 'conchylia' and by far the best for purple-fish. The 'dilutense,' that is, fed on varied ground. The one nourished on seaweed is the cheapest. It is most useful to catch purple-fish after the rising of the Dog Star, or before spring, since once they have bred they have discharges. And the strength of the dye is greater the fresher it is. Those of harder shell, like murices and purple-fish, produce their stickiness as the foam of the sea warms with the coming of rain. Likewise purple-fish adorn the banquets of kings, and dye their garments. It belongs to the waters, then, what is adored in kings, and of the waters is that hue which shines in garments.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: sea shellfish, which gather in springtime and, when rubbed, exude with their mouth the liquid they hold in the middle of their throat. The shells of these creatures reach full size within a year; if before this, in growing, they exceed it, they lose the power of mating and can no longer breed, so as to produce the precious dye in due season. Whence with the greatest care their shells are removed or broken in the first year, to prevent their growing further. With this liquid purple cloth is customarily dyed, a color that gleams beneath like a darkening rose. Purple-fish, according to Pliny, are caught by foul-smelling baits, and, when half-dead, revive once returned to the sea.

Pliny: the ash of purple-fish shell, mixed usefully with honey, is applied to ulcers of the head. The same ash with honey also effectively heals women's breasts; it also resists ringworm in both ways, whether used to disperse incipient cases or to discharge developed ones. The smaller kinds of purple-fish or murices are more effective, and preserve the freshness of the breath.

Dioscorides: the purple-fish, also called the sea 'blatta,' since it appears like a small blood-red bloom; its power is drying, whence it purges and heals putrid ulcers of the gums when reduced to powder and applied. And if bad flesh has grown up over them, the powder applied consumes it and roots it out; the burnt claws too do the same. The same claws and the white covering of the shellfish, fumigated, have the smell of castoreum, and by their fumigation free those laboring under suffocation of the womb, cure epileptics; drunk, they move the bowels. The shellfish itself, burnt, is known to do all the things said above.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the ray, called 'rais' in French, is a sea fish reckoned among the noble fish, yet quite cheap where fish are abundant; it is nearly round. It has horrible eyes. Its mouth, too, is discolored and misshapen, and this not in the place other fish have it, but toward the belly; where its head and eyes are, it has no mouth. It has a very long tail, like a snake's, and on it certain very sharp little spines. It sometimes has a stone in its head too, and we do not believe that nature created it in vain. Its flesh is indigestible, like beef. It grows fat, as Aristotle says, when the south wind blows.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba: there is, moreover, a fish called 'raha,' a numbing one, so that when it is carried in a net, its numbing power reaches the hand that carries it. This one hides in sand and mud, and hunts whatever fish come near it, since it numbs them so that they cannot move, and it then follows and eats them.
Ambrose: the frog, repulsive in the marshes, is beautiful in the waters, in which it excels almost all the elements.

Aristotle: the sea-frog has fins, like all the rest whose end tapers to narrowness. It also has gills inclining to one side, rough, similar to spines, and has a covering. In frogs the female is larger, as in other egg-laying creatures, like lizards and serpents. The sea-frog has, above its eyes, parts hanging down like hairs, having round tips, which nature has prepared for it for the sake of food. For when the frog stirs up something watery with mud and sand, then it raises those parts that are like hairs, and entangles small fish with them and draws them with these to its mouth, and thus eats. And if it does not hunt by means of those parts above its eyes, when caught it is found weak and sickly. Among those that hide is the frog too: and when it has hidden, it goes to the green area above the water and feeds on the small fish that are there: the frog is of continuous breeding and lays, besides, only one complete egg outside. And it is of hard shell, for the safety it needs on the outside: the reason for this is the nature of its body, since its head is manifold in size compared to its body and is spiny. And so it does not receive its young at the last. All fish, however, nourish their young, except the frog.

Pliny: the frog, like certain other sea creatures, has cartilage instead of a spine. In mating, the male comes over the female's front fins and grasps her hindquarters with his hind ones, as the tortoise does. Different kinds of fish do not mate together, except the angel-shark and the frog, from which is born a fish similar in its front part to the frog. Nor is the cunning of the frog small, which in the sea is called the 'fisher.' For it puts forth little horns projecting beneath its eyes, stirring the mud, drawing small fish that dart at them, until they come so close that it leaps upon them.

Pliny, book 32, in the same: the juice of sea frogs boiled in wine and vinegar is drunk against poisons and against the venom of the toad. Frog fat, dripped into the ears, at once removes pain. Frogs, too, are boiled singly in vinegar, so that the teeth may be rinsed with it and the juice held in the mouth. Some also steep the bodies of two frogs, feet cut off, in wine, and prescribe rinsing loose teeth with it. All these remedies, however, are more effective from the sea frog. A little bone from the tail of the sea frog is effective for scrofula, so that it does not wound. And this must be done daily, until the cure is complete.

Avicenna, in the third canon: the red sea frog, as the wise have reported, is malicious, attacking animals. For it leaps at them from a distance, to bite, and if it cannot bite, it blows a harmful breath at them. From its bite a great abscess and swift ruin follow. Its treatment is with great theriac and remedies of its own kind.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the red sea frog is venomous, and from drinking [a preparation of] it follow discoloration of the complexion and abscesses of the body and many other troubles.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: more will be said fully about the kinds of frogs below, in the treatise on worms.

Pliny: the turbot is a flat fish, like the flounder and the sole: these differ from flounders only in the position of their bodies. This one lies on its right side turned back, the flounder on its left.
Pliny, in the same: turbot flesh, crushed and given in honeyed water, benefits those with fever.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the turbot is a large, strong, and cunning fish, but slow. This fish too, like the sea-frog, preys in a similar way. For, hidden in stirred-up mud, it moves its exposed fins, and, wherever it sees fish approach, at once seizes and devours them. Proof of its cunning is this, that although it is the slowest of all fish, the mullet, the swiftest, is very often found in its belly.

Physiologus: the salmon is so called from its leaping: for it folds its tail back with its mouth and bends it, holding it firmly in its mouth, until, by the agility of its leap, it climbs even a steep place. But it is worth little in color or taste before it has tasted the sea. Heading toward it, against the river's current, it does not give up its purpose until it is refreshed, then returns to its familiar dwelling.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the salmon is a fish that grows to great length and breadth. It is also strong in power, but heavy and weighty, and all the agility it has comes from the power of its strength rather than from lightness of body: this fish, as Pliny says, was once preferred to all river fish, especially in Aquitaine. Its flesh is red, and although very sweet and pleasant, it brings on satiety quickly in those who eat it. This fish breeds and cannot live long in the fresh waters of ponds unless it has free passage to the fresh waters of rivers. Indeed, where it finds in its passage a weir or some such obstacle, it joins its head to its tail and, its body bent, flies through to its desired goal. It does the very same thing, too, when it senses itself caught in a net. The saupe is a foul and worthless fish. It presents this marvel of itself, that it can never be cooked unless first vigorously beaten with a club or rod.
Pliny: sea centipedes, similar to land ones, which they call centipedes, once they have swallowed a hook, vomit out all their innards, until they expel the hook: then they swallow them back in.

Isidore: the scorpion is so named because it harms [ledit] when picked up by hand. They report, moreover, that if ten crabs are bound with a bunch of basil, all the scorpions in the vicinity gather to that spot.
Aristotle: the sea scorpion lays eggs abundantly in spring, and again in autumn.
Pliny: dead crabs are transformed into scorpions on dry land.
Pliny, book 20, in the same: mint juice is taken against sea scorpions.

Pliny, in the same: the mullet too, applied or eaten as food, is taken and helps against sea scorpions. The sea scorpion's gall, moreover, fills in bald patches. Gall of the red sea scorpion with old oil or Attic honey disperses incipient cataracts. And again, gall of the sea scorpion removes scars. A sea scorpion, killed in wine and drunk to the weight of an obol, heals ailments of the bladder and stones. Likewise the stone found in the tail of the sea scorpion. When the sun is in Cancer, serpents are tormented by the stings of scorpions. The flesh of river snails, raw or cooked, resists the stings of scorpions. Some, for this reason, also keep them salted and apply them to the wounds themselves.
Dioscorides: sea scorpions purge bile, clear effusions of the eyes, remove dimness and cataracts.
Dioscorides, on the sea scorpion: its gall has great power, and is first among the galls of four-footed creatures; it works for effusion of the eyes and for dimness and roughness of the eyelids.
Avicenna, in the second canon: white lead, rubbed on the sting of a sea scorpion, is beneficial.

Avicenna: from the sea scorpion follow swelling of the belly and a dropsical appearance, and sometimes an involuntary passing of gas. Its treatment is the treatment for the sea-dragon and small venomous reptiles.

Isidore: the cuttlefish is so named because, shut in by hedges [sepes], it is more easily caught: in mating it is an obscene kind, for it conceives by mouth, like the viper: the power of its ink is so great that, added to a lamp, some report that Ethiopians appear to be seen, once the earlier light is removed.

Pliny: the cuttlefish is a fish of the soft-bodied, bloodless kind, whose head is between its foot and its belly; all have eight small feet. The cuttlefish and the squid have two feet among these that are the longest and roughest, with which they bring food to their mouths and steady themselves in the waves as if with anchors. The rest are short, and used for hunting. Cuttlefish mate by joining their tongues together, arranging their arms and swimming in opposite directions, and give birth through the mouth. The cuttlefish lays eggs in every month. Its eggs, held together by the glue of its ink, resemble a bunch of grapes. The male follows after them with his breath, otherwise they become sterile. It lays on land among reeds, or wherever seaweed has grown, and hatches them on the fifteenth day. Cuttlefish have neither bones nor spine. Burnt, its smell often draws fish, and for this reason it is placed in wicker traps, so they may be caught by it. Trebius says that on the shore of Carteia there are cuttlefish two cubits long. Nor do they live beyond two years. Among the male cuttlefish, they are varied and darker and of greater steadfastness; these, when the female is struck by a trident, come to her aid. But the female flees when the male is struck. Both, however, once they sense they are seized, hide themselves by discharging the ink that serves them in place of blood, darkening the water.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the cuttlefish conceives by mouth, like the viper too. Its eggs are hard; they do not swim in the sea except paired, male and female. They lay at every season and complete their eggs within forty nights; when the female lays, the male follows her and breathes his seed over the eggs, so that they may be brought to life.

Aristotle: the cuttlefish has a member placed beneath its mouth, called the 'mastim,' in which there is much semen, and when fear occurs, it ejects this into the water and clouds it. It also has, within itself, two vessels full of eggs, white in color, resembling hail. The bodies of the males, however, are rougher than those of the females. The chick cuttlefish is continuous with the egg at the front part of the body. Nor can it be otherwise, for the front and rear parts meet in the same place.

Dioscorides: the cuttlefish, cooked with its own ink, is bad for the stomach, but softens the bowels. What is soft of its bone is necessarily mixed into eye-salves for correcting the eyes. Likewise its crushed bones remove roughness from the teeth and restore full color to blemished flesh. They cure cataracts of men or animals in the eyes when blown in, especially with salt. Likewise its bone, ground and drunk with water, is entirely beneficial for ailments of the chest and for asthmatics.

Pliny: swelling and redness of the eyes are healed by the skin of the cuttlefish smeared with woman's milk, and by itself it corrects roughness. The ash of the same skin heals scars of the eyes and corrects white spots in beasts of burden. Cuttlefish loosen the bowels as food, and their shells, in the water used for salted fish, draw out embedded things stuck in the body. They also heal freckles and other blemishes with the burnt bones of cuttlefish. And so the ash removes excess flesh and moist ulcers.

Platearius: the bone of the cuttlefish, found in its belly, is effective for whitening teeth if rubbed with its fine powder placed in a linen cloth. Its powder is also mixed with citron ointment for whitening the face.

Isidore: the sponge is so named from 'fingere,' that is, to polish or wipe: whence Cicero: and blood was wiped [fingebatur] with sponges, that is, cleaned. It is taught, however, to be an animal, from the blood that adheres to the rocks. Whence, when it is cut off, it releases blood. For some living things in the waters move about, like fish, others stand fixed, like the oyster, the sea urchin, sponges. Of these, some are called male, since they have thin and denser tubes. Others female, which have larger and continuous tubes. Others are harder, which the Greeks call 'tragos' and we can call 'goat-like,' because of their roughness. The newest kind of these is called 'penicilli' [little brushes], since they are suited to swellings of the eyes and useful for wiping away watering eyes. White sponges are made by care: for in summer they are spread out in the sun and, like Punic wax, absorb whiteness.

Pliny: there are three kinds of sponges, as we have learned: the one called 'tragos,' thick and softer; the finer and denser kind, from which the 'penicilli' are made; and the 'achilleum,' all born on rocks. They are nourished on shellfish, fish, mud. It is clear that understanding is present in them, since, when they sense someone pulling them off, they contract and are removed with much greater difficulty; they do the same when a wave strikes. That they live by food is shown plainly by the tiny shells found in them. Around Toulon they say that even torn-off ones feed, and grow again on the rocks from the roots left behind. There are, moreover, certain hollow tubes, about four or five, through which they are believed to feed. It is also understood that a certain membrane lies beneath their roots: they live for a long time.

Pliny, book 31, in the same: in sponges there is male and female. Dyed with the foam of salt, in summer they are spread out inverted toward the moon and the frost, that is, so that the part by which they clung may drink in the whiteness. We have taught that it is an animal, from the blood that adheres to the rocks; some relate that they are governed by hearing and contract at a sound, showing an abundance of moisture, and that they cannot be torn from the rocks, and so are cut off and release matter. Northern sponges are preferred to the rest. Sponges usefully protect the head against the sun.
Pliny, book 32, in the same: in the sea near Campania they snatch up bread thrown to them, but there approach no food at all in which there is a hook.
Isidore: the softest kind of sponges are called 'penicilli,' since they are suited to swellings of the eyes and useful for wiping away watering eyes.

Pliny, in the same place: northern sponges, as said, are preferred to the rest, and physicians affirm that nowhere does their vitality last longer. The most noble kind of these, the 'penicilli,' calm swellings of the eyes, applied with honeyed wine; they are also most useful for wiping away watering eyes. Sponges themselves are also applied to eye discharges with vinegar-water, and to headaches with warm vinegar. Fresh ones disperse, soften, soothe. Old ones, however, glue wounds shut. They also dry moist ulcers and the like when applied. Fractures and wounds are most usefully treated with sponges, since blood is drawn out on the second application, so that the healing can be observed; they are applied to wounds now dry, now sprinkled with vinegar, now with wine, now with cold water. Applied moistened with rainwater, however, they dry fresh wounds and prevent swelling. They are also applied to disperse abscesses, smeared with boiled honey, and again for joint pains, soaked in salted vinegar or vinegar-water, if the attack is fierce, with the same salted water for calluses. They are also applied against the stings of scorpions with vinegar. In the treatment of wounds, moreover, they take the place of greasy wool, except that wool softens, while sponges constrict and draw out the impurities of wounds; besides, sponges, dry, are bound around dropsy sufferers and, applied, benefit the stomach. Likewise, applied with vinegar or cold water, they stop the flow of blood, and remove fresh bruising from a blow with salt water, warm, changed repeatedly. They also remove swelling and pain of the testicles with vinegar-water. For dog bites they are usefully applied, cut up, with vinegar or moistened with cold water or honey. African sponge-ash with leek juice benefits those coughing up blood, taken with a draft of salt in cold water. The same African ash disperses swelling with vinegar-water. The ash of all sponges burnt with pitch stops the bleeding of wounds. Likewise sponge ash with oil or vinegar, applied to the forehead, removes tertian fevers.
Pliny, in the same: a cold sponge, the brain moistened, also heals infants' 'syriasis,' that is, ulcers of the head.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'solaris' is so named because it gladly lies in the sun on riverbanks: it has a large head, a wide mouth opening, black and slippery skin, like that of eels. It has a most sweet liver, outstanding for eating, and it grows to a very great size and length.
Pliny: the sole is a flat fish, like the turbot.
Isidore: the sole is named from its shape, since it resembles the soles of shoes.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the sole, among sea fish, is according to physicians the most agreeable food for the infirm, since it is less phlegmatic than others. It is also pleasant in taste.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'spinachia' is small in body, but most usefully bristling all over with projecting spines, and is thus quite safe from the bite of any other fish.
Isidore: the 'squatus' is so named because it is rough with scales: whence wood is also polished with its skin.

Pliny: the angel-shark is of the kind of fish that have cartilage instead of a spine. All such are more fleshy and feed lying on their backs. Different kinds of fish do not mate together, except the angel-shark and the frog, from which is born a fish similar in its front part to the frog. And it takes its name, composed from both, among the Greeks. Some fish lay eggs three times a year, some twice, in spring and autumn. Of the flat fish, only the angel-shark does so twice, in autumn and at the setting of the Pleiades. The angel-shark, however, bears very soft eggs within itself, transferring them to another place of the womb and hatching them there. In the same way, too, all that we have called cartilaginous, so that alone among fish they both bear living young and conceive eggs.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the angel-shark is a sea fish, five cubits in length, with a tail a foot long: this one, hidden in mud, suddenly seizes fish. It has skin so rough that wood and ivory are polished with it: the hair of its skin itself is short and black. Nature made it so hard that it can scarcely be cut even by the sharpness of iron or steel.

Pliny: I see authors renowned for their learning marvel at the starfish in the sea: its shape is this - inside, a small amount of flesh; outside, a harder callus. This is said to have such fiery heat that it burns everything it touches in the sea and consumes all its food at once.
Pliny, in the same: the flesh of the starfish, applied, is effective against the strikes of the sea-dragon.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the starfish is a fish in the western sea, whose shape is like a star: this one, when it has eaten some creature, is soon found in its belly hard, like twice-baked bread. The sturgeon is a large fish dwelling in river waters that are great and broad. It cannot live long in ponds unless it has passage to the fresh waters of rivers. It takes in little or no food into its body. Indeed, sufficient nourishment for it is the very calm of clear air. Wherefore it also has a small belly, and is almost solid where the belly would be, as in the rest of its body. It has intestines, though small in proportion to its size.
