The rennet of the same seal is drunk by epileptics with mare's or donkey's milk. With the same rennet, those tending toward lethargy use it for smelling. It helps 'teutonic' [some ailment], the same rennet taken in wine. Likewise seal fat is dripped into the groin for the disease of a dead womb, and, with the same rennet, applied in a fleece.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the sea-calf, as said above, is itself the 'felcus,' of which fuller mention has been made; it is the same as what Aristotle calls the 'cocy,' of which mention has also been made above.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the hippopotamus is a beast born on land, but equally powerful in water and on land. It is generally larger than elephants. It has a turned-up snout, hooked teeth, grazes on crops at night, and goes to the water walking backward, as it were; it more readily receives wounds in its feet than in the rest of its body. It dwells in the Nile and is found especially in parts of India; spears are turned from its hide.

Isidore: the hippopotamus is so called because it is like a horse in its back, mane, and neighing, with a turned-up snout from its front teeth, and a twisting tail. By day it stays in the water, by night it grazes on crops; the Nile produces this creature.

Solinus: the hippopotamus has cloven hooves, and goes at night to graze on crops backward, by cunning, so that, its tracks deceiving, no ambush is prepared for it as it returns. This same creature, when distended with excessive fullness, seeks out freshly cut reeds, among which it turns about for so long until the sharp stumps wound its feet, so as to relieve its excess by the flow of blood; it then smears the wound with mud, until the wound heals into a scar.

Aristotle: the hippopotamus, that is the river-horse, has a horse's mane, cloven feet, soles like a cow's, and lacks a face, having on its feet a 'cahab.' Its tail is like a pig's, its neigh like a horse's, its size like a donkey's. Its hide is very thick, and so sandals and straps are made from it. Its innards resemble those of the horse and donkey. And although it lives on land, it cannot live without water, like the tortoise and the sea frog and the crocodile.

Pliny: the hippopotamus is a beast in the Nile, taller than the crocodile, with cloven hooves like an ox, a horse's back and mane and neigh, a turned-up snout, a twisted tail, and hooked teeth like a boar's, but less harmful, its hide impenetrable for shields and helmets, unless soaked in moisture; this creature became, in a certain respect, a master of medicine, for, made fat by constant excess, it comes out onto the shore, observes a recent cutting of reeds, and, where it sees the sharpest stump, presses its body onto it, wounding a certain vein in its leg, and thus, by the flow of blood, relieves its otherwise diseased body, and covers the wound again with mud.
Pliny, book 9, in the same: hippopotami are covered not only with hide, but also with hair, like seals too.
Pliny: [on] hippopotami. [The citation breaks off in the source after this heading word.]

Pliny: ash of hippopotamus hide, applied with water, heals ringworm; its fat, cold fevers. Its skin, bound on the left side of the forehead, checks the belly, and its ash cures baldness. A dram of its testicle is drunk in water against serpents; its dung, fumigated on the left side of the teeth, and, with the gums scarified, heals toothache.

div.head: DE CEDROSO ET ZIDRACH ET ZEPHIO

cit.quote: Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the Cedrosii are sea beasts dwelling in Arabia. Their bones are so large that doors in houses and palaces, and beams and other necessities of construction, are conveniently cut from them, for they are found to be forty cubits in size. The 'zidrach' is a monster marvelous in form, which suggests malice in its appearance, but is found harmless. It has a head like a horse's, but of smaller form; its body, however, is in every part most similar to a dragon's, and entirely colored in varied ways. It has a tail long in proportion to its body, slender and twisting, like a snake's; it also has fins like some fish. The 'zephius' is a sea beast most fearsome and very unlike the kind of all other animals, singular in form; for if you see its head, it is monstrous altogether. If you see the abyss of its mouth, you will flee as if from the image of death; if its eyes, you will shudder; if the rest of its body, you will confess you have seen nothing like it among things.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'zitiron' is a monster that common folk call 'the soldier,' and it is huge and most powerful. In its front part it displays, as it were, the form of an armed soldier, and a head as if helmeted with a casque, with wrinkled, hard, and very firm skin. From its neck hangs a long, broad, and great shield, hollow inside, so that it can be protected against the blows of combatants in it, in the manner of fighting men. For it is triangular in shape, and so firm and hard that it can scarcely ever be pierced by a javelin. From its neck and from its vertebrae certain veins and very strong sinews extend into its shoulder, by which the aforesaid shield hangs on its shoulder-blade. It also has very strong arms and, as it were, a cloven hand, with which it strikes most powerfully, whence it happens that it can very rarely be caught by man, and if caught, can be killed only with difficulty, and only with mallets.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: these things concerning the names of fish and of aquatic monsters and their natures we have run through in summary; now let us also add a few things about their sex and generation.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: female fish are larger than males and longer, and have harder flesh. Before the time of breeding and mating, males and females wander and swim together in shoals. At the time of mating and breeding, however, each walks paired with its own. All, moreover, keep nature's order in sex and kind. For a fish is never seen to mate with a fish of another kind. No fish has a neck or a penis or testicles or teats, as Aristotle says. From these, however, we except the dolphin and the whale and other sea monsters, and this because they generate offspring like themselves, whence they also have teats, with which they suckle their young, not above, however, but near the joints. And so they do not project, but have two channels, by which milk comes out, and the young follow their mothers. Male fish have passages full of semen, so that it often seems to run out externally; although the females are longer than the males and harder of flesh, the males, however, are better than the females, except among the [uncertain kind], and I do not call them females except in name, since in truth they are not so, but are diverse in appearance. For in certain fish there are no males and females, but certain kinds are only female.
Physiologus: [on] the moray. [The citation breaks off in the source after this heading word.]

Aristotle: of fish in which there are males and females, the males have a vessel in which there is semen, but the female a womb, and their eggs are not completed until they come outside, and then the males follow them and eject semen over them, so that they may receive their vital power and grow. But the hard-shelled sea creature has no male or female. Certain ones, too, are of hard hide, like trees, since in these what generates does so without the mating of male and female.
Pliny, book 9, on fish: female fish are larger than males. In the kind of certain ones, however, there are no males at all, as with sea urchins and the 'cromis.' For all are caught heavy with eggs.

Pliny, book 10, in the same: in all eels, moreover, there is neither a male nor a female kind, and they generate from themselves neither living young nor eggs, just as the kind is neuter also in oysters and other creatures attached to a shallow bottom or a rock.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: to fish, then, as to birds, from the beginning of their creation, God gave the blessing of propagating their own kind, saying: increase and multiply and fill the waters of the sea.

Ambrose: of fish, some generate eggs, like the varied larger ones, which they call trout; others send forth living young from their own body, like weasel-fish, dogfish, whales, dolphins, seals, and the like. And those that generate eggs do not weave nests, as birds do. Nor do they nourish them with such trouble, but entrust the eggs to the waters to be warmed. And the water itself gives life to and creates the offspring, as if a certain gentle mother of living things. As, then, the egg falls, the water, in a certain lap of its own nature, receives it like a gentle nurse and, by swift warming, renders it a living creature; for as soon as it falls, animated by the parent's cast, it becomes a fish and emerges. But those that send forth living young, once they have given birth, if they should sense any terror or that some ambush is being plotted around their young, by which they may protect them, either by the fear of their tender age or by maternal love, are reported to open their mouths and suspend their young with a harmless tooth, and also to receive them into the interior of their body and hide them in the womb, and again to give them life by a certain warmth of their own heat and nourish them with breath, and let them live safely within one body, until either they bring them to safety or, by interposing their own body, defend their offspring from danger. What human affection could imitate this devotion of fish? Behold, nature preserves in fish what it does not preserve in men.

Aristotle: large sea creatures generate a living animal, like the dolphin, and of these, even those that produce living young first generate eggs in their own womb. When these are completed, something like a worm is made from them, and when that worm is born, it takes on a perfect form, and from this a sea creature is made, which is called 'chelys' in Greek. The hard-shelled sea creature does not mate at all, but grows from mud and putrefaction. For universally, everything of hard shell is generated in mud by itself. Some fish, however, are generated in sand, some among stones, some by swimming on the surface of the water. And some that do not move, like the 'cheleti,' have something like roots growing in the earth. In a certain place dried by receding waters, when the Dog Star begins to appear, mud and putrefaction are taken away from it. And when water returns there, small fish that have neither egg nor semen are generated, and thus arise by themselves without mating and without eggs, and some from mud, some from sand, some through the putrefaction that is on the water's surface, like the foam that comes from water - when one dies, another is generated from it. Some fish, too, are generated from the earth, a sign of which is that when the weather is cold, it cannot be hunted. But when the day is clear, it rises from the earth and seeks warmth, and then can be hunted. Some fish, however, come from the foam that comes from rainwater, and are called 'foamy,' and are seen to bubble up in that foam, as worms bubble up in dung. And when the year is rainy and warm, there will be an abundance of this kind.

Pliny, book 9: scallops and 'vituli' arise spontaneously in sandy ground. Those of harder shell, however, like murices and purple-fish, from a sluggish salivary stickiness, as moisture increases, like gnats, and as the surface of the sea warms once rain has fallen. Those, however, that are covered with a stony shell, like oysters, from putrefying mud or foam standing for a long time around ships and fixed stakes and especially wood. It has recently been discovered that a fertile fluid, like milk, flows from oysters. Eels rub themselves against rocks, and these scrapings come to life, nor is there any other way they are generated; from the angel-shark and the frog mating together is born a fish similar in its front part to the frog. But other kinds do not intermix. Theophrastus reports that near Heraclea, when the river Lycus recedes, fish are generated from eggs left in the mud, which struggle toward feeding grounds with their tiny gills.

Pliny, in the same: fish mate by the rubbing of their bellies, with such speed that it deceives the eye. Dolphins and other cetaceans mate in a similar way, but somewhat longer; the female fish, at mating time, follows the male, striking his belly with her snout. During birth, however, the males follow the females, likewise feeding on their eggs, nor is mating by itself enough for generation, unless, once the eggs are laid, the males and females, moving among them, sprinkle them with vital fluid. This does not happen to all the eggs, in so great a multitude - otherwise the seas and pools would be filled, since each womb conceives innumerable eggs. Flat fish, whom the tail does not hinder, and spiny ones like tortoises and rays, mate coming from above, the octopus with one tentacle attached to the female's nostrils. Cuttlefish and squid, joining their arms together with their tongues and swimming in opposite directions, give birth through the mouth too, but octopuses mate with their heads turned to the ground. The rest of soft-bodied creatures mate back to back, like dogfish and prawns, lobsters. Crabs by the mouth, frogs, however, mount from above, the male grasping the female's front legs with his, and her haunches with his hind ones; they produce tiny black bits of flesh, which they call tadpoles, marked, however, by eyes and a tail; soon feet take shape as the tail splits into the hind legs. And, marvelously, after a six-month life they dissolve into mud, with no one observing it, and again are reborn from the spring waters, the same ones that had been born - just as it happens by a hidden principle every year. Different kinds of fish, however, do not mate together, except the angel-shark and the frog, from which is born one similar in its front part to the frog. And it takes its name, composed from both, among the Greeks.

Aristotle: all male fish have semen, except a certain one called [uncertain name], which has neither semen nor eggs. Fish are of quick mating, for they mate when one touches the other and eject semen quickly, and just as other animals hold their breath before the emission of semen, so too fish then do not take in seawater, and when they do this too quickly, they are spoiled more quickly. They have passages, however, like men, and semen is in the last part of the seed. And so large fish sometimes mate, and come close at the place called the navel, and from that passage the male draws out semen, the female eggs. Soft-bodied creatures and the 'vacca' and the eagle-ray and sea skates mate back to back. Females follow males at the time of lust and mating, and receive semen through the mouth, as is said, and place it beneath the belly. The kind of soft-bodied creature, like the cuttlefish, and of soft shell, like the lobster and the like, come from mating. And their mating, like that of ringed creatures, is slower, since they lack blood and so have a cold nature. Nor do they produce more than two eggs in summer, since the womb in them is divided into two. A certain fish generates without mating; a fish called 'enobares,' however, is generated from the mating of two species.

Ambrose: no fish mixes with another, but each with its own kind: the spurge-fish with the spurge-fish, the wolf-fish with the wolf-fish, the scorpion-fish too keeps the chastity of an unstained union with its own kind.

Isidore, on fish: some, as said before, conceive by the mixing of the male and bring forth young. Others lay eggs conceived without the reception of the male, which the same males, in a subsequent casting of their semen, suffuse, and thus they become capable of generation. Those, however, that have not been suffused with the male's semen remain sterile or putrefy.

Aristotle: just as, then, in certain female birds there are wind-eggs, so too in the kinds of fish there are eggs by themselves, which are not suited to generation except those over which the male ejects semen; not all fish, however, produce their young at one time, nor is the time of their impregnation equal. For some are impregnated over thirty days and some over twenty days, and all breed at a fixed time. Some, however, have small winged worms in their wombs, which destroy the impregnation before the time of breeding. Those are mistaken, however, who imagine that female fish conceive by swallowing the males' semen. Their error is aided by the swiftness of fish mating, and they do not consider that what enters the mouth passes into the stomach, not the womb, and is necessarily digested and turned into food. The soft-shelled sea creature, like the lobster, mates and is impregnated. The same happens to soft-bodied creatures. Fish of shelled or soft-shell hide, when impregnated, are good; but when the time since impregnation lengthens, some are good, some poor. All fish, however, lay eggs, except the 'cheleon,' which produces a living animal.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: eggs, however, are found only in those that mate. Some fish are impregnated by the south wind, some by the north. Marsh fish are impregnated for the most part after five months. All fish, generally, breed after one year.

Aristotle: eggs are not found in fish except in those that mate, and sometimes they are found without mating, as in river fish. The greater part of the eggs, as is said, is swallowed by the female. Many eggs perish in the water, and none of them survive except those laid in places where the young can emerge. But young are produced from eggs only from those over which the male ejects his semen. When the female has laid, the male follows her and ejects semen over the eggs, and whatever is touched by that semen becomes a small fish. The male fish stays in the place where the female lays, guarding the many eggs while the female wanders about; the male [of a certain longer-lived kind] stays over its eggs for forty or fifty days, since they are not completed quickly, nor are the fish that come from them. All the eggs that are touched by the semen soon appear whiter, after one day, and after a little time the eyes of the fish appear in them. The greater part of the eggs perish while the female lays them wandering about. Those eggs, too, that come out in the current of the water perish, unless they fall onto some matter. All scaled, that is scaly, fish lay eggs. Sea foxes and turtles called 'smooth' have eggs in the middle of the womb, like sea-dogs. Fish eggs are not of two separated colors, namely white and yellow-orange, but of one color, as if mixed from both. Nor are they complete like birds' eggs, but incomplete, since they receive growth. And so fish lay incomplete eggs, except one called the frog. They are completed outside, however, and the reason for this is that fish have many eggs. And so nature, because of their abundance, counters external corruption. And certain kinds of fish grow before laying, like the kind called the 'spiny' one, and the eggs of this kind are large, since nature, the more it diminishes in number, the more it increases in size. For fish that generate living young lay eggs internally first. And all fish lay eggs except the 'cheleon,' which produces a living animal, and which also first lays eggs within itself. Those, however, are mistaken who imagine that female fish swallow the males' eggs, since at the same time semen is found in the males and eggs in the females. The growth of the male's and female's semen is at the same time, nor do the females lay all at once, but successively, nor do the males eject semen all at once, but successively: the males' semen, however, is consumed together with the females' eggs. The generation of soft-bodied creatures, like the cuttlefish and its like, and of soft-shelled animals, like lobsters, guard their eggs only. Soft-bodied creatures lay outside, and the male ejects semen over the females, as male fish do over the eggs. Fish eggs grow in the sea, some with the greatest speed, like those of morays, some a little more slowly - the female, as said, laying, the male suddenly follows the eggs and ejects semen over them, so that they become living creatures. For the first motion is from the male. And so the completion of the eggs of birds and fish will not occur except from the males, but in birds inside, in fish outside, for the reason stated. Soft-bodied and soft-shelled creatures produce only two eggs in summer, since the womb in them is divided into two. The chick cuttlefish is continuous with the egg at the front part of the body. Nor can it be otherwise, for the front and rear parts meet in the same place. The 'cheleti,' indeed, lay one complete egg inside and bear it outside. Other fish, however, lay incomplete eggs outside, except the sea frog, which lays only one complete egg outside, and this is of hard shell, for the protection it needs on the outside. The reason for this is the nature of its body, since its head is manifold in size compared to its body and is spiny, and so it does not receive its young at the last. These eggs, after their smallness, grow quickly, like worms that are generated from a very small animal: then they grow by themselves. They grow, however, because of the heat of the semen... [the citation breaks off incomplete in the source here].

Aristotle, in the same: at the time of fish mating, as already said above, the male follows the female and swallows, as is said, the greater part of the eggs. And from the remaining eggs the generation of fish occurs. When, however, animals are formed inside fish, they are placed in a fine membrane, and at first their eyes will be large. But in fish that are generated from worms, the lower parts are larger at first, and at the end the eyes and head are generated. And when the moisture that is in the egg is used up, then the young is no longer fed from it. But once it has grown a little, it is fed from the water of the stream. Marsh and river fish breed on the banks of rivers and lakes, and especially where they find the material of trees and reeds. Some, however, breed in a place whose depth is one stadium. Small ones breed in places where there is little water, and especially where there are roots of willows or other trees or reeds. Likewise certain sea fish breed on the bank of a river, since that place is warm and there is no wind there, and they take in fresh water. There is a certain fish whose eggs, when the hour of birth comes, dissolve within it, and then the young come out. Fish generated from the eggs of small fish grow in three days; and eggs touched by much semen grow in one day. The fish called 'hallas' in Greek breeds all its young in a place of much water, and leads them behind it like a flock. A certain one, called the 'thylon,' however, breeds near the sea-shore in places where the wind always strikes, and this kind runs about in the manner of a flock. Some, however, at breeding time go to places of little water. A single female is sometimes followed by twelve or thirteen males. The diversity of regions, moreover, diversifies fish even in the frequency of mating and impregnation and birth, as with plants and trees and other things. And so many fish often lay or give birth in certain places, and in others not. Among aquatic animals, that which is of great body has few offspring, and that of small body, on the contrary, many. Breeding of fish occurs more in a sea calm from winds and warm, and where it receives much fresh water: and all fish nourish their young, except the frog. Some, however, feed on their own young at breeding time. The dolphin alone among fish produces a living animal having teats and suckles its young.

Pliny, in the same place: fish cross into pools and rivers so as to produce safe offspring, where there are none to devour the young, and the waves rage less. Of fish, the 'phycis' alone nests from seaweed and lays in the nest. The torpedo is found having eighty young. It bears very soft eggs within itself, transferring them to another place of the womb and hatching them there. In the same way, too, the other cartilaginous ones. So it happens that alone among fish they both bear living young and conceive eggs. The male catfish alone of all often guards the laid eggs for fifty days, lest they be consumed by others. The other females, however, hatch them in three days, if the male has touched them. The needlefish or garfish, one among fish, gives birth by the womb splitting open because of the abundance of young, and the wound heals after birth. The young of all aquatic creatures, moreover, lack sight at first.

Ambrose: therefore some fish generate eggs and entrust them to the waters to be warmed, like the varied ones and the like. Others produce living young from their own body, like weasel-fish, dogfish, whales, the dolphin and seals and the like, as already said above.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the greater part of fish breed on the banks of rivers if this suits them, when there is no wind in that place and it is warm in itself. Small fish breed where there is little water, and especially around the roots of willows or other trees. But the greatest part of the eggs perishes for various reasons, since if all survived, they would multiply excessively. And so, especially when the female lays wandering about, the greater part of the eggs perish. Some fish, moreover, weaken as they breed. And some have worms in their wombs, which destroy the young.

Aristotle: not all fish, however, lay or breed at one time. The sea scorpion lays once in spring and again in autumn: some lay only once, but since it lays its eggs successively, men think it lays twice, and indeed it lays first at the end of winter and finishes at the beginning [of spring]. Certain sea creatures lay at every season, and such females make small eggs. Afterward these crack open and grow very quickly. Hence the growth of all the eggs of sea fish is swift and rapid. Some lay on land among slender, green grasses that are in the water. Some near the courses of rivers. And some in the open sea; and this only in the season of spring. In the autumn season, however, they do not lay, except a little, but some lay in winter, some in summer, and of certain ones, like the 'fascari,' a certain part lay in winter, a certain part in summer. And some breed often, like the 'cheleti,' often within six months. Certain fish, however, twice a year, like the 'galeon.' Finally, egg-laying fish produce young only once a year, except the small 'sachadon,' which breeds twice a year: soft-bodied creatures lay on land. And certain other fish on stone. Certain fish, when they breed, weaken. Certain ones, before breeding, wander much in motion, and once they have bred, rest. Certain ones have small winged worms in their wombs, which destroy the impregnation and the young. Fish existing in the depth of the sea breed in summer, since they are not caught then.

Pliny: scallops, slugs, and swallows vanish at the same time. Of fish, the sea-bass and the sardine lay twice a year, and all rock fish. Some lay three times, like red mullets, the 'calchis,' the carp. Some twice, like sea-breams, namely in spring and autumn. Of the flat fish, the angel-shark alone in autumn, at the setting of the Pleiades. Most fish, in the three months of April, May, June. The saupe in autumn. Parrotfish and the torpedo around the equinox; soft-bodied ones, however, like the cuttlefish, in every month. Likewise octopuses mate in winter. Lobsters and the rest of thinner shell lay eggs upon eggs, or bear them, and brood them thus. The cuttlefish lays on land among reeds, and, kept in the deep, squid produce eggs. Likewise purple-fish and murices lay in spring. Sea urchins indeed have eggs at the full moons in winter, and snails are born in the winter season.

Ambrose: the fish knows, then, the seasons for giving birth, knows the time for going and returning, by the inspiration of nature, which is the true mistress of devotion. At the fitting time, from different places, they come together to very many bays of the sea in a joined company, as if by common counsel, and make for the northern sea. They cross to the strait of the Black Sea in summer, since the bay is sweeter there, because the sun lingers so long in this strait as to exhaust all the sweet and drinkable water in which sea creatures delight. There, suited by place and time, they breed and rear their tender young, and once this is done, all together return in the same company by which they came.

div.head: DE OPERE SEXTA DIEI ET PRIMO DE ANIMALIBUS

cit.quote: William of Conches: fish and birds having thus been created from water by the action of the higher elements, the water there was thinner, and was dried by the heat from these creatures' creation and from the higher elements. But the surface of the earth, which was muddy from the water lying over it, boiling from heat, created from itself the various kinds of animals. And if in some part the heat of fire predominated, from that were born choleric animals, like the lion; if the coldness of earth, melancholic ones, like the ox; if of water, phlegmatic ones, like pigs. But from a certain mud in which the qualities of the elements were balanced, man's body was made, indeed in the eastern region, for that region is more temperate than the others.

Petrus Comestor: all the higher parts of the world, that is heaven and air and water, having thus been adorned, God at last, on the sixth day, adorned the lowest part, that is the earth, producing from it three kinds of animals, namely beasts, reptiles, and beasts of burden. Knowing that man would fall through sin, God gave him beasts of burden as a penalty of labor, for work or for food. Reptiles and beasts, however, serve him for exercise. But it is asked, concerning these and other harmful creatures, whether they were created harmful, or were at first gentle and afterward made harmful. The answer is that they were at first created gentle, but after sin were made harmful to man, for three reasons, namely for man's punishment, correction, and instruction. For man is punished when he is harmed by them, or when he fears being harmed, since fear is itself a great penalty. He is corrected by them, when he knows that these things have happened to him because of his sin. He is also instructed by admiring the works of God — indeed admiring more the works of ants than the burdens of camels, so that, when man sees that even these smallest creatures can harm him, he may remember his own frailty and be humbled. Someone might perhaps say that certain animals harm others, which are neither punished nor corrected nor instructed by this. But even in these cases man is instructed by example, since they were created for this purpose, that they might serve as food for others. But someone might object that they also rage against dead men. And through this too man is instructed not to dread any kind of death, since, through whatever passage his body passes, not a hair of his head shall perish.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: before we assign the nature of land animals and the anatomy of their several members in general, it is fitting that we discuss, in our own manner, the several kinds by themselves and the species of each kind in particular, according to alphabetical order. That general treatment, however, we pass over here for the present, to avoid the tedium of length, and reserve it to be pursued more carefully and fully in the following work. Now, then, let us begin with those kinds that were made especially for man's help, that is, with flocks and herds, which Scripture, for this reason, also calls by the name of beasts of burden.

Isidore, book 12: the name 'pecus' [flock-animal] is properly applied to those animals that are either fit for eating, like sheep and pigs, or useful for man's service, like horses and oxen. Generally, however, every animal is called 'pecus' from grazing [pascendo]. 'Iumenta' [beasts of burden], moreover, are so called because they help [iuvent] men's labors or burdens, either by carrying or by ploughing. Likewise 'armenta' [herds], either because they are fit for arms [armis], that is, for war, or because men use them for this. Others understand 'armenta' to mean only oxen, so named from ploughing [arando], as if 'aramenta,' or because they are armed [armata] with horns. There is, moreover, a distinction between herds and flocks: for herds are of horses and oxen, but flocks are of sheep and goats.
Pliny: livestock grow fat by drinking; therefore salt is most suitable for them.
Pliny, book 24, in the same: the weight of loaded fruit is felt at once by beasts of burden, and unless it is shown to them beforehand, however small it is, they sweat immediately.

Solinus: the herds of the Gargarantes people graze with their necks turned aside, for if they should point their mouths straight at their pasture, their horns, bent down toward the ground, would get in the way.

Valerius Maximus: on the island of Cephalonia, whereas everywhere else livestock is refreshed daily by drinking water, on this island the livestock, for the greater part of the year, quench their thirst by standing with mouths open, taking in the wind from on high.

div.head: DE EISDEM IN SPECIALI SECUNDUM ORDINEM ALPHABETI ET PRIMO DE AGNO

cit.quote: Isidore: the Greeks call the lamb [agnus] from the sound 'agnos,' as if 'pious.' The Latins, however, think it has this name entirely because it recognizes [agnoscat] its mother before other animals, so much so that even if it has strayed in a great flock, it recognizes its parent's voice at once by her bleating.

Ambrose: the lamb, most simple of creatures, when it sometimes strays from its mother, often calls to her absence with its bleating, and although it may be surrounded by many thousands of sheep, it recognizes its parent's voice and hastens toward her. For although it is held by desire for food and drink, it passes by the udders of others, however much they overflow, swollen with milk, and seeks only the fountains of its own mother's milk.

Pliny, book 8: many prefer winter lambs to spring ones, since it matters more that they be strong before the solstice than before midwinter, and this alone among animals is usefully born in midwinter. To castrate lambs before three months old, however, is premature.
Pliny: [on] lambs or rams, as [with] calves and kids and boars. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]
Aristotle: a lamb, if its kidneys are entirely covered around with fat, will die.

Palladius, in the passage above, book 15: the first generation of lambs is in the month of November, but the newborn lamb must be brought to its mother's udders at once by hand, though first a small amount of the milk, which is thicker by nature, should be milked out, which shepherds call the beestings, for this will harm the lambs unless it is removed; and for two days after birth it should be shut in with its mother, and then kept in dark and warm pens. Likewise, once the flock of young ones is separated off, the mothers should be sent out to pasture. It is enough, however, to let the lambs drink from the udders before the mothers go out in the morning and again in the evening when they return sated. Until they are strengthened, they should be fed within the fold on bran or lucerne, or, if there is a supply, barley flour, given to them until, through the strength of their growing age, they can share the common pasture with their mothers within the enclosure.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the lamb is the simplest and gentlest of all animals, since it is skilled in no trickery or cunning, and harms no one with teeth or claws. It is also most patient, since it does not cry out when about to be sacrificed, and is silent when being shorn. It is also most useful for many purposes. For it provides milk for nourishment, wool for clothing, flesh for eating, hide too for making shoes or for writing, and dung for enriching and fertilizing the field. It is, moreover, a clean animal according to the Law, since it both chews the cud and has a cloven hoof; it naturally fears, dreads, and flees the wolf. Rightly, then, and because of these many good qualities mentioned, Christ, who is good above all, wished to be represented especially in the figure of the lamb, just as the Holy Spirit is in the dove.

Isaac Judaeus, in the Diets: the suckling lamb, in its viscosity, is close to the wild pig, because of the closeness of the womb and the moisture of the milk on which it is nourished. Accordingly its flesh is not praiseworthy, since it is indigestible and, by its own slipperiness, descends from the stomach undigested. It is especially indigestible if those eating it have a moist stomach from a deficiency. And so Galen criticized suckling lambs; yearling lambs, however, have a more moderate complexion, between the moisture of the suckling and the dryness of the young adult. And so they are better than the rest and easier to digest. For they produce better blood, and especially benefit the young, who have a hot and dry complexion and dwell in a hot and dry region.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: lamb's flesh is very good for the strong and healthy, but harmful to the weak, since, although it descends easily from the stomach, it is dissolved from the limbs only with great difficulty, and so it generates a viscous humor.
Lamb's rennet is powerful against all harmful medicines, and is effective against the bites or stings of sea creatures.
Avicenna: lamb's blood, with wine, heals epilepsy. Its rennet, indeed, heals all poisons and bites.

Isidore: the boar [aper] is named from ferocity [feritas], with the letter f removed and p substituted; whence too, among the Greeks, it is called 'syagros,' that is, 'wild.' For everything that is wild and fierce we improperly call 'agrestis' [rustic]. Wild pigs are very warlike at mating time, and contrive to make their hides hard at that time by rubbing themselves against trees and afterward entering mud and drying it on. From this they fight, so much that one or both may die; the bear too fights with wild pigs. It is, moreover, very ill-tempered and unintelligent, receiving no training in good manners, and no change occurs in it even if it is castrated. The female boar too is castrated, so that, needing no mating, she may quickly grow fat, though food is withheld beforehand for two days.

Pliny: boars show the greatest roughness at mating time. Then they fight among themselves, hardening their sides by rubbing against trees and coating themselves with mud. The females too are rougher in giving birth, nearly as in every kind of beast. Male boars breed only from the age of one year. Boars are not found on the island of Crete, only in Africa; in India boars have twin tusks of a cubit's curve on the snout, and as many again on the forehead, projecting like a calf's horns.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: the boar's tusks project; rarely in the female, and even then to no use. And so, when boars strike, the female pigs bite. Males have more tusks than females, and tails like goats. Boars' blood does not clot.
Pliny, in the same: boars heal themselves in sickness with ivy, and by eating crabs, especially those cast up by the sea.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: it is remarkable how slowly boars and stags, unless raised from infancy, become tame. In Macedonia many boars are reported. In Pamphylia and in the mountains of Sicily, however, those who eat a salamander that has been devoured by boars die.

Physiologus: the boar, hard-pressed when forced to flee, does not repeat its strike; a boar's tusk, separated from it while the animal lives, retains its sharpness, which it loses once the animal is dead.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the boar is a strong, black-colored beast, which never receives any training in good manners, but is always fierce and savage; it has large, curved tusks fit for cutting, in which this is remarkable, that while the beast is alive they can do what iron can, but once removed from the dead animal they are proven to have lost their cutting power. This animal, if attacked by hunters in the morning before it has urinated, is easily tired out. But if it has urinated before or during the hunt, it yields to capture only with difficulty. Yet even when tired it does not yield, but stands its ground in the rear, and by its rigid ferocity conceals its weariness, offering combat to the hunter; it does not, however, dare to strike or attack a man unless it has first received a blow from him. Let a man, however, beware, for unless he deals a fatal wound with the first thrust of his sharp spear-point, between the shoulder and the ribs on the side, he may risk his life, unless perhaps he finds a nearby tree to climb for refuge, or presses his whole body flat to the ground in some lower spot of the level earth. For its tusks, turned backward and curved, by which, as if by the most terrible weapons, it is able to deal death, cannot reach anyone except one standing upright and straight. He will endure, however, the trampling of its feet until help comes to him as he lies there from someone nearby. The boar surpasses all beasts in hearing; on its right side it has a mouth like a shield, which it turns against hunting-spears and blades.

Pliny, book 8: boar's brain is praised against serpents, taken with blood. Aged liver too, drunk with rue and wine; likewise fat with honey and resin, and boar's liver too, with only four ounces' weight of the fibers removed, and brain drunk with wine. Likewise boar's brain or blood heals carbuncles of the private parts. Its liver rouses the lethargic. In the liver of a female boar little stones are found, which, crushed and drunk in wine, expel stones. Boar's lung wards off drunkenness, roasted and taken that same day by one fasting. Boar's gall disperses scrofulous swellings, and calms the spleen when drunk. The same, with fat, applied as lung-poultice, heals chilblains. Boar's gall too, with resin and white lead, heals spreading ulcers. Ash of boar's jaw heals spreading ulcers, and the same also benefits fractures. Its lard, boiled and bound around, also heals them with remarkable speed. Boar's urine, and the bladder itself taken as food, heal pains of the bladder and of stones, if both are first steeped in smoke. Likewise boar's bladder, if roasted and eaten, checks incontinence of urine; boar's urine, or even the bladder, given gradually in drink, helps the dropsical. It is more effective when it has dried within its own bladder. Likewise boar's urine with vinegar benefits the falling sickness. It also benefits to have drunk boar's testicles in mare's milk or in water. Boar's urine too, kept in glass, heals ear pains and ailments; finally boar's urine is so offensive to the boar itself that it cannot bear to flee from it, unless, once passed, it is, as it were, overcome and buries it; whence it is reported they burn it away. Fresh boar dung, sprinkled into a draught of warm wine, heals dysentery sufferers; the same dung, and fresh foam from a boar, with vinegar, also benefits those with loose bowels. In the dung of a sow that has not given birth the use is more effective, and even more so in boars. The use of lard is effective, rubbed on the limbs, for softening, warming, dispersing, and purging away the weariness of travel.
Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: fresh, warm boar dung is a chief remedy against bleeding from the nose.

Isidore: the ram [aries] is named from the Greek 'arren,' that is, 'from the male'; whence among us too the males of flocks are called 'mares,' or because this animal was first sacrificed on altars [aris] by the pagans. Whence the saying: 'the ram is slain at the altars.'

Aristotle: horns quickly appear on the heads of rams, and, as Homer says, horns are also found on the heads of female sheep. Among northern peoples, however, in a certain place rams have no horns. Animals that have horns naturally have cloven hooves, like the bull, the stag, and the ram. And, for the most part, the ram is the leader of the flock. For shepherds place one ram as leader in the flock, and thus train him from lambhood, so that, when the shepherd calls him by his own name, he goes ahead of the rest.
Aesculapius, in the book on the limbs: the elephant, when it sees a ram, fears it and flees.

Pliny: it is natural for the ram to disdain old ewes and to seek out young ones. And the ram himself is better and more useful in old age. His ferocity is checked by boring a hole in his horn near the ear. Tying off the right testicle produces females, the left, males; to castrate him before five months old, however, is premature.
Pliny, in the same: a ram whose veins beneath the tongue are of a certain color will have offspring of the same wool-color, and mottled, if there are several colors.
Pliny: to the ram kind horns were given, coiled in a spiral.
Pliny: rams should be castrated while the moon is waning.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the ram, leader of the flock, attacks a rival with his horn, and first steps back so as to strike better with his horns.

Palladius, book 8: rams should be chosen and admitted to mating in the month of July, the whitest ones with soft wool, in which not only the whiteness of the body is to be considered, but also the tongue, which, if spotted with dark patches, produces variegated coloring in the offspring. From a white ram offspring of another color is often born; from dark rams, however, as Columella asserts, a white one can never be produced. The ram to choose is one that is tall, well-formed, with a broad belly and covered in the whitest wool, a very long tail, a low fleece, a broad forehead, large testicles, and of prime age, though he can usefully mate up to eight years old. They should be admitted to mating, as said, in July, so that the offspring born may grow strong before winter. Aristotle asserts that if you wish to produce more males, the breeze of the north wind should be chosen at mating time, and the flocks pastured facing that same wind; if females, the breath of the south wind should be sought, and the pasture directed accordingly, and thus you may direct the unwitting mothers so that the number of those dead or defective may be restored by new offspring. Some, however, keep rams from mating for two months beforehand, so that the delay of pleasure easily increases their desire. Others, however, let them mate without restriction, so that offspring may not be lacking to them by this method throughout the whole year.

Aristotle: a ram of one year mates, but produces something feeble; before mating season rams walk together, but at mating time they separate and fight, and have their own distinctive voice, by which they call to one another at that season.

div.head: DE USU EIUS IN CIBO ET MEDICINIS

cit.quote: Isaac Judaeus: rams have hotter and less moist flesh than sheep, and harder to digest. Rams remaining in their youth are of lesser moisture and viscosity, because of the dryness that predominates in their complexion at that age. And so their flesh is better than that of lambs and ewes, since, if well digested, they produce good and abundant blood, especially if they are castrated, since their heat and moisture are then tempered, whence they are of good flavor, except when they are decrepit with age, which are without doubt the worst, and uncastrated ones are better than these. For all decrepit animals are naturally deficient in heat. This deficiency comes from age and from lack of the testicles. Yearlings have a moderate complexion, between the moisture of the suckling and the dryness of the young adult. And so they are better than the other rams and easier to digest. For they produce better blood, and especially benefit the young, who have a hot and dry complexion and dwell in a hot and dry region. The decrepit, as said, are worse than the rest. For all decrepit creatures, following a dry generation, are colder and drier, and so are woody and tasteless. But although they are unpraiseworthy because of old age, yet, being naturally hot and moist, they are better than other decrepit animals.

Avicenna: burnt ram's flesh is usefully applied to vitiligo and impetigo. It also benefits the bites of serpents and scorpions, even with the dung of a rabid dog. Its ash benefits the white film of the eye. Warm ram's lung, applied, heals chafing of the heel from footwear.
Aesculapius: the liquid that drips from a boiled ram's lung heals tertian fevers and kidney disease arising in them.
Pliny: [on] ram's cantharides. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]
Haly Abbas: ram's gall heals ear pain that comes from cold.

Isidore: the donkey [asinus] is named from sitting [sedere], as if 'asedus,' since, before men caught horses, they began to sit upon this animal. For, being a slow creature offering no resistance by reason, it submitted itself to man as soon as he wished.

Pliny: the donkey performs generous services, ploughing too, but especially for the breeding of mules; its homeland is noted among these - the Arcadians in Achaia, in Italy the people of Reate - an animal most impatient of cold. Males are worse when work is slackened. Their affection for their offspring is the greatest, but their aversion to water is greater still. They go through fires to reach their young. Likewise, if even the smallest stream lies between, they shudder, so much so that they take care not to wet their feet at all. Nor do they drink except at accustomed springs found on the farms, and in such a way that they go to drink by a dry path and do not cross bridges, through rivers made transparent by the scarcity of plants. And, remarkable to say, they suffer thirst, and if the water is changed, they must be forced or coaxed to drink.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: beetles are born from the body of a dead donkey; the donkey's blood is very thick, just as man's is very thin. The hair of donkeys' tails is longer than that of horses', but bristly for pack-animals. Donkey's milk is the thickest, so that it is used in place of rennet. It is also thought to contribute something to whiteness in women's skin. Among solid-hoofed animals, the only single-horned animal is the Indian donkey.

Pliny, book 24, in the same: fennel-giant is most pleasing food to donkeys, but present poison to other beasts of burden. For this reason this animal was assigned to Father Liber, to whom the fennel-giant is also a sacrificial victim.

Aristotle: the donkey has hooves like the horse, and lacks gall entirely, but has thick and very black blood, like the bull. The donkey and other great-hearted animals are more fearful than all other animals; it fears cold, lacks gall, eats thorns when they are soft, mates much, though less than the horse. And if it has not begun to breed after the shedding of its back teeth, it will never breed at all. It eats fruit, feeds on plants, and fattens on water. And the more it drinks of water, the more its food benefits it; it has a single belly, like other solid-hoofed animals. It often falls ill with a disease called 'milide,' which begins in the head. Much phlegm runs from its nostrils, and if it descends to the lung, it dies. The female donkey, like the cow, discharges much in her menses, because of the size of her body. The bear fights with the donkey, since it eats raw flesh. The crow too fights with it and flies above it, harms it, and pecks its eyes with its beak. The Indian donkey has both a horn and hooves at once, contrary to the habit of other animals.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the donkey is a stupid, slow, and lustful animal. It has a cross-mark on the front part of its back, above the shoulders, and there it is weaker. On the hindquarters, however, above the kidneys, there it is stronger: it brays horribly, eats burdock, delights, it is said, in the sound of the lyre, carries wheat and does not eat it.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the donkey is an ugly, base, and despised animal, with a large head, long and broad ears, a lean body, unable to grow fat. On its shoulders it bears the marks of Christ's cross. The donkey is, then, a gentle animal, ignorant of discord, willing to bear burdens and not rebelling even against loads placed on it beyond what it can carry, dull and irrational beyond all animals. Slow and sluggish too in its gait, patient and most enduring of blows, walking along a road it does not know how to yield to those it meets; it mates after thirty months, but does not breed until after three years; it gladly eats thorns; it is naturally cold and impatient of cold, especially at the time of conception. And so it is not bred in cold places, and in Scotland and neighboring regions, nor at the equinox as horses mate, but in summer. Nor is it found in the northern land, which is coldest, since it cannot live there. It carries in the womb for a full year. A donkey's foal has some grace in its youth, but the older it grows, the uglier it becomes. If you remove a female donkey placed next to her foal and keep the foal from following, she will remain in the same place and will not move five paces elsewhere, but will wait where she left him. Donkeys' bones are more resonant than others, as Pliny says; donkey's milk is the whitest, and is thought to contribute something to whiteness of the skin. Whence it is found that Nero's wife Poppaea used to bathe in donkey's milk. The same, warm, also strengthens the teeth and eases their pain. Donkeys mostly fall ill on one side, having a catarrh, and if it flows from the nostrils down onto the lung, they die.

Ambrose: the donkey, sluggish and exposed to prey, and rather slow of sense, teaches us that we ought to be more alert, and not grow sluggish in idleness of body and mind, but take refuge in faith, which is accustomed to lighten heavy burdens.

Physiologus: the donkey is a beast of burden, a slave bound to servitude, which, in view of the multitude of labors it endures, receives little gratitude; it understands the accustomed voice of man, and knows the road it has often walked, sometimes even becoming a guide for its driver when he has gone astray. But when it sees a wolf coming, it looks back over its loins, and thus, unaware, is seized by the wolf.

Isaac Judaeus: donkey's flesh, if eaten, is digested with difficulty, harms the stomach, and causes vomiting. It is, however, of finer nourishment than the horse's. The horse, however, is finer than the camel's, the mule's worse than the rest.

Aristotle: the donkey mates after thirty months, but does not breed before three, or two, or two and a half years are complete. In mating, however, it ejects semen more quickly than the horse. Female donkeys, however, do not retain the male's semen, but urinate it out at once. And mares similarly. And so, after a donkey has mated, the female is struck with straps and prevented from urinating; she has, moreover, distinctions of teats under the armpit, like the female camel and the mare. In cold regions the donkey does not breed, since it naturally feels much cold. And so it does not mate at the equinox, as the horse does, but at the onset of summer, so that the breeding and birth of donkeys occurs in warm weather, since they give birth at a time similar to the time of conception. For they are pregnant for one full year. The donkey's nature, however, is cold, and its semen is cold. Whence if a horse mates with a female donkey already impregnated by a donkey, the conception is not spoiled. But if a donkey mates with a mare already impregnated by a horse, the conception will be spoiled, because of the coldness of the donkey's semen. And so if a horse mates with a female donkey, the mixture will be preserved because of the heat of the one semen, namely the horse's; the donkey's semen, as said, is cold, but the mare's matter is hot. And when hot is mixed with cold, it becomes temperate, and conception will result from them. But when the donkey's semen is colder, generation from it will occur only with difficulty, or will be sterile.

Pliny: the donkey is an animal most impatient of cold. And so it does not breed in the Black Sea region, nor is it admitted to mating at the spring equinox, but at the solstice. The female donkey's gestation, from the thirtieth month, is at its quickest; from three years old, normal. The same number of months as the mare, and in a similar way. It rarely bears twins. About to give birth, she flees the light, seeks darkness, so as not to be seen by man. She breeds her whole life, which extends to thirty years for her. Their affection for their offspring, as said, is the greatest; they go through fires to reach their young. A female donkey that has not conceived before shedding her foal-teeth is understood to be sterile, and one that has not begun to breed at her first mating.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: pregnant female donkeys grow thin at once, and their udders ache from the pregnancy. And so they prevent birth in the sixth month, whereas mares carry almost the whole year. It is fatal for their foals to taste the mother's milk within two days of birth.

Avicenna, in the same place: the donkey heals leprosy; those contracted from dryness sit in the broth of its flesh, and its flesh too helps. Its liver, roasted and eaten while fasting, benefits epilepsy, and likewise its burnt hoof. Ash of its flesh and liver with oil is effective applied to cracks from cold. Likewise ash of its liver with oil is effective on scrofula. It is said, moreover, that its urine benefits pain of the kidneys. The urine of the wild donkey, as Galen says, breaks a stone in the bladder. Donkey's blood prevents bleeding from the nostrils by a covering. Its fat is effective for marks on the skin. Donkey's urine benefits creeping and moist ulcers and pain of the kidneys. Its dung is administered in every kind of bleeding. It is smelled for strong bleeding of the nostrils, and its moisture is expressed into the nostril and held there. Likewise dried dung of a grazing donkey with wine is very good for a scorpion's sting: donkey's milk too, being less buttery, is fine and watery, and is effective for cough, wasting, and coughing blood, and for dropsy and hardness of the spleen; it soothes the bowels and is good for hectic fever. It is also said that when the mouth is rinsed with it, it strengthens the teeth and gums. It is not suitable, however, for those having head-ache, vertigo, and ringing in the ears, and especially for sleeping upon, and generally harms those with weak heads.

Aesculapius: donkey's blood, drunk with wine, heals daily fevers, three or four drops given; its milk is effective for the weary, those with sighing breath, tremors, dysentery sufferers, and ulcers of dark eyes. Its fat stirs mating. Its spleen, ground with water and applied to the breast, draws forth milk.

Dioscorides: [donkey fat] is said to restore the color of scars; its milk softens the bowels and, taken by mouth, strengthens teeth and gums. It also excellently cures wounds of the belly and rheumatism. Its urine, drunk, heals frenzied sufferers.

Haly Abbas: donkey lung, and that of its foal, if dried and ground and drunk, benefits difficulty of breathing and cough. The liver of a domestic donkey, if an epileptic eats it, benefits him. Donkey dung, if pressed on it, stops or checks bleeding from a cut vein or artery. In like manner, if some of its water is dripped into the nostrils, it entirely checks bleeding in those suffering from it. Donkey's milk is harmful against deadly medicines and benefits ulcers of the intestines and tenesmus; sheep's milk is likewise beneficial, but less so.

Pythagoras, in the book of the Romans, and Pliny, book 28: a ring made from the hoof and legs of a donkey without any black on it, if an epileptic wears it, prevents him from falling. Besides, if you fumigate a house with donkey's lung, you clean it of every creeping thing and serpent. All venomous creatures are said to flee from a burning donkey's lung. Poisons too are neutralized by drinking donkey's milk, especially if henbane has been drunk, or mistletoe, or hemlock, or sea hare, but it must be fresh, for nothing loses its power more quickly. Wild donkey remedies are more effective than the donkey's in every way; broken and boiled donkey bones are given against the poisons of the sea hare; water left over from a donkey's drinking, drunk, soothes headache. Ash of donkey hoof disperses scrofula, applied with oil or water. Also hot dung with vinegar. Likewise ash of donkey hoof mixed with its own milk removes scars and white spots of the eyes. Donkey liver heals rheumatism when ground with two parts parsley and three walnuts and honey and taken as food. Likewise liver, mixed with a little panacea-herb, dripped into the mouth, protects infants from epilepsy and other diseases. A donkey's skin, thrown over them, also makes infants fearless: its brain, smoked with honeyed water, benefits epileptic disease, or the ash of its hooves, drunk in two spoonfuls for a whole month. Likewise donkey hooves induce miscarriage - for they kill the living fetus; donkey flesh, taken in broth, heals consumptives; donkey marrow especially removes human scabies, and its urine mixed with its own mud, applied. Donkey tallow restores dark scars to natural color. Donkey kidneys, ground in undiluted wine and drunk, prevent incontinence. Likewise, aged and ground and steeped in wine, they heal the bladder and expel stones. Donkey urine, around the rising of the Dog Star, removes blemishes on the face; a drink of its milk with honey greatly benefits dysentery sufferers. Tenesmus, that is, frequent and futile urge to evacuate, is removed by drinking donkey's milk. Its dung rouses the lethargic, applied to the nostrils with vinegar. The same, applied fresh, is said to marvelously calm bleeding. The ash of the same dung, too, applied, stops bleeding. Its power, however, is more effective from males, mixed with vinegar and applied on wool for every kind of bleeding. Dung of a donkey foal, the very first it produces after birth, given in the size of a bean in wine, also heals jaundice, and this within the third day.

Isidore: the Greeks call the ox 'ton boun,' the Latins call it 'trio,' as if 'terio,' since it wears down the earth [terram terat]; the breadth of its skin from the chin to the legs is called the dewlap ['palearia'], from the skin, as if 'pellearia,' which is a sign of good breeding in an ox. Oxen have exceptional devotion toward their companions. For one, they say, seeks another with which it is accustomed to draw the plough under a shared yoke, and, by frequent lowing, faithfully testifies its affection, should the other happen to fail.

Ambrose: the ox seeks out its companion with love, and if another is substituted, does not know how to pull the yoke. Further, when rain is imminent, oxen know to keep to their stalls. But when, by natural instinct, they have gathered that the sky will change, they look outward and stretch their necks beyond the stalls, all with one shared eagerness, so as to show that they wish to go out.

Helinand of Froidmont: [on a certain deer-like ox creature] with the shape of a stag, from the middle of whose forehead, between the ears, a single horn rises, taller and straighter, and from its top these branches of ours are known, spreading like palms and boughs. The nature of male and female is the same, the shape and size of the horns the same.

Pliny, book 8: Indian oxen are reported to have the height of camels, and horns four feet broad. There are, moreover, Indian oxen with one horn and with three horns. Among these too there are solid-hooved oxen with one horn. Bulls have smaller and thinner horns than oxen. Oxen alone among animals graze walking backward; among the Garamantes, indeed, not otherwise. Their life for females is fifteen years at longest, for males twenty; their strength is at its peak at five years: they are said to grow fat from bathing in warm water, and if, the skin cut, one drives breath into their innards through a reed.
Pliny, book 5, in the same: oxen and animals having continuous teeth drink by sucking, like horses.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: oxen have no upper front teeth, just as sheep do not, nor do all ruminants; oxen, however, do shed their teeth. Their tails have a very long stalk, shaggy on one side. Among the kind of oxen, only the females have a deeper voice, whereas in every other kind it is thinner than in the males. Theophrastus proves that oxen feed on pitch, but only while alive; farmers treat oxen's worn hooves and heal them by anointing their horns with fat. And their nature is so pliable that, while the animals are still alive, their horns can be bent with hot wax, and, cut in the newborn, twisted into different directions, so that four horns are made on a single head.

Pliny, book 18, in the same: there is in the Narbonensian province a famous spring called Orga, in which grow herbs so sought after by oxen that they seek them with their whole heads submerged. But it is certain that those growing in the water are nourished only by rain [continued in a following, untranslated fragment].
Pliny, book 24, in the same: oil, poured into oxen through the anus until they belch, relieves bloating.
Pliny, in the same: oxen are killed by black hellebore, and so they avoid it when they feed on white hellebore.

Pliny, in the same: for the diseases of oxen, tallow, bran, wine, wild garlic, and boiled egg are remedies. In Cyprus oxen treat colic in themselves with human excrement. Oxen's feet, too, are treated, if their horns are first anointed with liquid pitch.
Pliny, book 30, in the same: the 'buprestis,' a creature similar to a beetle, deceives the ox among the grasses, and, once devoured, its gall, once touched, so inflames the ox that it bursts.
Pliny, in the same: salt removes oxen's mange, applied and given to be licked.

Pliny, book 24, in the same: a small, mute, voiceless, green frog, if swallowed, distends the belly of oxen. Oxen, smelling the sky and licking themselves against the grain of their hair, signal a storm.
Aristotle: the ox mates after a year, or perhaps after eight months. After two years, however, it is pregnant for nine months: it lives fifteen years, but castrated, twenty.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the ox is a clean animal according to the law, for sacrifice and for eating, since it chews the cud and has a cloven hoof; it eats straw, is pressed under the yoke, driven by the goad, ploughs the earth.

Palladius, on agriculture, book 4: oxen should be purchased in March, since their bodily condition is not yet at its fullest, so that the seller's deceit cannot hide either their faults or their stubbornness in resisting training, which the confidence of full strength can otherwise exercise. These things, however, should be looked for in oxen: that they be young, with square and large limbs and a solid body, muscles rising everywhere, large ears, a broad and curly forehead, black lips and eyes, strong horns without any deformity of curvature, crescent-shaped and open nostrils, well-dried, a muscular and compact neck, ample dewlaps hanging down toward the knees, a large chest, broad shoulders, a belly not small, spreading flanks, broad loins, a straight and flat back, solid, sinewy, and short legs, large hooves, long and bristly tails, the hair of the whole body flat and short, mostly of red or dark color. We will do better, moreover, to buy oxen from nearby places that are not affected by any variation of soil or climate. Or, if this is not available, let us transfer them from similar places to similar ones. This, however, must generally be attended to, that they be bought equal in strength for pulling, lest the strength of the more powerful one bring about the ruin of the other. In their temperament, this should be considered: that they be alert, gentle, fearful of the encouragement of shouting and the whip, eager for food; if the region's conditions permit, no food is better than green fodder; but where it is lacking, it should be administered in whatever order the abundance of fodder and the increase of labors requires.

Pliny: oxen should not be judged inferior even for a less praised appearance, especially those with the most milk, the Alpine ones, which have the smallest body and the greatest capacity for labor, joined at the head rather than the neck. Syrian oxen have no dewlap, but a hump on the back. The Carian oxen too, in a part of Asia, are ugly to look at, with a lump projecting above the shoulders from the neck, their horns loose, but are said to excel in work. The rest, of black or white color, are condemned for labor.

div.head: DE BOBUS EDOMANDIS ET IUGO PREPARANDIS

cit.quote: Palladius, in the same place: oxen should also be tamed in the same month, at three years of age, since after five years they cannot be well tamed, the hardness of their age resisting. Once caught, then, let them be tamed at once, though it is better if, while they were still young, they were made tame by frequent, gentle handling of the hand. But the stall for new oxen should have more spacious quarters, and likewise the area before the stall should be enclosed with no narrowness, and, once led out, they should not be marred by any injury. In the stall itself, moreover, crossbars should be fixed seven feet from the ground, to which the untamed oxen may be tied. Then you should choose a day free from storms and every hindrance, on which the caught oxen are led to the stall, and if their fierceness is excessive, let them be calmed for a day and a night among their bonds and by fasting. Then, with gentle calls and enticements of offered food, the herdsman, approaching not from the side or the rear, but from the front, should soothe them, handling their nostrils and back, and sprinkling them repeatedly with undiluted wine. With this precaution, however, that he not be touched by a kick or a horn - a fault which, if he senses he has overcome it at the outset, he will keep overcome. Then, calming its mouth and palate, rub them with salt, and let balls of well-salted fat down its throat, and then pour in, through its throat, a pint each from a horn, which practice will dissolve the anger of all its fierceness within three days. Some join them together and teach them to try lighter loads. And what is useful, if they are being prepared for ploughing, they should first be exercised in a well-worked field, so that new labor does not shatter their still-tender necks. A quicker method of taming, however, is to yoke a fierce ox with a gentle and strong one, by whose example they will easily be driven to all their duties: if, after taming, an ox lies down in the furrow, it should not be plied with fire or the whip, but rather, when it lies down, its feet should be so bound with cords that it cannot go forward or stand or feed. Once this is done, worn out by thirst and hunger, it will be free of this fault.

Pliny, in the same place: the taming of oxen is at three years; later than this is too late, earlier too premature. It is best, however, when a young steer is broken in alongside an already-tamed one, for we have this animal as a companion in labor and agriculture. Among the ancients it is reported that a certain man was condemned because he had killed his own ox, and was driven into exile as if he had killed his own tenant farmer.

Isaac Judaeus, on diets: beef, compared to the flesh of other herd animals, is the driest, and so generates thick, turbid, and melancholic blood, and gives much nourishment. It is disobedient to digestion, is expelled slowly from the stomach, and constipates the bowels. And if those of melancholic constitution become accustomed to it, they become spleen-afflicted, or subject to quartan fevers, or dropsical, or scabby, or leprous, according to the constitution it finds already prepared for these diseases in them. The flesh of a suckling calf, however, generates praiseworthy nourishment and is easy to digest, since its heat and moisture are present in great quantity, because of the closeness of the womb and the drinking of milk. Accordingly it makes good blood. It expels red bile from the stomach, especially if natural heat dominates in those eating it. For convalescents, however, although it does not harm them, it is nevertheless heavy for digestion because of the deficiency of their strength.

Avicenna: ox gall with soda and thyme-oil is effective for dandruff, when the head is washed with it. The same gall also opens the openings of hemorrhoids; from the same, mixed with honey, the palate is anointed for suffocation.

Dioscorides: [ox marrow] leads fresh wounds of the mouth to health. Ox dung helps against the stings of bees and wasps. A dropsy sufferer too is helped by it applied, if it lies long in the sun to dry. But the greatest benefit is provided by the dung of a male ox for women's hysterical fits, fumigated for those with a prolapsed womb.

Pliny: ox tallow with goose fat and basil juice heals ulcers and cracks of the mouth. Likewise, against poisons that kill through ulceration, ox tallow helps. Ox marrow, too, from the right foreleg, ground with blood, counters faults of the eyelashes and eyelid corners. But if there is heaviness of hearing, ox gall benefits with goat's or he-goat's urine. An ox's ankle-bone, burnt and applied, strengthens loosening, painful teeth. The same ash, too, with myrrh, makes a tooth-powder for oxen [sic - presumably 'for men']. Ox spleen is given and applied in honey for pains of the spleen. Ox milk is more medicinal than others. Indeed they report that all poisons are overcome by vomiting after ox milk. Besides, tenesmus is removed by drinking ox milk. A drink of ox milk restores an ulcerated stomach, and its gnawing pains are eased by beef mixed with vinegar and wine and cooked; for a human bite too, cooked beef applied is effective. Mange in dogs is healed with fresh ox blood, and again, once it has dried on and is washed off the next day, with lye ash.
Haly Abbas: [on] ox, bulls, wasps, ox, ox, ox, ox. [The citation is a fragmentary heading list in the source.]
Isidore: buffaloes are so named by derivation, since they are similar to oxen, yet so untamed that, out of wildness, they do not accept a yoke on their necks; Africa produces these.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the buffalo is an animal larger than the ox and taller in body, black in color; it has long, twisting horns, a long neck, a huge head, lean limbs, a small tail, and a benevolent and simple appearance. But it is of the greatest swiftness and cruelty when provoked to anger. It is most suited to human uses, and is endowed with the greatest strength. The buffalo endures labor patiently, has little hair, a terrible voice, a very rough forehead, very hard skin, and scatters earth with its foot. In its nostril a bronze ring with a small rope is placed, so that it more easily yields to man for the work imposed on it. But if the load is heavy and imposed beyond its willingness, it is at once disturbed and lies down on the ground. Nor is it easily forced to rise by blows, unless the load weighing on it is lightened: this creature is called by another name, the bison, of which Solinus says that it is a beast similar to the ox. Buffalo milk easily softens the bowels, heals fresh wounds, and benefits those who have drunk poison. Its gall too is medicinal, since it heals scars of wounds, and, mixed with milk, calms ear pains.

Solinus: bisons are in the northern region, oxen similar to wild ones, with bristly necks, shaggy manes, surpassing bulls in swiftness; once caught, they do not know how to grow tame - the unskilled common folk call these buffaloes.

Pliny: among the kinds of northern oxen, maned bisons and 'uri,' outstanding in speed, to all of which the unskilled common folk give the name of buffaloes, whereas Africa produces that animal, rather resembling a calf in a certain likeness of the neck.
Pliny: the blood of buffaloes does not thicken.
Haly Abbas: [on] buffalo young, mushrooms. Hemlock rennet. [Fragmentary heading list in the source.]
Dioscorides: the dung of a grazing buffalo, applied, removes swellings of wounds and is suited to sciatic suffering. Placed in poultices, it purges hardnesses and scrofula and dissolves pustules.

Isidore: it gave the name to camels either because, when they are loaded, they become shorter and lower, since the Greeks call low and short 'chamai,' or because it is curved in the back, for 'kamos' in Greek signifies 'curved': other regions too send these, but Arabia the most. They differ from one another, for the Arabian ones have two humps on the back, those of other regions single ones. The region of Bactria also sends the strongest camels, which never wear down their feet.

Solinus: Bactrian camels never wear down their feet, since they have, as it were, certain flexible little cushions and fleshy pads of their footprints. Some, indeed, are suited to carrying burdens. Others, however, are swifter. But the former do not take on weights beyond what is just, nor do the latter wish to go beyond their accustomed distances. They hate the horse kind. They also endure thirst for four days. But when the occasion for drinking is so great, they fill themselves only as much as satisfies past desire and long benefits the future; they seek out clear waters, and shun pure ones. Finally, where the liquid is muddier, they themselves, by constant trampling, stir up the mud so that it becomes turbid. They last, however, up to a hundred years, unless perhaps, transported to foreign lands, they contract diseases from the strangeness of a changed climate.

Pliny: the East pastures camels among its herds, of which two kinds, of Bactria and of Arabia, differ, in that the former have two humps on the back, the latter single ones, and, under the chest, another on which they can lean; in the upper row of teeth they lack teeth, as oxen do, in both kinds.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: camels alone, among horned-lacking animals, have no front teeth in the upper jaw; only the lion and the camel walk foot by foot, that is, so that the left foot does not pass the right, but follows it; buffaloes are similar to such a camel, but somewhat smaller. For it is a cloven-hoofed animal, with a slight distinction, its foot flat, with a fleshy footprint like a bear's. For this reason, on a longer journey, they wear out without shoes.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: camels have four stomachs. The first receives raw food. The second, somewhat digested. The third, more digested. The fourth, completely digested.
Ambrose: since the camel is tall, so that it may feed on the smallest plants, it has been given a neck long enough to reach the ground for the purpose of grazing.

Basil of Caesarea: the camel has a tenacious memory of wrongs; finally, if it has been struck, having long concealed its resentment, when it finds the opportune time, it at once repays the injury done to it. Hear this, then, you irascible men, to which beast you are shown to be similar.

Aristotle: camels are like horned animals, since their bellies are like those of horned creatures.
