Pliny: [horse and mare's dung, except that of virgin mares,] has an astringent power. It corrodes, edges, ulcerates: the flesh and dung of a horse fed in the field are used for wounds. Poisons of the sea hare and toxic substances are overcome by mare's milk; besides, if there is great heaviness of hearing, horse's foam or the ash of its fresh dung is dripped in with rose oil. In a horse's heart is found a bone similar to large canine teeth, with which aching teeth are rubbed. 'Hippomanes' too heals teeth; ash of horse's hoof, applied with oil or water, disperses scrofula, and hot dung with vinegar. The spleen, however, is soothed by aged horse's tongue with wine. Its rennet loosens the bowels, and so does a drink of mare's milk. Likewise horse's rennet benefits celiacs and dysentery sufferers, even if they draw blood, or the ash of its dung, or the flour of its ground teeth: the bladder, moreover, is healed and stones expelled by horse's spleen drunk in honeyed wine or wine for forty days. Ash of horse's hoof in wine or water is also beneficial. Likewise a drink of mare's milk is given for epileptic diseases; sprinkled on creeping ulcers, horse's blood eats away flesh with astringent power, and again the ash of aged horse dung. A dead fetus is expelled by horse's spleen drunk in fresh water, or fumigation with the hooves, or dry dung.

Isidore: the he-goat [hyrcus] is a wanton and lustful animal, always burning for mating, whose eyes, from lust, look sideways, whence it also took its name. For 'hyrci,' according to Suetonius, means the corners of the eyes. Its nature is so hot that only its blood dissolves the adamant stone, which neither fire nor the substance of iron can tame. Larger he-goats are called 'cunfii,' from the river Cunfe in Libya, where large ones are born.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the he-goat is a foul-smelling animal, as Isaac says; if taken as food it generates worse blood than the goat.
Pliny, book 8: males of the goat kind, that is he-goats, are approved of when they are as snub-nosed as possible, with long ears and broken-looking shoulders, and as shaggy as possible.
Pliny, book 11, in the same: sharp, thick hairs grow on he-goats, but finer ones on the females. Likewise male goats have more teeth than females.

Pliny: they say that, if its beard is stroked, the he-goat's rage is soothed. And that if the same is cut off, they do not go over to another flock. He-goat's blood is of such power that the fineness of iron tools is bent, or hardened, or polished of roughness by nothing else, not even more vehemently by a file.

Palladius: he-goats should be admitted to mating in the month of November, so that the offspring may be nurtured first by the rising of spring. But the he-goat, as said above, should be chosen that has, as it seems, two small warts hanging from its jaws, of large body, thick legs, a short and full neck, folded and heavy ears, a small head, a shiny, thick, and long coat, suited to covering the females, and, before a year old, is not yet fit; it does not last beyond six years. A female kid similar in body should be chosen, but with large udders.
Thomas Cantimpratensis: the male goat, that is the he-goat, is a spirited, warlike, and robust animal. Its greatest strength is in its forehead and flesh.

div.head: DE OPERATIONE HYRCI IN CIBORUM REMEDIO

cit.quote: Avicenna: he-goat's flesh is absolutely bad and causes quartan fevers to occur. Its blood quickly matures hot abscesses and is administered after congealing. The same, drunk, breaks a kidney stone. Fried and drunk with wine, it benefits the harm of an Armenian arrow-wound. He-goats' liver reveals whether one is epileptic, for when an epileptic eats it, he has an attack. Water of goat's liver benefits, eaten and applied to the affected area, and leaning over its vapor. He-goat's fat is of more vehement dissolving power than others. He-goat's gall roots out bad flesh, benefits ulcers growing in the ear. It also benefits elephantiasis and varicose veins when applied. The gall of the wild he-goat is a theriac for venomous bites. The he-goat's heel-bone, that is its ankle bone, as is said, with oxymel removes the spleen and stirs mating.

Isaac Judaeus, on diets: he-goat's flesh generates even worse blood than goat's flesh. Hot he-goat's blood, applied, as Dioscorides says, checks spider-bites and bad wounds. Dissolving he-goat's tallow, if dissolved with blood-red wool and applied with unwashed wool, helps gout sufferers, especially if it has received saffron. He-goat's gall, applied, removes thickness of the eyelids and suits scrofula sufferers. Applied on wool and placed on the navel, it loosens infants' bowels.

Pliny: he-goat's blood, boiled on coals, heals the spleen, since some think night-blind people are healed by it, or by goat liver boiled in dry wine. He-goat's warm liver, applied, removes leprosy, as goat gall removes elephantiasis. Likewise warm he-goat's liver, applied, removes freckles, mixed with sponge ash and native sulfur, to the thickness of honey. The bite of a rabid dog is healed by applying he-goat's liver. He-goat's tallow, with an equal part of chickweed, a third part mustard, heals gout. Women develop distaste for love if given he-goat's urine to drink, mixed with spikenard for the disgust of it, as Eschines reports; goat's blood, as said above, with marrow, helps dropsy sufferers, and is more effective if the he-goat is fed on mastic.

Pliny, in the same: ibexes or roe deer are animals of the goat kind of marvelous swiftness, although their heads are burdened with vast horns like sword-sheaths. In this they balance themselves so that, as if whirled by some engine, especially on rocks, and wishing to leap from one mountain to another, they spring back nimbly wherever they please.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the ibex is a small, most swift animal, its head burdened with vast horns: it dwells among rocks and breeds there, of which indeed fuller mention has already been made above. There is also a kind of bird called 'ibis,' of which mention has likewise been made above in the treatise on birds: whence this verse: the ibex is an animal, the ibis a bird, and the envious ibis. So mention of the ibex animal has been made above under the name 'caprea,' in this same book, where indeed herd animals are treated.
Isidore: fawns are the young of stags, so named from 'nodding' [innuendo], since they are hidden at their mother's nod.

Solinus: for stags, as said above, carefully hide their tender young, that is conceal them, among the depths of thickets of trees or grasses, or chastise them with a blow of the foot to keep them hidden. And once strength has matured for flight, they teach them by the exercise of running, and accustom them to leap over steep places. The rennet of a fawn killed in its mother's womb, however, is generous against poisons.
Avicenna, on the rennet of stags' fawns: it heals from all poisons and bites.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the fawn too, as is read, is agile, swift of course, sharp of sight, has a cloven hoof, dwells in high places, and feeds on the heights. Whence it is written: be like, my beloved, a roe deer or a fawn of stags upon the mountains of Bethel.
Ambrose, in the Hexaemeron: the fawn does not yet have horns, and yet practices beforehand with its forehead, and threatens with weapons it has not yet experienced.

Aristotle: if stags' fawns are castrated before the growth of their horns, horns do not grow on them at all; but if after the horns have appeared, they do not grow further, nor do they shed them any more.
Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: a stag's fawn, caught by a man and led a short time in a bond, follows him even unbound afterward.
Isidore: the hare [lepus], as if 'levipes' [light-foot], since it runs swiftly; for it is a swift animal and quite timid.
Ambrose: the hare turns white in winter, and returns to its own color in summer.

Pliny: there are several kinds of hares. In the Alps they are white, and it is believed they eat snow as food in the winter months. Certainly, as the snow melts, they turn reddish every year. Of the hare kind too are those Spain calls rabbits, of countless fecundity, bringing famine to the Balearic Islands by devastating the crops. They cast ferrets into the burrows, which are full of holes in the ground - whence the animal's name too - and thus catch them as they are driven out above.
Pliny: [on] the hare. [The citation breaks off in the source after this heading word.]

Pliny, book 11, in the same: hares sleep with open eyes and do not grow fat, just as partridges do not. The hare is the most despicable of animals, and Trogus reports that it has hairs inside its cheeks, and likewise on its feet.

Aristotle: the hare, indeed, is of much hair, and has hairs inside its jaws and likewise on its feet. Alone among those having teeth in both jaws it has rennet. The female hare sometimes mounts the male at mating time. Its fur, moreover, is soft, but very fine. It has a large heart, like other animals that are timid. The vulture catches and kills the hare. Hares too, if brought to the land of Ithaca, will not live, but sometimes seem to return to the sea.
Ambrose: we have learned that hares turn white in winter, but return to their own color in summer. We say this so that we may believe in the future transformation of the good at the resurrection.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the hare is a most gentle, weak, timid, and fugitive animal, long-eared; it has longer hind legs, whence it climbs more easily than it descends. It is unclean according to the law, since it does not chew the cud, though it does have a cloven hoof. It places its resting-place on a rock, and sleeps with open eyes. It has, moreover, both sexes at once, whence the comic poet Terence: you, he says, are a hare and seek soft flesh, as if to say: since you now play the part of a woman, now of a man, why do you seek a woman to caress? The hare, moreover, has lips always in motion.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the hare, vigorous in speed, is the most timid of beasts, and so rarely goes out to feed except at night; at harvest time it exults and is moved to play. On Pliny's testimony, it never grows fat. But if it is raised within the roof of a house with men, and lacks the exercise of speed, an unnatural fatness grows over its kidney and it dies. Much exercise, then, reduces in the animal the fatness it might otherwise gain from much food. Since the hare is born prey for all, it was fitting that it multiply beyond measure. Whence, alone almost among animals producing young, it carries at once one offspring clothed in fur in the womb, another without fur, and another still laid up in seed. And so Basil says that wherever they have begun to dwell, their kind is not easily wiped out. In certain regions, however, according to Ambrose, they turn white in winter and return to their original color in summer. It is said that the weasel plays with the hare and, when it is finally worn out, seizes its throat with its teeth and grips most fiercely. The hare, feeling the bite, tries to escape by fleeing, but is weighed down by the treacherous burden. And at last, as it collapses, the wicked little beast kills and eats it. The hare, moreover, changes its sex every year.

Physiologus: [on the female] of the hare mounting the male in mating. Grains of gold are gathered at the hare's feet, lest they perish. But let not your mouth be full of hair, as the inside of a hare's mouth, but let your feet be hairy beneath without weight, like a hare's feet, lest they be hurt in leaping.

Alexander Neckam: [it is said] that the hare, having the character of the nobler sex, carries young hares in its womb. Is it not a hermaphrodite? They add too that once it has conceived, even while the young hares are already growing large, it conceives again.

Isaac Judaeus: although the hare is dry and generates thick blood, it is nevertheless better than he-goats and young goats. Accordingly it suits those wishing to have dry constitutions. It is contrary, however, to those keeping a light diet.

Avicenna: the wild hare is cold and dry, and cleanses the stomach. Its blood cleans ringworm, and the ash of its head heals baldness. Its brain, applied, benefits tremor occurring in the course of illness. Likewise, with the same brain, children's gums are anointed. The property that is in it is that teeth arise quickly and come through easily without pain. Its rennet is better than all rennets of its kind; this, drunk with vinegar, benefits epilepsy. The same, with vinegar, is a theriac for poisons. Likewise fried hare's blood benefits dysentery and abscess of the intestines and old resolution [of the sinews], and also the poison of an Armenian arrow. Hare's flesh is hot and dry; roasted, it is good for ulcers of the intestines. In its broth, gout sufferers and those having pain of the joints sit. And its effect is close to the effect of fox broth. Warm hare's blood, applied to ringworm and vitiligo, benefits them. The same, eaten, matures hot abscesses and light ones.

Dioscorides: [hare's blood] checks spider-bites and bad wounds. Hare's lung marvelously removes eye pains, applied and bound on. Likewise crushed and applied, it heals chilblains and feet injured by shoes. Hare's urine, drunk with spikenard and water, cures dropsy sufferers. In infants it provokes urine, softens the bowels, checks ear pains.

Dioscorides, the same: a hare's little brain, eaten, removes bodily tremor. Ground and eaten, it strengthens infants' teeth. Its head, burnt with bear fat and applied as a poultice, corrects baldness. Its rennet, drunk, checks the menses and stanches flux of blood. It heals epileptics, helps against poisons. With vinegar it dissolves milk curdled in women's breasts. Drunk, it also does not allow a viper's bite to harm. Its warm juice, applied, corrects blemishes. Likewise hare's brain, ground and drunk, corrects bed-wetters and does not allow urine to be passed.
Rhazes, the physicist: hare's flesh generates melancholy more than others.

The Physicus: hare's rennet is cold and dry, and has a constricting power from its coldness, and, from the property of milk, a cleansing and purifying power. It checks any flux, and strengthens the members: it has the greatest power against epilepsy.

Aesculapius: hare's lung, placed over the eyes, removes pain. Its fresh heart, hung on the neck, helps those with quartan fever. Dried, ground, and drunk, it suits epileptics. Its gall clarifies the eyes. Its kidneys, dried and drunk, expel stones. Its blood with warm water does the same.

Zeno, in the same place: and for one afflicted with chills from fever, if a hare's heart or a shrew's foot is hung on him, it helps. In colic ailments too, 'orcob,' that is hare's rennet, hung over the sufferer, helps him.
Aristotle: among animals, as said, having teeth in both jaws, rennet is not found, except in the hare alone; the rennet of the hare is especially effective against flux of the bowels.

Pliny: some use hare's rennet with vinegar against the scorpion and the shrew-mouse and the spider, and they say those anointed with it are not stung. It is likewise effective against the bites or stings of sea creatures, and against drunk bull's blood. And it is added to antidotes against poisons; poured into the ear, it is effective against toothache. It also benefits heaviness of hearing; and, applied to the udder, checks infants' bowels. Hare's brain in wine checks incontinence of urine. Its roasted testicles, or its rennet with goose fat in barley meal; its aged kidneys too expel stones, and its feet, bound on, benefit gout. Ash of hare's fur benefits feet burned by cold. And its lung, cut open, is applied to bruises, or lung-ash. Hare's rennet also checks bleeding, and the ash of its fur. Hare's ash with myrtle oil calms headache. Cato judges that sleep is induced by eating hare in food. Ash of hare's dung in warm wine also benefits dysentery sufferers.

Isidore: the mule [mulus] has a name drawn from the Greek, namely because, driven under the yoke of millers, it draws the slow millstones in a circle, grinding. The Jews assert that Anah, great-grandson of Esau, first had herds of mares mounted by donkeys in the desert, so that from this new kinds of mules might be born, distinct from other animals.

Pliny: from a donkey and a mare, indeed, as said above, a mule is produced in the thirteenth month, an animal outstanding in strength for labors. For such offspring, they choose mares neither younger than four years nor older than ten. And they say each kind is kept from the other, except in the infancy of the offspring, which they approach once nursed with milk. For this reason they bring stolen foals in darkness to the udders of mares or the young donkeys to the udders of female donkeys. And so it has been observed that what is born from two different kinds becomes of a third kind, and resembles neither parent. And these very creatures, so born, do not breed - true of every kind of animal - and so mules do not give birth: a mule's tendency to kick is checked by more frequent drinking of wine; it is recorded in Athenian monuments that a mule lived eighty years. This animal is most impatient of cold, and so is not bred in the Black Sea region, nor at the spring equinox as other herd animals are, but at the solstice.
Pliny, in the same: mules' hooves alone are unaffected by poisons, or even by the poison of the river Styx, by which Alexander the Great is said to have perished, but every other material is.
Pliny: mules do not kick when they have drunk wine.

Alexander Neckam: the mule is a cunning animal, for, by kicking backward, it lays a trap for the muleteer and strikes with its foot the master goading it. It is also disobedient to goads, and when it sees a farmhouse where it thinks it will spend the night, it suddenly feigns lameness, pretending it is unable to go further. But the rider, to whom its tricks are known, restores its former strength by repeated use of the spurs.

Physiologus: the mule is, as it were, midway between the horse and the donkey; whoever rides it is carried, as it were, by temperance. For whoever is carried by pride is carried, as it were, by a horse; whoever by sloth, as it were, by a donkey: this animal is domesticated at every season, as man is.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the mule, born from a donkey and a mare, has certain traits proper to the donkey, namely long ears, a harsh bray, a cross on the shoulders, small feet, and a lean body. The rest, however, it has like the horse. Mules never conceive, since the surplus of menstruation in them, along with food, passes into the nourishment of the body; likewise the blood that nature does not need exits with the surplus of the bladder. There is also another reason, since this animal is generated outside nature, and its nature is made diverse, in the horse, which is of hot nature, and the donkey, which is of the utmost cold. And so, in an offspring generated so diversely and of poor constitution, there cannot be a harmony of parts and an ordered nature, such that it might generate, as if from its own kind, one like itself, since the mule has the substance proper to its own kind. And so in the annals of the Romans, mules giving birth was regarded as a portent.

Aristotle: the mule is a hairy animal: in it the front parts of the neck extend close to part of the head and the tip of the shoulder-blades, and it has a mane, as the horse does. Nor does it have a cloven foot, but a hoof-covering at the end of the foot. It sheds its teeth, as the horse and donkey do, and has gall attached to the liver. It too eats fruit and feeds on plants, and the mare is impregnated by it. And the more it drinks of water, the more its food benefits it. It has soft hair, a narrow spleen, like man and the donkey; a single belly, like other hoofed animals. The kind of mules discharges menstrual moisture, which other four-footed creatures, bending their feet backward, do not do. And mules' bodies are large, since the menstrual surplus passes into the formation and nourishment of their bodies. The blood they do not need exits with the bladder's surplus. And so male mules do not smell female mules' urine, as other hoofed beasts do: finally, the kind of mules burns in mating, although male and female mules cannot breed, yet it is possible for a female mule to be impregnated, though rarely, which has happened in the past, but she cannot nourish and feed it until its formation is complete: the male, however, can breed at certain times, since he is hotter than the female. And what is generated from them will be extraordinary, an incidental occurrence. Though the mule is great-hearted, it is timid, and does not have gall at all, unlike the horse and donkey.

Pliny: mules, as said, are bred at the solstice. Their gestation from the thirtieth month is quickest, but from three years old is normal. They report that female mules do not give birth. Theophrastus, however, reports that in Cappadocia they do give birth, but that this animal there is of its own separate kind. Mules swift in running are bred from a mare and tamed wild donkeys: outstanding hardness of hooves, but with a wrinkled body and an untamed yet noble spirit. One bred from a wild donkey and a female donkey, however, surpasses all.
Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: from a donkey and a mare, indeed, as said, mules are bred. From a female donkey and a horse, however, hinnies or 'burduli.'

Palladius: to produce the kind of mules, one should choose a mare of large body, solid bones, and outstanding form, in which one seeks not speed but strength. The proper age for this mating is from four years old to ten. If a male donkey, once admitted, disdains the mare, we bring in a female donkey, shown beforehand, until the pleasure of mating is aroused, and once she is withdrawn, the mare's lust, now stirred, will not reject him, and, seized by the allurements of his kind, will consent to the alien union. If, raging, he wounds the mares presented to him with his bite, he may be somewhat tamed by labor. They are bred from a horse and a female donkey, or a wild donkey and a mare, but no such animal is nobler than that born when a donkey sires it. Useful breeding stallions, however, will be born from a wild donkey and a female donkey, which will later restore agility and strength in the offspring that follows. The breeding donkey, however, should be of this kind: a large, solid, muscular body, tight and strong limbs, black or mouse-grey or reddish in color. If, however, he bears hairs of a different color on his eyelids or ears, he will pass on this variation. Younger than three years, or older than ten, he should not be admitted. A yearling female mule should be weaned from her mother and pastured through rough mountains, so that, finding labor at a tender age, she may grow accustomed to it and not despise it once grown. But a smaller donkey is especially necessary for the farm, since it both endures labor and does not refuse neglect, in a manner of speaking.

Avicenna: ash of mule hide and the like is applied to burns from fire, and to hot ulcers when they are not accompanied by an abscess. It is also a remedy for chafing of the feet from shoes and of the hips, and for fistulas.
Belbetus, in the book On the Senses: if you fumigate a house with a mule's left hoof, no shrew-mouse will remain in it.
Pliny: ash of mule or she-mule hooves with myrtle oil fills in bald patches.
Aesculapius: if a she-mule's ear-lobes and a hinny's testicles are sewn onto a woman, she will not conceive.

Isidore: the sheep [ovis] is a soft herd animal, unarmed in wool and body, of gentle flesh, named from offering [oblatio], namely because among the ancients, in the beginning, not bulls but sheep were slaughtered in sacrifice. Some of these are called 'bidentes' [two-toothed], since among eight teeth they have two taller ones, which the pagans especially offered in sacrifice.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the sheep, harmed by scent alone, avoids it; at the approach of winter it insatiably tears at grass.

Aristotle: sheep are more peaceful than other animals and closer to men. In them a lack of understanding abounds more than in other four-footed animals; they have feet cloven in two, and, at the tip, hoof-coverings in place of claws, like the he-goat and the stag; they have more milk than their young need, as also suits cows, so that it may be the matter of cheese, especially both kinds of milk. Sheep's kidneys fatten quickly. They fatten from drinking, and so shepherds often give them salt. But when fat multiplies too much in their kidneys, they die. Sheep in Germany have a large tail, so much so that its length is one cubit. Among other animals, indeed, sheep give milk for a long time, namely for seven months. Shepherds train sheep to walk quickly at the hearing of a certain voice. They also recognize which can endure winter, since the weak one is that which does not shake ice off itself. In Libya, horns quickly appear on the heads of rams. And according to Homer, horns are also on the heads of the females. Sheep's eyes are black, more so than those of other animals. Their fat is greater than the fat of other animals; the cow and the goat and the sheep have many stomachs.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: sheep fatten by drinking much, this especially after midday, if they drink muddy water; from fat, however, they become sterile. Likewise sheep led to pasture in dry places live longer. In marshy places, however, if they take pasture frequently, they become diseased and cannot live long. In May, however, or after May, if honeyed dew falls on the grasses at night, they say sheep die quickly from this. But in August, if they eat dry ears of grain to satiety and afterward drink, their innards burst at once and they die. A sheep from a burning house can scarcely be driven out, and if driven out, unless held back by force, runs back into the fire. Sheep of good stock are those that recognize their own shepherd apart from others and flee thieves. Shepherds are accustomed to give sheep salt in their food, so that they drink more and thereby give more abundant milk. They also take a sign of those that can endure winter thus: in winter they throw icy water on their tails. For the one that shakes it off is strong, but the one that does not shake it off is altogether weak.

Physiologus: sheep, for the most part strong, go out to desert places and stay under the rain. Nor do they move, until the shepherd comes to them with the rams, and then they follow the rams themselves. Sheep, moreover, are washed with clear water; shepherds recognize which sheep can endure winter, since the weak one among them does not shake ice off itself; a diseased sheep taints the flock. From the skin of a slaughtered sheep, too, good parchment is never made, nor ever from thick skin. The sheep does not feel or grieve the shearing of its fleece, and feeds the one who shears it with its milk and flesh.
Pythagoras, in the book of the Romans: sheep and domestic four-footed animals, when they see the eye of a wolf gouged out, fear and flee.

Belbetus, in the same place: if sheep eat grass where leeches mate, leeches are generated in them and eat their liver: pestilence too befalls all herd animals, when, in spring and at the end of summer, spiders breed in their webs among the grasses of the fields. For whatever creature tastes from that dies.

Palladius: for the herd's sake, whether for the appeasement of the gods or for the use of fleeces, and just as oxen serve men's labors, so bodily care is owed to the flock. In the sheep considerable good breeding is shown by the shortness of the legs and the covering of the belly. Those you see with these bare, they used to call 'tapitae' [bare-bellied] and condemn. The head is the weakest part of the flock, wherefore they must be made to graze with heads turned from the sun. Indeed the woolly creatures are the most foolish of animals. Where they have feared to enter, they will follow if one is seized by a horn and led. Their life is longest at ten years. In Ethiopia, thirteen.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: it is clear that the sheep is simple, calm, very gentle, harming no one, timid, chews the cud and has a cloven hoof, feeds on dry fodder, provides milk and flesh for food, wool for clothing, hide for writing and for many other uses. Its dung too for fertilizing and enriching the soil. These indeed are called 'pecora' or 'pecudes' [herd animals] in natural philosophy, and their flesh is called 'carnes pecorum' or 'pecorinae,' as will appear below.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: there are four kinds of all these. For some cannot go far to pasture, and these need gardens and streams. Some too are pregnant and heavy, and need an attentive shepherd, who carries the pregnant ones so they are not burdened in crossing. Some, too, are fat and strong, and equally need a shepherd to look after them, so that they never lack wholesome pasture, lest they weaken and die. Some, however, are prone to running off and wandering, and these too need a shepherd to catch them with a staff or by hand and bring them back to the flock. In many parts of the world, as said, sheep produce two broods, especially in Ethiopia.

Peter Comestor: the sheep of Mesopotamia and Italy are said to be the same, so much so that they lamb twice a year. Whence the poet: those twice pregnant, that is, the spring offspring, are better. The last, that is those conceived in autumn, are worse. Similarly too those born at the very end of spring, since in those slower to seek mating, nature is less vigorous. Whence, at the late mating, Jacob did not place his rods in the water troughs, but only at the first mating, so that in their sight sheep might conceive such offspring.

Valerius Maximus, book 1: further, as already said above, on the island of Cephalonia, whereas all herd animals everywhere are refreshed daily by the use of water, on this island the herd animals, for the greater part of the year, quench their thirst with their mouths open, taking in the winds from on high.

Pliny, on herd animals, in the same place: there is in Spain, and especially in Corsica, a kind not much unlike the sheep, the mouflon, with a goat-like fleece closer to a goat's coat than to a sheep's, from whose kind, and from sheep, the ancients called those born 'umbri.' In Syria, sheep's tails are a cubit long, and most of the wool production is from that region. Of sheep, there are then two chief kinds: the 'roofed' and the 'farm' kind. The former is softer, the latter more delicate at pasture, feeding among brambles while roofed.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the sheep, as said above, according to Ambrose, at the approach of winter is insatiable for food and tears at grass without restraint, since it senses the harshness of winter beforehand, so as to stuff itself with fodder before it fails, scorched by frost; sheep often graze grass down to the roots. But if they graze on trees, these scarcely ever thrive again. Their bite, too, is deadly to many trees. Pastured in dry places, they live longer.

Aristotle: for these, in autumn, cucumbers prepared with salt are given for the increase of milk. They fatten, moreover, on lentils and chaff with salt. They also fatten by drinking water. And in summer, cold northern water benefits them; in autumn, warm southern water. Pasture at the end of the day, and movement along paths, benefits them; but by labor they grow lean. A sheep or lamb, if its kidneys grow fat so that they are covered all around with tallow, dies; whence, since through good pasture tallow multiplies in the kidneys, sheep are often moved from their pastures, so that they do not take more than necessary. In Egypt sheep are very large, since there they have much food.

Palladius, book 12: pastures useful for the sheep kind are those roused either in fallow land or in drier meadows, but marshy ones are harmful, and wooded ones injurious to woolly animals; frequent sprinkling of salt, however, mixed into the pastures or often offered in troughs, is said to relieve their distaste for food. For through the winter, if there is scarcity, hay or chaff or vetch, or the easier fare of elm leaves kept in store, or ash, should be offered. In summer months they should graze at the first light of dawn, when the mixture of dew commends the sweetness of the tender grass. At the fourth hour, as it grows warm, a drink of muddy river or well water should be offered, or of a spring. In the noonday heat a valley or a shady tree should be sought. Then, when the day has already turned and the tree's shade lengthens, and the ground first grows moist with the evening dew, let us call the flock back to pasture. But on the dog-days and in summer days, sheep should be pastured so that the heads of the flock are always turned away from the sun's glare. In winter or spring, however, unless the frost has thawed, they should not go out to pasture. For frost-covered grass will bring disease to this kind, and then watering once will suffice. It is the custom to raise Greek sheep, like the Ascanian or Tarentine kind, in the stable rather than the field, and to line with boards the ground alone on which they are shut in, so that their resting places are safe, because of the harm to the precious fleece, lest moisture spoil it. But for three days throughout the whole year, on a sunny day, it will be necessary to wash the sheep and anoint them with oil and wine, because of the serpents that often hide beneath the mangers; cedar or galbanum, or a woman's hair, or stag's horns, should often be burnt.

Aristotle: the sheep mates after a year and lambs up to nine years, or up to eleven, or its whole life if well cared for; sheep drinking salt water mate earlier. In mating they must turn their faces toward the north, so that they conceive males. And if there are white veins under its tongue, it will produce a white lamb; if black, a black one; if both, likewise of two colors; and if red, reddish. Toward Thrace there are two rivers, of which one, drunk before mating, makes lambs' colors black, and the other white, and another still reddish. When goats and sheep grow fat, they are more sluggish. The sheep proper to Ethiopia lives fourteen years, and the goat eleven, and they bear twins. And if the food is suitable, the ram or he-goat will be vigorous: sheep and goats, if impregnated in a place facing the force of the north wind, bear males. But facing south, they bear females: a sheep, indeed, if thunder occurs and it alone remains impregnated, will miscarry.

Pliny, in the same place: the mating of sheep is from the setting of Arcturus, that is from the third day before the ides of May, to the setting of the Eagle constellation, that is up to the thirteenth day before the kalends of August. They complete gestation in a hundred fifty days; those conceived later, however, are weak, and offspring born after that time the ancients called 'cordi.' Thunder causes miscarriage in solitary sheep. The remedy is to gather them together, so they are helped by company. Males should be conceived with the blowing of the north wind, females with the south, and in that kind the faces of rams are especially observed, since whatever color of veins they have under the tongue, that is the color of the wool in the offspring, and varied if there are several; a change of water and drink also causes variation.

Ambrose: the sheep, however, among many thousands of little lambs, recognizes only its own offspring; there is one bleat and the same appearance among the many, yet she distinguishes her own offspring from the rest; the shepherd errs in distinguishing the sheep and is deceived by appearance, but the sheep is not deceived by devotion. There is one scent for all. But nature nevertheless has its own domestic scent, which the offspring seems to give off by a certain special property.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: [when] sheep hasten to mating, it is a very bad sign, namely that there is plague among them. Likewise if an old sheep seeks mating after the due time, it is a bad sign. In many parts of the world sheep produce two broods, and especially in Ethiopia: and just as a lamb recognizes its own mother among other sheep by her bleating, so the mother admits the lamb to her tail and udders once she has smelled it.

Isaac Judaeus: mutton, or the flesh of herd animals, is hotter and drier than pork. It is also hotter and moister than beef and goat's flesh, whence it is more tender and easier to digest, and descends most easily from the stomach; it moistens the bowels more than goat's or sheep's flesh does, yet is less moist than pork, for it does not have moisture opposed to digestion as pork does, nor lubricating moisture, so that it emerges before full cooking. But its nourishment varies according to the diversity of age and constitution. The variation of nourishment by age is fourfold. For there is the suckling and the yearling or young one. The adult, or already fully grown, and the decrepit. The suckling is viscous and indigestible. The young one is of less moisture and viscosity. The adult, however, of moderate constitution. The decrepit, however, worse than the rest, since colder and drier: and so woody and tasteless. Sheep eaten generate viscous phlegm, unless those eating them are of dry constitution.
Avicenna: mutton is good when, along with heat, it is fine, and is altogether drier than the flesh of a [certain other] four-footed animal.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: [on] ram's and lamb's flesh, mention has already been made above; these animals, of the same kind as the sheep, nevertheless differ in flesh as food according to the difference of sex or age.
Palladius, book 5: sheep in warm places should be shorn in the month of April, and the late-born should be marked in the same month.

Palladius, the same: further, in temperate places, the shearing of sheep should be held in the month of May. But sheared sheep should be treated with this ointment. You will mix the juice of boiled lupine, dregs of old wine, and olive lees, in equal measure, and take care to spread all of it, blended into one substance. Then, after three days, if the sea is nearby, let them be dipped at the shore's edge; if we pasture inland, rainwater boiled with a little salt should, under the open sky, wash the sheared and anointed limbs of the flock. Treated this way, the flock is said neither to become mangy throughout the year, nor to fail to produce long and soft wool.

Pliny: sheep are not sheared everywhere, but in certain places the custom of plucking the wool persists, and, matted together by itself, it makes clothing, and if vinegar is added, it resists iron, indeed even fire. In Syria, as said above, sheep's tails are a cubit long, and most wool production is from that region; black wools take no dye.
Aristotle: the wool of sheep that a wolf has eaten, after shearing, receives more lice in the cloth made from it.
Thomas Cantimpratensis: sheep that are especially woolly in their tails are notable for goodness; their wool is praised for the exceptional fineness of the fleece and its curled, twisted density.

Isidore: wool [lana] is so named from tearing [laniando], that is, plucking. Hence too the fleece [vellus] is so named, since wool was formerly plucked, not sheared. The pagans say Minerva first showed the use of wool-working. They also report that she arranged the loom and dyed wools, and that she was endowed with many talents besides.

Pliny: [wool] applied to the bites of a rabid dog is removed after the seventh day. The same wool, dyed with soda, sulfur, oil, vinegar, and boiling pitch, applied as hot as possible twice a day, calms pains of the loins. Wool from the neck is most praised of all. Its ash, ground, is applied to the wounded, to burns, and is added to eye medicines. Likewise for fistulas and suppurating ears, its power is astringent, and it very effectively cleanses the cheeks. It also benefits ailments of the genitals.

Dioscorides: [wool grease] with goose fat added heals ear pain, removes itching of the eyelids, clears roughness and scabbiness of the eyelids. It counters falling hair. This same juice, if burnt in a new earthen vessel over a slow fire, until the fat is rendered out by the fire - the powder of this burning is mixed into eye-salves. Taken with wine, three obols' worth, it counters venomous bites. It heals celiacs and dysentery sufferers. It checks a woman's flux of blood. It dissolves coagulated blood. It cleanses wounds of the chest, and, drunk by a woman after childbirth, makes her fertile. That grease which is gathered from unwashed wools is called 'hyssopus,' and is mixed into emollient plasters and pessaries.

Avicenna: 'hyssopus' is a moist filth gathered on the wool of sheep grazing in Armenia, and it is spread over spurge plants and takes on their power, and their milk. It is hot in the fourth degree, moist in the first: it is maturing and dissolving. It dissolves hard abscesses when a plaster is made from it. Applied and drunk, it benefits coldness of the liver and abscesses of the eyes. It dissolves hardnesses that are in parts of the bladder and womb, and benefits their coldness and that of the kidneys.
Thomas Cantimpratensis: [these things] of the sheep are useful, namely wool, hide, flesh, and sheep dung too is judged better than the dung of all other animals.

Haly Abbas: a sheep's head, if boiled, and an enema made with its broth, moistens the lower intestines and kidneys, fattens the body, increases mating if it is prepared from hot and dry things. Sheep's liver, roasted and eaten, constricts the bowels. Sheep dung, if ground and mixed with vinegar, heals ant-like varicose sores and benefits excess flesh.

Pliny: rennet of a herd animal, and likewise ram's-flesh broth, is effective against blister-beetle poisoning. Itching of the head, too, is removed by sheep's gall with Cimolian chalk applied to the head until it dries: sheep's milk too is effective for many things when warm, effective against all poisons except for those who have drunk the blister-beetle called 'buprestis' or aconite. The gall of a herd animal, too, with honey, cleans the ears. Its liver benefits eyes suffused with blood. Ash of herd animal dung with cyprus oil and honey fills in bald patches.

Avicenna: fresh sheepskin, applied to a bruise at once, that is immediately, prevents harm from it. It is also suited to deceptive [i.e. slow-healing] ulcers and to scabies and itching. Sheep dung benefits erysipelas. Burnt, however, especially when prepared with vinegar, it is applied to the bite of a rabid dog. Likewise with vinegar it benefits ant-like warts. And, applied to burns from fire, with wax and rose oil. Sheep's milk is thick and rich, of much cheese-content and buttery quality. It helps coughing blood even more than goat's milk.
Isaac Judaeus: milk of herd animals is heavier in smell than cow's milk, and so more phlegmatic.
Dioscorides: sheep's cheese nourishes more than others, and constricts the bowels less, since it is sharp.

Isidore: the pig [porcus] is so named as if 'spurcus' [filthy]. For it gorges itself in mire, plunges into mud, and smears itself with slime; hence too we speak of filth [spurcitia] or bastards [spurii]: we call its hairs 'setae' [bristles], named from the pig [sus], whence shoemakers [sutores] too are so called, since they sew [suunt] with bristles.

Aristotle: the pig has thick hairs, because of the thickness of its skin, and a spleen similar to man's spleen, and a belly likewise, that is intestines. Flux of the bowels in it has no remedy, however; it has a single belly, like other animals having teeth in both jaws and cloven hooves. The males have tusks; the females do not have projecting tusks; and they bite only because of sharpness [of hunger]. The pig has teeth in both jaws and does not shed its teeth entirely; it also has hoof-coverings on its feet. Its heart has little blood, having a division at the joint; it fights with the wolf, and if one of its eyes is removed, it will die in most cases. Scorpions bite black pigs and kill them. In certain regions the pig's belly is large and it does not have a cloven foot: the pig is very irascible, since in its blood there are many 'hairs,' that is fine, hair-like particles; the pig, more than all animals, eats roots, and quickly fattens on them; it also eats serpents.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the pig, that is the domestic boar, is a savage and unclean beast, and dwells most gladly in filthy places. Among these one is always stronger and dominates the rest, and if a stronger one comes upon it, it strives to gain victory by strength, and once the defeated one yields, the victor dominates the rest. At its dung the whole herd, rushing up, is roused to a frenzy, and it is dangerous to walk among them in their anger. At the last quarter of the moon, the pig's brain is reported to shrink more than in any other animal.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the pig does not chew the cud, and so is reckoned among the unclean animals according to the law. It feeds indiscriminately on clean and unclean things, and delights in mud. It digs mud with its snout, grunts horribly, and especially, when one is struck, the rest grunt and gather there as if sympathizing. But at once, forgetting their lament, they return to the mud or to food. It is said, moreover, that no animal's internal body resembles the human body so closely, in disposition and number of parts, as the pig's body: whence physicians and others investigating the interior of the human body examine the interior of pigs as a kind of model.

Physiologus: the pig's eyes have a natural formation such that it always looks toward the ground from necessity. The pig, as is reported, mostly dies, if one of its eyes is removed. In the region of Jerusalem there are pigs of marvelous size, having tusks a cubit long.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: it is proper to the pig to seek food from ground it has rooted up, and to sweat, mouth to the ground, over vile and filthy things. For it feeds indiscriminately, as said, on clean and unclean, and delights in mud.

Aristotle: the pig is among the four-footed animals, having a broad snout-appendage for hollowing out the earth and eating roots; more than all animals it eats roots, and quickly fattens on them; it also eats serpents. It has a belly larger than the dog's, having a coiling within itself, so that the digestion of food takes a long time; it fattens on barley and millet and apples, but especially fattens and grows delicate at rest, and various food fattens it, and mixed food helps it. And certain foods bloat it, some generate flesh, some fat. It delights in eating acorns, which render its flesh moist; it has two tusks. Its impregnated female, however, if she eats much of the acorns, will miscarry: chickpeas too are effective for the pig. Barley is good food for leaping males. Boiled barley too for impregnated females; a sixth part of the pig's food passes into hairs and blood and the like.

Palladius, book 3: in pigs, besides other benefits, this advantage too is found, that, let loose in vineyards not yet budding, or after the harvest with the grass cut, they imitate the diligence of a digger.

Aristotle: the pig mates at eight months, but generates something weak then. It produces many offspring, because of the abundance of semen: other cloven-hoofed animals produce few, and it lives up to fifteen years. When fattened, it can mate at any time, summer and winter, night and day; the sow is pregnant for four months, is fertile in offspring, for she bears twenty young and cannot suffice to nurse them all: she has teats over her whole belly, and not all equal. The first of these, that is the one nearest the armpit, she gives to the first-born piglet, the male pig soliciting the female; she raises her ears, and before she has lowered them, does not consent. The pig produces many offspring, because of the abundance of semen. It also breeds many times a year: because of heat and abundance of food: after eight months the male pig leaps: and the one-year-old sow gives birth. In certain regions, however, the male pig mates after four months, and the sow gives birth after six. When she gives birth, however, she grows lean. Likewise, if a sow was previously a virgin, she will bear offspring of small body. And once she reaches fifteen years, she will not give birth. If she is very fat and pampered, then her milk after birth will be scant. Likewise, better offspring of the sow are those born in her youth, and better too those born in winter: worse, however, those born in summer, small and lean and moist.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the pig has much power of mating beyond other animals, provided it is fat; sows, however, are said to become so wild in mating that they tear at a man, especially one dressed in white clothing. They are castrated, however, with the crest cut away, and thus fatten more quickly, abstaining from mating. If it eats many acorns while pregnant, it will miscarry. When it has many offspring, its milk is very scant: the worst sows, indeed, are those that tear apart their own newborn young. In warm regions, the sow's offspring is better in winter than in summer. In cold regions, however, the opposite, and this because of the harshness of these regions.

Physiologus: wild pigs at mating time are warlike, and, so as to have a hard hide, rub themselves against trees and afterward enter mud. Then they dry the mud, afterward they fight so fiercely that both, or one of them, dies. The pig mates in the morning, but what the wild pig sires after it enters that age is poor.

Aristotle: three kinds of illness befall pigs. One, indeed, called 'brancos,' is an abscess in the ear and jaw, or in any other member, though it often occurs in the feet; thus the flesh of that place decays, and the decay passes gradually until it reaches the lung, and afterward it dies: this illness increases quickly, and at once, at the start, when it is recognized, the member in which it is must be cut off; otherwise it cannot be healed. The second is heaviness and pain in the head, and from this the greater part of pigs die. The third is flux of the bowels, and this they think has no remedy. The illness of the ears occurs when the pain is great. When the pig is fat, eating blackberries helps it. A bath and warm water also help it. The vein under the tongue should also be opened. Soft-fleshed pigs get pustules on the leg and neck and shoulders, and often on the tongue and under the armpits too. And if the hairs of its head are pulled out, something like poison will come out from the roots of the hairs: chickpeas and figs are effective for it as food, and it delights in eating acorns, and these render its flesh mild and moist. But if impregnated sows eat much of the acorns, they will miscarry, as sheep do. When a pig is bitten by a scorpion, it feels little, and if after the bite it enters water, it will die quickly.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: it seems to belong also to the illnesses of the pig, as said above, that having lost one eye it dies more quickly, and that the sow, when she gives birth, grows lean.

Isaac Judaeus: pork is much nourishing. It generates good chyme, moistens the bowels because of its abundance of moisture and viscosity, provokes urine, however, and is unsuited to those keeping a light diet: yet it is of varying quality, because of the variety of the constitution of its ages. Suckling pigs are more moist than the rest and so are convertible into bad humors and putrefaction: especially, however, if they find the stomach already occupied by bad humors. But they are useful for those having a strong stomach, since they are well digested and give perfect nourishment: for those of moist nature, however, they are naturally the worst, especially if their stomach is full of bad humors. For they generate viscous phlegm, and from it gout, pain of the flank, stones in the kidneys, paralysis, and the like, according to the constitutions and natures they find. Adolescent pigs, however, are indeed better and well nourishing: for they generate praiseworthy blood. Young ones are better than the rest, especially if castrated: decrepit ones, however, are the worst. For they are cold and have hard flesh, woody and tasteless, and those accustomed to them fall into melancholy and long-lasting fevers, like quartan fever. Pork is colder and moister than other animals' flesh, especially domestic pork, since wild pork, by comparison with domestic, is hot and dry, whence it is of less nourishment. Domestic pork, then, should be taken only rarely. And only its extremities should be eaten, like the feet and buttocks, which are always in motion, but even those eating it should exercise after the meal. For those living quietly, wild pork should be avoided, and domestic much more so.

Avicenna: the flesh of the wild and domestic pig, according to what is said, is of quick digestion and descent, and strong, viscous, and thick nourishment. The Christians and their imitators say, moreover, that wild pork is better than domestic pork, since, along with being lighter than domestic flesh, it is of strong and most abundant nourishment and quick digestion, and is better than it can be in winter. The flesh of piglets, however, is of little nourishment, because of the strength of its dissolving power and the vehemence of its moisture.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: pork is harmful to eat in summer, up to the autumn equinox, since the pig sleeps more in warm weather than suits its nature. Indeed, a weak pig gapes for sleep so much that, unless roused meanwhile, it will die as if from a lethargic sleep.

Avicenna: the blood of the pig and of man are similar in every way; likewise the flesh of both, so much so that some have sold human flesh for pork, and it went undetected, until human fingers were found in it. The pig's blood, however, is of weaker power than man's blood. Pig's gall is weaker than other galls, yet it is laxative for bad chyme. In it there is a certain astringency, and it generates melancholic blood and is said to be of slow digestion because of its astringency. Pig's fat is effective for abscesses and for burns from fire. It also benefits the sting of venomous worms and calms the gnawing pain of the intestines more vehemently even than goat's fat. Pig's dung with water and wine benefits coughing blood and pain of the side. Likewise dry dung with vinegar is drunk for weakness of the arms. It is also placed, with wax-salve, on twisting of the sinews and on all hardnesses.

Dioscorides: old, salted, and hot pig's fat is more softening. When taken with wine, it is useful for pleurisy sufferers and for the womb and for burns from fire; mixed with ash or with heat, it removes swellings and leads wounds to health. Pig's gall, applied on wool and placed on the navel, loosens infants' bowels.

Haly Abbas: pig's gall benefits ulcers of the ears. Pig's fat is less hot than lion's fat, but inclines toward moisture, maturing and moistening. It benefits the bite of venomous creatures. Pig's and lamb's lung, too, burnt and powdered, benefits chafing from greaves. Wild pig's liver, eaten with vinegar, benefits the bite of reptiles. A pig's ankle-bone, if burnt and the teeth rubbed with it, strengthens them; it also especially benefits twisting and bloating of the belly: pig's urine benefits whiteness of the eyes, but its special property is that it breaks stones, and the rest.

Isidore: the sow [sus] is so named because it roots up pastures, that is, seeks food from ground it has worked. Of which Horace: it is a friend to mud. From the sow, moreover, bristles [setae] are named, whence shoemakers [sutores] too are so called, since they sew [suunt], that is stitch together, hides with bristles.
Solinus: the Scenite Arabs, who dwell in tents of goat-hair cloth, abstain entirely from pork. Indeed, if this kind of animal is found there, it dies at once.

Pliny, book 8: pigs fatten in sixty days, but more so from a three-day fast begun before the fattening. This is the most stupid of animals. Females are castrated after a two-day fast, hung by the forelegs, their womb cut out, and they fatten faster this way. They breed once a year. They think a pig dies quickly once it loses an eye. For some the lifespan is fifteen years, for others up to twenty, but they are wild; otherwise this kind is subject to diseases, especially quinsy and scrofula. A sign of a weak pig is blood at the root of a bristle pulled from the back, and a crooked head in walking. Very fat ones feel the scarcity of milk, and are less numerous in their first litter. Wallowing in mud is pleasing to this kind: its tail is twisted. It has also been noted that it more easily lies on its right side than on its twisted left.

Pliny, in the same: horses and dogs and pigs are said to seek a morning neigh or bark; and more attentive females, they report, coax after midday. Pigs, too, they say, foam at the mouth only during mating. And the boar, hearing the voice of a female in heat, if not allowed to mate, refuses food to the point of wasting away. Females become so wild from mating that they tear at a man, especially one dressed in white clothing. This rage is soothed by sprinkling their genitals with vinegar. Eagerness for mating is thought to arise from food, as arugula does for a man, onion for a herd animal. Among pregnant four-footed creatures, all avoid mating except the mare and the sow. Solid-hoofed and cloven-hoofed pigs are nourished on every kind of food and on roots.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: the boar indeed has projecting tusks, but the female rarely, and even then without use. And so, when boars strike, female pigs bite. Males, too, have more teeth than females, as in the goat and man. Pigs' teeth never fall out. The throat swells only in man and pigs, generally from a flaw in the water they drink. In most animals fat is without sensation; for this reason they report that pigs, while breathing, are gnawed by mice. Pigs have many teats over the whole belly, in a double row. Well-bred sows have twelve, common ones fewer, at two years old. The first-born, on each side of the sow, press for the first teats. And although they are all equally close for feeding, each piglet nevertheless knows its own, according to the order in which it was born, and is nourished by that one and no other. Once her nursling is taken from her, the sow becomes sterile at once and dries up. Then, from the whole litter, with one left, she alone, the provider, who had been assigned to the one born, comes down. Pigs twist their tails. In certain places in Illyria they have solid hooves.
Pliny, book 25, in the same: black hellebore kills pigs, and so they avoid it when they feed on white hellebore.

Pliny, book 29, in the same: the salamander, eaten by a pig with the same dominating over the other, is a case of the opposition of things - it is likely that its venom is neutralized first of all by that which feeds on it.
Pliny, in the same: pigs struck by serpents heal themselves by eating crabs.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: the sow, fiercer than the boar, meets the hunter with a bite, repeating its strikes most sharply, whereas, as said above, the wild boar does not repeat its strike.

Pliny, in the same place: the swine herd breeds twice a year. The time in the womb is four months; the number of fecundity up to twenty, but they cannot raise so many. Males do not breed beyond three years old. Females, worn by old age, mate lying down.

Palladius: in the month of February boars should mate with females especially; those chosen should be of vast and large body, but round rather than long, with a large belly and haunches, a short snout, thick glands of the neck, lustful, one year old, able to mate with females up to four years old. We should choose sows of long side, and those whose belly extends greatly enough to sustain the burden of gestation, otherwise similar to the boars. But in cold regions, thick and black bristles occur; in warm ones, of whatever kind they turn out. A female will suffice to bear the burden of offspring up to seven years. To conceive, she should begin at one year old. Once the fourth month is past, they give birth as the fifth begins. They begin, as I said, in the month of February, and those born should be fed on more solid plants, with straw succeeding, where it is easy to manage, and, once those subsequently born are sold, the mothers' breeding is more quickly restored. This kind can be kept in any place, but is better in marshy fields than dry ones: especially where a forest of fruit-bearing trees is available, which may help, with alternating fruit ripening through the year. They are nourished especially in grassy places and on reeds, rushes, and roots. But when food runs short, in winter they must sometimes be given fodder of acorns, chestnuts, or the cheap leftovers of other grains. In spring, new green shoots often tend to harm pigs when they are hungry. Nor should sows be shut in together in a herd, as other flocks are, but we should make pens with partitions beneath separate sections, in which the mother may be shut in with her piglets, so that she herself may better protect her nursling brood from cold. Wherefore they should be uncovered on top, so that the shepherd may freely check their number, and often come to the aid of offspring crushed by the mother by removing them. He will take care, however, to shut each mother in with her own offspring, and, as Columella says, she should not nurse more than eight. To me, however, from experience, it seems more useful that a sow with sufficient fodder should nurse at most six, since although she can raise more, she will often run dry in number.

Pliny: pig's brain and blood heal carbuncles of the genitals. Its marrow is used to rub the eyes against watering. Pig's gall too heals ear pains from faults; likewise, drunk, it soothes the spleen. With fat and flour applied, it heals chilblains. Ash of its jaws heals creeping ulcers. Ash of its hooves, too, sprinkled in a drink, checks incontinence of urine, as does its burnt and drunk bladder. Boiled lard, bound around, heals broken bones with marvelous speed. Pig's milk is most useful for dysentery sufferers and consumptives too. The same milk, drunk with honeyed wine, helps women's childbirth; by itself, drunk, it fills the failing breasts of women who have given birth. This same animal's spleen, that is aged, applied with vinegar to the breasts produces abundance. A draft of pig's medulla stimulates mating. Its roasted lung, taken that day while fasting, wards off drunkenness. In a pig's liver small stones are found, which, crushed and drunk in wine, expel stones. Pig fat was greatly praised among the ancients. It is aged in two ways, either with salt or pure; the older it is, the more useful; the Greeks call it 'axungia'; its use is for softening and warming, dispersing and cleansing burnt and rubbed limbs: it also relieves weariness and fatigue. In pig dung there are countless uses. Wherefore, not to speak of the boar, that of a female is much more effective, and one that has not borne young, and it is much more outstanding still in wild boars. Pig dung, warmed under a roof and ground with oil, is effective for swellings. Likewise its juice, applied, heals creeping ulcers. The same dung, too, fresh or aged, is applied with flour to wounds made by iron. Ash of pig dung, sprinkled in a drink of warm wine, heals dysentery sufferers: if blood flows in beasts of burden, pig dung should be poured in with wine. Pig dung is also effective for dislocations, and fresh boar's foam with vinegar; ash of pig dung, applied with water, also benefits pustules. Boar's liver and brain, drunk in wine, are effective against serpents.
Isidore: the name 'taurus' [bull] is the same as 'bos' [ox]. It is said, moreover, that drinking bull's blood is deadly to man.

Ambrose: bull's blood is indeed deadly to man, nor should it be thought that so laborious an animal ought not to have been born, or generated without blood, since its power is useful for the cultivation of fields, suited for the use of wagons, pleasant for nourishment.

Pliny: bulls have smaller and thinner horns than oxen. Bulls have a noble appearance, a fierce forehead, and bristly ears. With their horns poised for combat, yet all the threat rests on their front feet: thus, growing fierce, alternating their feet and scattering sand into the air, and, the only animal kindled by that goad, alone among animals. We have seen them, at command, whirl in combat with their horns, fall and be caught up, rise again, sometimes lie on the ground and be lifted, and even stand on a swift chariot as if charioteers on a two-horse team.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the bull is a lustful, insolent, fierce animal, attacking with its horn; it protects and fertilizes the herd.

Aristotle: the bull, like the pig, is very indiscriminately irascible at the time of anger and mating, since in its blood there are many 'hairs.' For this reason too it is bold, because of the irascibility that stirs its heat. Bull's blood, too, congeals or coagulates faster than all other bloods. For it is thick and very black. Crows fight with bulls and fly over them and peck their eyes with their beak. The bull sheds its teeth after two years, and not all at once, as the horse does. The bear sometimes throws itself upon the bull and falls onto its back. And when the bull wishes to strike it with its horns, the bear holds the horns with its hands and shoulder-blades, and then throws it to the ground. The bull eats plants and fattens on fruits that generate wind, like barley and beans, and also fattens on sweet foods, like figs and raisins, or if someone splits its hide and blows into it, then gives it food to eat, it also fattens greatly if it remains without mating. Bulls live many years, for the most part fifteen years. And if castrated, twenty. Animals having equal teeth, which do not make a saw of them, suck water, like the bull and the horse, but bulls do the opposite of horses, since they do not wish to drink water unless clear and cold. Horses, however, love muddy water. In Egypt there are certain very large animals, like bulls and sheep, since there they have good food; some bulls even have hairs over their shoulders, like camels. The bull dreams too, as the he-goat and the dog do: bulls, like he-goats, walk together before mating time, and at mating time separate and fight. The horns of wild bulls are closer to being harmful to them than beneficial. For it fights with its horns against what is weaker, but sometimes flees wolves and creatures weaker than itself.

Pliny, in the same place: bulls, if they mate on the right side, are said to produce males; if on the left, females; conception occurs in a single mounting. If it should happen to fail, the female seeks the male again after twenty days.
Pliny: [on] bulls. [The citation breaks off in the source after this heading word.]
Pliny, book 2, in the same: the herb 'laser' inflames bulls when applied to their nostrils.
Pliny: the wild fig tree, wound around the neck of fierce bulls, restrains them so much as to render them immobile.
Pliny, book 28, in the same: fresh bull's blood is a poison, and against this poison kid's rennet is helpful.
Pliny, in the same: soda too, with 'laser,' is given to those who have drunk bull's blood.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the bull is a robust animal and, among all social beasts, quite gentle, except toward those hostile to it in rapacity like others; joined together, these fight most often, and in fighting hold their tongues extended; they do nothing with their teeth, but only with their horns; they have a strong forehead for every battle, and their strongest members are the head and neck, for which reason yokes are bound on them at the head and shoulders, as with horses. And their neck, too, is of cartilaginous and strong flesh, and for this reason somewhat inflexible under due weight; they gladly drink clear water, and when they graze on plants, they do not harm the roots, but take only what appears on the surface. Those that are castrated, kept from lust, are better and suited to every task and especially fit for the yoke. Bulls' horns, if heated, can be bent at will. The bull alone among animals is kindled by a goad. The older it is, the more tender its flesh, if it has been fattened: the ox has stronger and harder heart-sinews than other animals, but the bull has stronger ones still. If a bull remains many years without mating, it fattens greatly, and when excess comes upon it, it will suddenly die.
Aristotle: in Amphirus they guard bulls for nine years to prevent mating, and they do this only if they grow at the start of a flash of lightning.
Physiologus: the bull, fearing thunder, at the start of a flash of lightning stays grazing in the meadow, but the cow flees. A wild bull, tied to a fig tree, grows tame, and so on.
Isidore: the Indian bull is of tawny color, of swift speed, with hairs turned backward. When it wishes to turn its head, the hardness of its hide rejects all blows, untamed in its ferocity.
Hrabanus Maurus: the Indian bull, untamed in ferocity, has a large head and a gaping mouth opening from ear to ear.
Solinus: Indian bulls turn their horns with the flexibility they wish, and are of such untamed ferocity that, once caught, they all throw themselves about in a frenzy.

Pliny: and so on. Among the Indians there are most savage wild bulls, larger than the wild kind, with sky-blue eyes and hair turned backward, their mouth gaping to the ears. They hunt all wild beasts, and, caught only by pits, always die of their own ferocity.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: Indian bulls have a large head and thick, bristling hairs. Their horns are useful for their flexibility, by which they turn them as they wish, either for pleasure or for battle, and lower or extend them: they have another benefit too, namely the casting of dung to a great distance, whose heat and stench slows dogs and hunters. There are also, in the East, oxen having only one horn. Others, however, having three; these do not have cloven hooves, but solid ones, in the manner of horses.

Aristotle: the bull grazes alone, unless the time of mating approaches; for then it grazes with the cows and fights against all other males. Bulls fight, indeed, over a cow, and the victor mounts the female, but the cow flees the mating, because of the hardness of the male's member.
Pliny: bulls complete their generative development at four years old. They give birth, however, in the tenth month. Whatever is bred before that is of no use.

Palladius: and so, in the month of March, whoever wishes to build up a herd should submit young bulls by these signs: that they be tall and of huge limbs, of middle age. And rather one that is younger in youth than one declining into old age, with a fierce face, small horns, a muscular and vast neck, a drawn-in belly; we shall also then prepare cows especially, but we shall choose ones of the tallest form, of long body, a capacious and large womb, a high forehead, black and large eyes, beautiful and especially black horns, hairy ears, very large dewlaps and tails, short claws and black and small legs, especially of three years of age, since up to ten years their breeding produces more useful offspring, nor should bulls be admitted to them before three years of age. But it will be the diligent farmer's care, once the older ones are removed, to bring in young ones in succession, and to assign the sterile ones to the plough and to labor. The Greeks assert that if you wish to produce males, the bull's left testicle should be tied at mating; if females, the right. Bulls, however, should be kept abstinent for a long time, so that, when the time comes, they bear down more keenly on the object of their delayed ardor. But for these herds we should prepare maritime and sunny places in winter, shaded and cold ones in summer, mountainous ones especially, since they are better satisfied with shrubs and the grass growing among them, since, although they graze rightly around rivers because of the pleasant places, their breeding is nevertheless helped by warmer waters, whence they graze better and more usefully where rainwater forms warm pools. This kind of herd, however, tolerates cold and can easily winter under the open sky. For them, however, more spacious enclosures should be made, because of the injury to pregnant ones. Stables, however, are useful when strewn with stone or gravel or sand, sloped somewhat so that moisture can drain away, facing the southern side, because of icy blasts, against which some barrier must stand.

Palladius, book 8, the same: in the month of July especially, bulls should be submitted to cows, since a ten-month gestation can thus be concluded by ripe spring, and it is certain that they, growing eager for the wantonness of mating after the fatness of spring, love it. Columella asserts that one bull can suffice for fifteen cows. And care must be taken that they cannot conceive from excess of fatness. If there is abundance of fodder in the region where we graze, a cow can be submitted for breeding every year. But if this kind is needed for other work, they should be burdened in alternate seasons, especially if they are accustomed to serve some other task.

Aesculapius: bull's horn drives off serpents, and its blood kills them, and also removes blemishes of the face. Its gall with honey and balsam cures ailments of the eyes. Its tallow with resin and wax softens all hardnesses. Its marrow, tempered with wine, cures those with tremors. Its dung dissolves swellings and hardnesses.

Pliny, book 28: warmed with Egyptian alum, bull's gall is applied to baldness. For ulcers of the head, too, eye-salves are made from the same gall with egg white, dissolved in water, applied for four days; the same, with soda added, removes leprosy and dandruff and hangnails of the fingers; the same, dried, dissolved in warm water, removes them. Rinsing the teeth with the same gall benefits them. Bull's gall heals ulcers. The same, too, with leek juice, is applied to fistulas. It also heals fresh wounds made by iron, applied as melted bull's glue, dissolved on the third day. Likewise bull's glue, dissolved in warm water, calms inflammations, and bull's gall, applied on unwashed wool, also aids women's purgations. Dried bull's blood, ground, represses parotid swellings, heals ailments of the rear. Bull's gall in shredded linen cloths leads cracks to scarring. Its tallow and dried, ground bull's blood heal inflammations in that part. Bear fat and bull's tallow are also effective for gout; bull dung's liquid helps dropsy sufferers. And they say cheeks redden with the same dung. Bull's urine effectively heals oozing ulcers of the head.

Avicenna, in the second canon: bull's gall benefits fresh ulcers in the ear, and ulcers of the anus too. A liniment is made from it for pain of the womb and testicles, and it is applied to bony abscesses. Bull's urine, dissolved with soda and finely dripped into the ear, is a theriac for venomous bites, and calms its pain, and, washed with it, benefits dandruff. Bull dung quickly drives off venomous worms and bedbugs, when fumigation is made with it. From the same, too, fumigation is made for prolapse of the womb. Warm bull's blood is applied to hard abscesses.

Avicenna, book 3, the same: fresh bull's blood is a poison, and to one who drinks it there follow difficulty of breathing and pain of the throat and gullet, and redness of the tongue, and clots of coagulated blood in the teeth and gums, and vehement nausea and distress; then erosion appears on the tongue, then it leads to suffocation and spasm; one must hasten, then, to an enema and loosening of the bowels, for vomiting is dangerous: since sometimes it is expelled, whose expulsion is sometimes not tolerated, and so suffocates. Medicines that benefit the coagulation of blood should be given, like unripe figs, full and raw, cabbage seed, and the rest.

Dioscorides: bull's gall, mixed with he-goat's gall, cures quinsy, heals wounds and scars; mixed with milk, it soothes ear pains, and even more when mixed with woman's milk. Bull's blood is diaphoretic and softening, dissolves hardnesses, and, applied as a poultice, is effective.
Isidore: the cow [vacca] is named as if 'boacca.' For it is of the class of movable nouns, like lion/lioness, dragon/she-dragon.

Aristotle, in the book On Animals: the cow is a gentle animal, of little irascibility, but of much lack of understanding. Its kidneys, in appearance, seem composed of several small kidneys; it has many stomachs, so that the use of food is completed, and what diminishes from it because of digestion has one stomach after another. The first stomach, then, receives raw food, the second digested food, the third food already improved by digestion. The fourth, however, well digested. The cow's horns, if heated, bend in any direction. Females' horns are stronger than males' horns. Cows' desire for mating is shown by swelling of the groin and their continuous lowing; two illnesses befall cows in herds. Gout, namely, since their feet are constricted, but they do not die from this, and if their horns are anointed, they will indeed be healed. The other, however, is 'crocator,' which, when it occurs, quickly returns their breath, and this is likened to fevers in men; the sign of this illness is when they lower their ears and do not eat, and quickly die from it. When cows fatten, however, they are more sluggish, and graze toward the rear. The cow has a bone in its heart, like the horse, because of the heart's size. And four teats, like the female camel. Its voice, and especially the young cow's, is deeper than the male ox's, whereas in other animals it is the opposite: for drinking it loves clear water, the horse muddy water. Bulls fight over a cow, and the victor mounts her. But when he is weakened by frequent mating, the defeated one fights against him again, and whoever wins mounts the female. She herself, by fleeing, does not endure the mating, as said above, and at mating time cannot be tamed. Cows also have a leader, and live longer because of good pasture. If a cow is separated from the herd, it is lost, since it is eaten by wild beasts. The wild cow has horns curving toward each other, and for this reason nature gave it another benefit, namely the casting of dung to a distance, so that the hunter is held off by it. In the region of Greece around the Phasis, wild cows abound. They are black, very strong, having feet cloven into two hooves, long hair, and drooping faces. Cow's milk, among other things, is very thick; it has more milk, moreover, like the sheep, than the offspring needs. And so it is fitting for cheese to be made from it. In the region called Ephesus in Greek there are small cows, from which milk is drawn in abundance. There are, moreover, certain bloating foods that multiply milk, like beans, which suit cows and goats. At mating, the cow follows the bull and mounts him.
