And the bull's own mounting of her is heavy, so that she must bend. The time fitting for mating and birth is after two years. And the cow's time of pregnancy is nine months, and birth occurs in the tenth. And when cows breed often, they think it signifies much rain to come in winter. The cow lives, for the most part, fifteen years. Cows and female donkeys menstruate and discharge much, because of the size of their bodies.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: Pliny denies that pregnant cows carry except in the right side of the womb, and when they bear twins, menstruation appears both in cows and mares, especially in warm regions, where humors and surpluses abound more in animals. But the menstrual matter is sometimes expelled through the bladder in the urine. Cow's urine is very sharp. A cow grazing in a meadow at thunder time flees from the face of the lightning, the bull remaining and not afraid.
Rhazes: beef is thick and nourishes much, generates foul and thick blood, and is unsuited except to those who take much exercise: those subject to melancholic illnesses should abstain from it.

Avicenna, in the second canon: beef is of very abundant nourishment, thick, melancholic, generating melancholic illnesses. Better than it is the flesh of calves. Beef generates vitiligo, cancer, scabies, bad impetigo, leprosy, elephantiasis, and varicose veins, and quartan fevers. Likewise beef and other such flesh cause mental derangement through dryness, and thicken the spleen. Sour broth of beef is good for choleric looseness, for it checks it. Melon rinds dissolve beef, namely when it is cooked with them. The better season to eat it, however, is spring and the beginning of summer.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: beef is dry and generates turbid and thick blood, yet nourishes much, but is digested slowly, unless taken with wine and garlic. Cow's milk is very thick and does not easily freeze from cold, but its wateriness separates from it, and the thick residue is formed. By fire, however, it thickens. In the region of Ambedor cows are of such large body that the milker must stand on his feet; these provide an abundance of milk beyond measure, and dogs too in that region are large, and all animals except donkeys.
Avicenna: cow's milk has the most butter, and is thicker and richer than sheep's.

Isaac Judaeus: cow's [milk] is less watery than others and sharp, and more nourishing. It suits the stomach, strengthens the members, cools the heat of the liver and stomach. It is also good for other things, once its buttery quality is removed. For, given to drink, it eases the gnawing pain of hot humors, strengthens and tempers natural heat, increases flesh, removes choleric diarrhea and choleric tenesmus, and aids ulcers of the intestines and bladder and womb. It should be given thus, and it will be best when as much cold water as there is milk is added, and it is cooked so long until all the water is gone. And the more often you do this, the better it will be for these purposes.

Avicenna, in the second canon: cow's gall is stronger than the other galls of four-footed animals. It is put in plasters for wounds that are erysipelas and of vehement pain. Cow's shins, that is the burnt bones of the legs, check bleeding and looseness of the bowels. Cow dung is among those things given for the lung and consumption and the like. From it a plaster is made for sciatica. Likewise, applied with vinegar over hot boils, it calms them. It also suits abscesses that are behind the ears. Necks of cowhide, applied with vinegar, benefit impetigo and scabies that can be scraped off when not of vehement depth. Likewise applied with honey and vinegar over wounds, and burnt and washed, they are effective for curing nits.
Belbetus: cow's blood, if poured over a wound, checks bleeding.
Aristotle: cow's horns, if heated, bend in every direction, as said, and if anointed with oil and pitch, are effective against foot pain and against harm from snow.
Pliny: cow's liver, too, heals celiacs and dysentery sufferers.
Isidore: the wether [vervex, castrated ram] is male, or named because it has worms in its head, which, roused by an itch, cause them to butt one another, and, fighting, strike with great force.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the wether, or ram, has horns curled in the manner of a circle, with which it strives to defend the flock. From natural fierceness it strikes the ground with its right foot, when it is angry or stunned or afraid, and this especially at mating time: for half the year it lies on one side, and for half on the other. Its flesh is hotter and less moist than that of ewes, and harder to digest. The lamb, naturally abhorring the wolf, though it has never seen one, flees at once, whereas it would neither flee nor fear a horse or another animal it saw. Its flesh does not easily submit to excretion, yet descends easily from the stomach, but is dissolved from the members with great difficulty. For it generates a viscous humor. A yearling lamb, however, is more praiseworthy because of the temperateness of moisture and dryness. Everything in the sheep is useful, namely wool, hide, flesh, milk.

Dioscorides: wether-fat has a power similar to pig's. It usefully cures hysterical or anal ailments, and helps burns. Wether's gall, applied on wool and placed on the navel, loosens infants' bowels. Wether dung, applied as a poultice with vinegar, corrects black blemishes: it removes growing corns from the body. Applied, it cures erysipelas. Mixed with wax and oil, it heals burns.

Isidore: the calf [vitulus] and heifer [vitula] are named from greenness [viriditas], that is from a green age, like 'virgo' [maiden]. The heifer, then, is young and has not yet calved. For one that has calved is a young cow [iuvenca] or a cow. The young bull [iuvencus], however, is so named because it begins to help [iuvare] the uses of men in cultivating the land, or because among the Jews only a young bull, never a full-grown bull, was ever sacrificed to God. For age, too, is considered in sacrificial victims.

Palladius, book 5, on calves: calves are usually born in the month of April; their mothers should be aided by abundance of fodder, so that they can suffice for the burden of labor and milk. To the calves themselves, however, roasted and ground millet mixed with milk should be given, in the manner of spelt-porridge.

Aristotle: they say the gestation of calves is ten months, and if born before this time, it will not live, since its hooves will not be complete. If a calf is castrated, it can live twenty years and more, if only its body happens to be so. The calf alone, among every kind of animal, has a deeper voice than that of older oxen. For all other creatures have a sharper voice in youth, thicker in old age. When male calves reach a certain age, they go alone and graze without females until the time of mating. But when the time of mating approaches, they no longer graze alone, but with the cows. They begin to mate after two years, but then their offspring are few, weak, and small.

Pliny: to this alone, among all animals whose tail is rather long, is it not, as with the rest, of full measure as soon as born, for it grows until it reaches the ground. Wherefore the testing of sacrificial victims rests on the calf's tail, that it should reach the joints of the hocks.

Palladius: calves, however, as the Carthaginian [Mago] says, should be castrated in May, at a tender age, so that, with a split rod, the testicles are compressed, and, gradually crushed, are dissolved. But he prescribes this be done as the moon wanes, in spring or autumn. Others, with the calf tied to a frame, grasp with two narrow tin rods, as if with forceps, those very sinews, which the Greeks call 'cremasters.' Having gripped these, they cut the stretched testicles with iron and cut them out with force, so that something of the heads of these sinews is left clinging. This procedure both prevents excessive bleeding and does not entirely unman the young bulls by removing their manly vigor. Nor should it be overlooked, as many do, that they force them to mate immediately after castration. For it is certain, indeed, that offspring is generated by them, but that they themselves perish from the flow of blood; the wounds of castrated animals, however, should be smeared with ash of vine-cuttings and silver dross. The castrated animal should be kept from drink and fed sparse food. And for the following three days it should be given tender treetops and soft shrubs and green herbs, sweeter foliage, fattening or riverine. With liquid pitch too, mixed with ash and a little oil, the wounds should be carefully anointed after three days. But a better kind of castration, subsequent practice has found. For, the young bull tied and thrown down, the testicles are enclosed in tightened skin, and there, with a wooden rod pressing, they are cut off with heated axes or hatchets. Or, what is better, with an iron tool shaped for this purpose, so that it holds the likeness of a sword. For thus the edge of the falling iron is pressed around the rod itself with each blow, and so it removes the delay of pain by the benefit of speed, and, the veins and skins burnt and constricted against bleeding, the scar, formed in a way together with the wound itself, protects the wound.
Aristotle: calves should be castrated after one year. Otherwise they will be small. Castrated ones, however, live longer.
Pliny, book 18: further, young bulls should be castrated as the moon wanes.

Pliny: they apply calf's flesh to a human bite and do not remove it before the fifth day. All marrows, indeed, soften, fill out, dry, and warm. Among the rest, however, calf's marrow is praiseworthy. Calf's tallow too, ground with salt, is praised as most useful for ulcers of the head. But also for ulcers and cracks of the mouth, calf's or ox's tallow with donkey's fat or basil juice heals. Besides, swelling of the testicles is checked by calf's tallow, with soda added, or even with the same animal's dung boiled with vinegar. For bloating that occurs in the area of the rear, too, calf's tallow with rue is effective. Likewise, against poisons that kill through ulceration, calf's tallow helps, and against aconite and hemlock. Warmed calf's gall thins dark scars. Calf's gall too effectively heals oozing ulcers of the head. With this, warmed with vinegar, nits too are removed. Calf's spleen, boiled and ground with honey in wine and applied, heals oozing ulcers. Calf's dung too, boiled in wine, benefits ailments of the intestines. Fumigating those stung by a scorpion with the same dung is useful for them. The dung of a calf that has not yet tasted grass benefits gout sufferers. And dropsy sufferers are helped by applying the dung of a male calf. Fresh calf's dung is also applied to erysipelas. Ash of the same dung, applied with vinegar, checks bleeding. Ash of the same dung, too, boiled with lily bulbs with a little honey added, calms the pains of varicose veins, and all inflammations and suppurations threatening to develop. It also benefits gout and joint diseases, especially from male calves.
